Spin and SpinKubeFermyon (now Akamai); CNCF sandbox · Platform · Emerging · Intermediate Developer framework for Wasm microservices and its Kubernetes operator and shim for running them on clusters. spin new, spin build, spin up gives a working HTTP Wasm app; SpinKube deploys it to AKS. wasmCloudCNCF project (Cosmonic and community) · Platform · Emerging · Advanced Distributed platform for running Wasm components across clouds and edges, linked by capability providers. A retailer runs the same pricing component in its cloud and in 300 store servers through wasmCloud.

docs.title: Glossary of Terms
A
docs.text: Access control list (ACL) A list attached to a file or object granting specific permissions to named users or groups, beyond the basic owner/group/others model. API server The Kubernetes control-plane component that exposes the cluster's REST API, validates requests and is the only component that talks to etcd. ASLR Address Space Layout Randomization — placing code, stack and heap at random addresses so memory-corruption exploits cannot predict where things are.

docs.title: B
docs.text: Bootloader Small program started by firmware that loads the kernel (and initramfs) into memory and starts it, for example GRUB or systemd-boot.

docs.title: C
docs.text: cgroups Control groups — a Linux kernel feature that limits and accounts for the CPU, memory, I/O and process count used by groups of processes. CIS Benchmark A free consensus configuration guide from the Center for Internet Security describing how to harden a specific OS, cloud or application. cloud-init The standard first-boot tool for cloud and VM images that applies user data: users, SSH keys, packages, files and commands. Container A set of processes isolated with namespaces, limited with cgroups and started from an image, sharing the host's kernel. Container runtime Software that creates and runs containers — high-level runtimes such as containerd and CRI-O manage images, low-level ones such as runc start processes. Context switch The kernel saving one thread's CPU state and restoring another's so they can share a CPU core. Copy-on-write (COW) Sharing memory pages or data blocks until someone writes, then copying only the changed part — used by fork(), snapshots and some file systems. CRI / CNI / CSI Kubernetes plug-in interfaces for container runtimes (CRI), pod networking (CNI) and storage drivers (CSI).

docs.title: D
docs.text: Deadlock A state where two or more threads each wait for a resource held by another, so none can ever proceed. Deployment A Kubernetes object that keeps a set number of identical Pod replicas running and rolls out updates gradually. Device driver Kernel code that lets the operating system control a particular piece of hardware through a standard interface. DMA Direct Memory Access — hardware moving data between a device and memory without the CPU copying each byte.

docs.title: E
docs.text: eBPF A Linux technology for running small verified programs inside the kernel, used for tracing, networking and security tools. EEVDF Earliest Eligible Virtual Deadline First — the Linux kernel's default CPU scheduler since version 6.6, replacing CFS. Error budget The amount of unreliability an SLO allows (100% minus the target), spent on releases and experiments. etcd The consistent, distributed key-value store that holds all Kubernetes cluster state.

docs.title: F
docs.text: File descriptor A small integer a process uses to refer to an open file, pipe or socket, such as 0, 1 and 2 for standard input, output and error.

docs.title: H
docs.text: Hypervisor Software that creates and runs virtual machines; Type 1 runs directly on hardware, Type 2 runs on top of a host OS.

docs.title: I
docs.text: Idempotency The property that running an operation repeatedly gives the same result, essential for safe automation. Infrastructure as code (IaC) Defining servers, networks and settings in version-controlled files that tools apply automatically, such as Terraform, OpenTofu or Ansible. Init system The first user-space process (PID 1) that starts and supervises services; systemd on most Linux distributions, launchd on macOS. Inode A file-system record holding a file's metadata and data locations — everything except its name. Interrupt A signal from hardware (or software) that makes the CPU pause its current work and run a handler in the kernel. IOMMU A memory-management unit for devices that restricts which memory each device can reach by DMA, used for security and device passthrough to VMs. io_uring A Linux asynchronous I/O interface using shared ring buffers between applications and the kernel to cut system-call overhead.

docs.title: K
docs.text: Kernel The core of the operating system that runs in privileged mode and manages CPU, memory, devices and security. Kernel module Code, often a driver, that can be loaded into or removed from a running Linux kernel without rebooting. kubelet The agent on every Kubernetes node that starts Pods through the container runtime and reports their status. KVM Kernel-based Virtual Machine — the Linux kernel's built-in hypervisor, normally paired with QEMU.

docs.title: L
docs.text: Least privilege Giving every user, process and service only the permissions it needs, for only as long as it needs them. Live migration Moving a running virtual machine from one host to another with little or no interruption. Live patching Applying critical kernel fixes to a running system in memory without an immediate reboot, for example kpatch or Canonical Livepatch.

docs.title: M
docs.text: Microkernel An OS design that keeps only minimal services in the kernel and runs drivers and file systems as user-space servers. Monolithic kernel An OS design in which the scheduler, memory manager, file systems and drivers all run together in kernel space, as in Linux. Mutex A lock that lets only one thread at a time enter a critical section of code.

docs.title: N
docs.text: Namespace (Linux) A kernel feature giving a process its own private view of a resource, such as process IDs, network interfaces, mounts or users.

docs.title: O
docs.text: OCI Open Container Initiative — the Linux Foundation project publishing the image, runtime and distribution specifications for containers. OOM killer The Linux kernel mechanism that ends processes when memory runs out, either system-wide or inside a cgroup limit. Operator A Kubernetes controller plus custom resources that encode the operational knowledge for running a specific application. Overlay file system A union file system that stacks read-only image layers under a writable layer — the basis of container images.

docs.title: P
docs.text: Page cache RAM the kernel uses to cache file data so repeated reads and writes avoid slow storage. Page fault A CPU exception raised when a program touches a virtual page that is not currently mapped, which the kernel then resolves or rejects. Paging Dividing memory into fixed-size pages (commonly 4 KiB) mapped through page tables from virtual to physical addresses. Paravirtualization Virtualization where the guest knows it is virtualized and uses efficient interfaces such as virtio instead of emulated hardware. Pod The smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes: one or more containers sharing a network namespace and storage volumes. POSIX The IEEE family of standards defining a common Unix-like system interface, shell and utilities. Process A running program with its own address space, open files, credentials and one or more threads. Process control block (PCB) The kernel data structure holding a process's state, registers, memory map, open files and scheduling information.

docs.title: R
docs.text: RBAC Role-Based Access Control — granting permissions to roles and binding users or service accounts to them, as in Kubernetes. Real-time OS (RTOS) An operating system that guarantees tasks respond within strict, predictable time limits, such as FreeRTOS or Zephyr. Reconciliation loop A controller's continual cycle of comparing desired state with actual state and acting to close the gap.

docs.title: S
docs.text: Scheduler The component that decides what runs next — which thread gets a CPU in an OS, or which node gets a Pod in Kubernetes. SELinux Security-Enhanced Linux — a mandatory access-control system that confines processes using labels and policy. Semaphore A synchronisation counter that limits how many threads can use a resource at once. Service (Kubernetes) A stable virtual IP and DNS name that load-balances traffic across the ready Pods matching a label selector. Shell A command-line interpreter such as bash, zsh or PowerShell that runs commands and scripts for the user. SLI / SLO / SLA Service level indicator (a measurement), objective (an internal target) and agreement (a contract with penalties). Swap Disk space (or compressed RAM, as with zram) used to hold memory pages that do not fit in physical RAM. System call The controlled entry point through which a program asks the kernel to do privileged work, such as read(), fork() or mmap(). systemd The init system and service manager used by most Linux distributions, with units, targets, timers and the journal.

docs.title: T
docs.text: Thread An independent flow of execution within a process, sharing its memory but with its own stack and registers. TLB Translation Lookaside Buffer — a CPU cache of recent virtual-to-physical address translations.

docs.title: U
docs.text: User space The unprivileged CPU mode and memory region where applications run, separated from kernel space.

docs.title: V
docs.text: VFS Virtual File System — the kernel layer giving one common interface (open, read, write) over many different file systems. Virtual memory Giving each process its own private address space, mapped by hardware and the kernel onto RAM and disk.

docs.title: Z
docs.text: Zombie process A process that has exited but whose parent has not yet collected its exit status with wait().

docs.title: How to read this guide
docs.text: Each topic follows the same simple pattern, so you can jump to any page and understand it without reading the rest first.

docs.title: How each topic is built
docs.text:
In plain English A jargon-free explanation of what the topic is. Think of it like… An everyday analogy that makes the idea click. Real-world example A short realistic story or worked example showing it in action. How it works The key steps, in order. Who uses it The people, jobs and industries that rely on it. Key takeaway The single most important thing to remember.

Many topics include a Try it box with a safe command or snippet. Then a table lists the most important entries — with what each one does and a concrete example.

docs.title: Entry type labels
docs.text:
Concept, Kernel, Operating System, Component, System Call, API, Standard, File System, Software, Tool, Command, Runtime, Platform, Service, Object, Specification, Language, Attack, Organisation, Certification, Career, Resource

Concept = an idea to understand. Kernel / Operating system / Component = the OS itself and its parts. System call / API / Standard / Specification = programming interfaces and official specs. File system / Runtime / Platform / Service / Object (a Kubernetes resource) = building blocks you run or configure. Software / Tool / Command / Language = things you install, run or write. Attack = a known weakness. Organisation / Certification / Career / Resource = bodies, credentials, jobs and learning material.

docs.title: Status labels
docs.text:
Current, Legacy, Emerging

Current = widely used today. Legacy = still found and worth knowing, but being replaced or mainly historical. Emerging = new, announced or just being adopted.

docs.title: Level labels
docs.text:
Beginner, Intermediate, Advanced

Beginner = learn this first. Intermediate = needed for coursework and most jobs. Advanced = specialist depth.

docs.title: About this guide
docs.text: This guide is for students and self-learners. Product names, versions, standards and dates were checked for accuracy as of late 2026, but operating systems, virtualization, containers and Kubernetes changes quickly — confirm details with official documentation and standards bodies. Product names and trademarks belong to their owners.

docs.title: Chapter 8: Kubernetes in Depth
docs.text: Kubernetes is the operating system of the data centre: it schedules containers across many machines and keeps them running the way you declared. This chapter opens it up piece by piece — architecture and the reconciliation loop, Pods and workload controllers, Services and the Gateway API, CNI networking and policies, storage and configuration, scheduling and autoscaling, security, operators, Helm and GitOps, observability and service mesh, AI and GPU workloads, and the distributions and release cycle as of October 2026 — with real YAML and kubectl commands you can try on a laptop cluster.

docs.title: 8.1 Why Orchestration and the Declarative Model
docs.text:
Running one container is easy; running hundreds across dozens of machines, restarting them when they crash and updating them without downtime is not. Kubernetes is an orchestrator: you write down the state you want (for example 'three copies of my web app, version 2.4'), and it works continuously to make the real cluster match that description.

The reconciliation loop. Every controller runs this loop forever; it reacts to the current difference, not to a list of past events.

Think of it like…

Kubernetes is like a thermostat rather than a light switch: you do not turn the heater on and off yourself, you set 21 °C and the thermostat keeps correcting the room until it matches.

Real-world example

Lumen Bikes, a fictional bike-rental start-up, ran 40 containers on six VMs with shell scripts and 3 a.m. pager alerts. After moving to Kubernetes, their Deployment simply says replicas: 3. When a VM dies, Kubernetes notices the missing Pods and recreates them on healthy nodes, usually within about five minutes and without anyone waking up.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. You describe desired state in a YAML manifest: an object with apiVersion, kind, metadata and spec.
  2. kubectl apply sends the object to the API server, which validates it and stores it in etcd.
  3. Controllers watch for objects they own, compare desired state (spec) with actual state (status) and act on any difference.
  4. The scheduler picks nodes for new Pods and each node's kubelet starts the containers.
  5. The loop never ends: crashes, deleted Pods or failed nodes all create a difference that controllers repair.

Who uses it

Platform engineers, DevOps engineers, SREs, backend developers and cloud architects use Kubernetes daily; it is the default way to run containers at most mid-size and large organisations.

Key takeaway

Interview line to memorise: Kubernetes is a declarative, API-driven system of independent control loops that continuously reconcile actual state towards desired state.

Going deeper

  • Kubernetes grew out of Google's internal Borg and Omega cluster managers; Google announced it in June 2014, released 1.0 on 21 July 2015 and donated it to the new Cloud Native Computing Foundation.
  • Controllers are level-triggered, not edge-triggered: they compare whole states rather than replaying events, so a missed notification or a controller restart cannot leave the cluster permanently wrong.
  • Every object carries metadata.resourceVersion; updates use optimistic concurrency, so if two clients edit the same object, the second write fails with a 409 Conflict instead of silently overwriting.
  • metadata.generation increases when spec changes and status.observedGeneration shows which generation a controller has processed; Pods gained both fields as a stable feature in v1.35.
  • Server-side apply (kubectl apply --server-side) records which field manager owns each field, so a human, a GitOps tool and an autoscaler can share one object without overwriting each other's fields.
  • Owner references link children to parents (Pod to ReplicaSet to Deployment); the garbage collector deletes orphaned children, and finalizers can block deletion until cleanup work is done.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Mixing kubectl edit on live objects with Git-managed YAML: the next apply or GitOps sync silently undoes manual changes. Change the source file instead.
  • Thinking Kubernetes replaces your container runtime or cloud: it orchestrates them, and still needs nodes, a runtime, networking and storage plugins underneath.
  • Adopting Kubernetes for one small app: for a handful of containers a PaaS or a single VM with Compose is often cheaper and simpler.

docs.title: Try it: Spin up a throwaway local cluster with kind and watch self-healing
docs.text:
kind create cluster --name lab          # needs Docker or Podman
kubectl create deployment hello --image=nginx:1.27 --replicas=3
kubectl get pods -l app=hello -w &       # watch in the background
kubectl delete pod -l app=hello --wait=false   # delete all three...
# ...and watch three new Pods appear almost instantly
kubectl get deployment hello -o yaml | less    # compare spec with status
kind delete cluster --name lab

docs.title: Key kernels, commands, tools, standards & concepts
docs.text: Name What it does Example Kubernetes (K8s)CNCF; originally Google (2014) · Platform · Current · Beginner Open-source container orchestrator that schedules, scales, heals and updates containerised workloads across a cluster of machines. A retailer runs 600 microservice Pods on 40 nodes; Kubernetes spreads them, restarts crashes and rolls out new versions several times a day. Borg and OmegaGoogle (internal) · Software · Legacy · Intermediate Google's internal cluster managers whose lessons (Pods, labels, controllers, a central state store) shaped Kubernetes' design. The 2015 'Large-scale cluster management at Google with Borg' paper explains why Kubernetes groups containers into Pods with a shared IP. Desired state vs actual stateKubernetes API conventions · Concept · Current · Beginner spec holds what you want; status holds what controllers observed. Kubernetes works to close any gap between them. A Deployment's spec.replicas is 5 but status.readyReplicas is 3, so the ReplicaSet controller creates two more Pods. Control loop (controller)Kubernetes architecture · Concept · Current · Beginner A program that watches objects of one kind and repeatedly acts to move real state towards desired state. The Job controller sees a failed Pod in a Job with backoffLimit: 6 and creates a replacement after a back-off delay. Manifest (YAML object)Kubernetes API · Concept · Current · Beginner A YAML or JSON file describing an object with four top-level parts: apiVersion, kind, metadata and spec. deploy.yaml with apiVersion: apps/v1, kind: Deployment, metadata.name: web and a spec with three replicas is applied with kubectl apply -f deploy.yaml. kubectlKubernetes SIG CLI · Tool · Current · Beginner The official command-line client: it turns your commands and YAML into REST calls to the API server. kubectl get pods -A, kubectl describe pod web-7d9f, kubectl logs -f web-7d9f and kubectl explain deployment.spec are daily commands. Imperative vs declarative managementKubernetes object management docs · Concept · Current · Beginner Imperative commands say 'do this now' (kubectl create, scale); declarative files say 'this should exist' and are re-applied safely. Ana tests with kubectl scale deploy web --replicas=5, then records replicas: 5 in Git so the change survives the next apply. Server-side applyKubernetes SIG API Machinery (GA v1.22) · Command · Current · Intermediate kubectl apply mode where the API server merges changes and tracks which manager owns each field, reporting conflicts. kubectl apply --server-side -f app.yaml warns of a conflict because the HPA owns spec.replicas, avoiding an accidental scale-down. NamespaceKubernetes core/v1 · Object · Current · Beginner A named partition inside one cluster that scopes object names, RBAC rules, quotas and policies. Teams 'payments' and 'search' each get a namespace, so both can own a Service called api without clashing. Labels and selectorsKubernetes API · Concept · Current · Beginner Key-value tags on objects plus queries over them; they are how Services, Deployments and policies find the Pods they manage. A Service with selector app: web, tier: frontend sends traffic only to Pods carrying both labels. AnnotationsKubernetes API · Concept · Current · Beginner Non-identifying key-value metadata for tools and humans; unlike labels they cannot be used in selectors. kubectl annotate deploy web team-contact=ops@lumen.example records an owner for whoever is on call. API groups and versionsKubernetes API conventions · Concept · Current · Intermediate Resources live in groups (core, apps, batch, networking.k8s.io) with versions that mature from v1alpha1 to v1beta1 to v1. kubectl api-resources lists deployments under apps/v1 and cronjobs under batch/v1. Garbage collection and owner referencesKubernetes SIG API Machinery · Concept · Current · Intermediate Child objects record their owner; when the owner is deleted, the garbage collector removes children in cascade. Deleting Deployment web removes its ReplicaSets and Pods; kubectl delete --cascade=orphan would leave the Pods running. kind (Kubernetes in Docker)Kubernetes SIG Testing · Tool · Current · Beginner Runs each Kubernetes node as a container, giving a disposable multi-node cluster on a laptop in about a minute. A student runs kind create cluster --config three-nodes.yaml to practise node draining before a CKA exam attempt. minikubeKubernetes SIG Cluster Lifecycle · Tool · Current · Beginner Local single- or multi-node cluster on a VM, container or bare metal, with handy add-ons like ingress and a dashboard. minikube start --driver=docker then minikube addons enable metrics-server gives a laptop cluster with kubectl top working.

docs.title: 8.2 Cluster Architecture: Control Plane and Nodes
docs.text:
A Kubernetes cluster has two halves. The control plane is the brain: an API server, a database called etcd, a scheduler and controller managers. Worker nodes are the muscle: each runs a kubelet agent, a container runtime and a network proxy, and that is where your application containers actually run.

Who talks to whom. Every arrow goes through the API server; etcd is never accessed directly by nodes or controllers.

Think of it like…

The control plane is an airport control tower with its flight log (etcd); each node is a gate whose ground crew (the kubelet) follows the tower's instructions and reports back what is really happening at the gate.

Real-world example

Rivera Logistics runs a production cluster with three control-plane VMs spread over three availability zones and 25 worker nodes. One zone has a power cut: etcd keeps quorum with two of three members, the API server stays reachable through a load balancer, and Pods from the lost zone's workers are recreated on the surviving nodes.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Every client — kubectl, controllers, kubelets — talks only to kube-apiserver over HTTPS; nothing else reads or writes etcd.
  2. The API server authenticates and authorises each request, runs admission checks and persists the object in etcd.
  3. kube-scheduler watches for Pods with no node and binds each one to the best node.
  4. kube-controller-manager and cloud-controller-manager run dozens of control loops (ReplicaSets, nodes, endpoints, load balancers).
  5. On the chosen node the kubelet sees the Pod, asks the container runtime via CRI to start it, and reports status back.
  6. kube-proxy (or an eBPF replacement) programs the node so that Service IPs reach healthy Pods.

Who uses it

Cluster administrators and platform teams operate these components (or pay a cloud to); every Kubernetes engineer must know them for troubleshooting and for the CKA exam.

Key takeaway

Remember the rule 'only the API server talks to etcd' — everything else, including the scheduler and kubelets, is just an API client.

Going deeper

  • etcd uses the Raft consensus algorithm and needs a majority to accept writes: three members survive one failure, five survive two; even member counts add cost without adding fault tolerance.
  • etcd's default request size limit is about 1.5 MiB, which is why a single ConfigMap or Secret is capped at 1 MiB; the default backend quota is 2 GiB and 8 GiB is the usual recommended maximum.
  • The API server keeps a watch cache in memory, so thousands of controllers and kubelets can watch objects without each request hitting etcd; v1.37 added etcd RangeStream support as beta to cut memory on large lists.
  • Nodes renew a Lease object in kube-node-lease roughly every 10 seconds; if the node controller sees no renewal within its grace period, it marks the node NotReady and taints it, and Pods are evicted after a default 300-second toleration.
  • Kubernetes' tested scalability limits are about 5,000 nodes, 150,000 Pods and 110 Pods per node by default; managed clouds publish their own, sometimes higher, limits.
  • Scheduler and controller managers run one active copy elected through a Lease; standby replicas take over in seconds if the leader stops renewing.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Running two etcd members 'for redundancy': quorum of two is two, so losing either one stops all writes. Use three or five.
  • Assuming a NotReady node's Pods move instantly: by default the cluster waits roughly five minutes before evicting them, unless you set tolerationSeconds lower.
  • Exposing the API server or kubelet port (10250) to the internet without strong authentication; scanners find open clusters within hours.

docs.title: Try it: Inspect the control plane and nodes of any cluster
docs.text:
kubectl get nodes -o wide
kubectl get pods -n kube-system -o wide       # static control-plane Pods on kubeadm/kind
kubectl get --raw='/readyz?verbose' | tail -5   # API server health checks
kubectl get leases -n kube-system              # scheduler/controller leader election
kubectl get leases -n kube-node-lease          # one heartbeat Lease per node
kubectl describe node <node-name> | sed -n '/Conditions/,/Addresses/p'

docs.title: Key kernels, commands, tools, standards & concepts
docs.text: Name What it does Example kube-apiserverKubernetes SIG API Machinery · Component · Current · Beginner The REST front door of the cluster: authenticates, authorises, validates and stores every object, and serves watches to clients. kubectl get pods becomes GET /api/v1/namespaces/default/pods, answered by kube-apiserver from its watch cache. etcdCNCF graduated project (etcd-io) · Software · Current · Intermediate Strongly consistent, Raft-replicated key-value store holding the entire cluster state under keys such as /registry/pods/. An admin takes etcdctl snapshot save backup.db nightly so the whole cluster's objects can be restored after a disaster. kube-schedulerKubernetes SIG Scheduling · Component · Current · Beginner Assigns each unscheduled Pod to a node by filtering out unsuitable nodes and scoring the rest. A Pod requesting 2 CPUs and a GPU skips 18 CPU-only nodes and lands on the GPU node with most free capacity. kube-controller-managerKubernetes SIG API Machinery / SIG Apps · Component · Current · Intermediate One binary running many built-in controllers: Deployment, ReplicaSet, Job, node lifecycle, EndpointSlice, ServiceAccount and more. When a node dies, its node-lifecycle controller taints it and the ReplicaSet controller replaces the lost Pods elsewhere. cloud-controller-managerKubernetes SIG Cloud Provider · Component · Current · Intermediate Runs cloud-specific loops: creating load balancers for Services, labelling nodes with zones and removing deleted VMs. Creating a type: LoadBalancer Service on AKS makes the Azure cloud-controller-manager provision an Azure Load Balancer and public IP. kubeletKubernetes SIG Node · Component · Current · Beginner Node agent that runs Pods assigned to its node through the container runtime, runs probes and reports node and Pod status. The kubelet restarts a container after its liveness probe fails three times and records a 'Killing' event. kube-proxyKubernetes SIG Network · Component · Current · Intermediate Per-node agent that programs iptables, nftables or IPVS rules so traffic to a Service IP reaches a backend Pod. On a node, nft list ruleset shows kube-proxy's rules translating 10.96.12.7:80 to three Pod IPs. Watch API and watch cacheKubernetes SIG API Machinery · Concept · Current · Advanced Clients open long-lived watches to receive object changes as a stream; the API server serves them from an in-memory cache. kubectl get pods -w uses a watch; thousands of kubelets and controllers watch the same way instead of polling every second. Node and Lease heartbeatsKubernetes core/v1 and coordination.k8s.io/v1 · Object · Current · Intermediate Each node has a Node object with capacity and conditions, plus a lightweight Lease renewed every ~10 s as a heartbeat. kubectl get node worker-7 shows Ready=False after its Lease stopped renewing during a network partition. Static PodsKubernetes SIG Node · Concept · Current · Intermediate Pods defined as files on a node that the kubelet runs directly, without the scheduler; used to bootstrap the control plane. kubeadm writes kube-apiserver.yaml into /etc/kubernetes/manifests, and the kubelet keeps that API server running. kubeadmKubernetes SIG Cluster Lifecycle · Tool · Current · Intermediate Official tool to bootstrap a conformant cluster: generates certificates, static Pod manifests and join tokens. kubeadm init --control-plane-endpoint lb.lab:6443 --upload-certs then kubeadm join on each worker builds a lab cluster. Highly available control planeKubernetes docs (kubeadm HA topologies) · Concept · Current · Advanced Three or more control-plane nodes behind a load balancer, with etcd either stacked on them or run as a separate cluster. Stacked etcd on three control-plane VMs suits most teams; a bank keeps five external etcd nodes for extra failure tolerance. Leader electionclient-go leaderelection, coordination.k8s.io Lease · Concept · Current · Advanced Replicas of a controller compete for a Lease; only the holder acts, and a standby takes over when renewals stop. kubectl get lease kube-scheduler -n kube-system -o yaml shows holderIdentity naming the active scheduler's host. API request pipelineKubernetes SIG Auth / API Machinery · Concept · Current · Intermediate Every write passes authentication, authorisation, mutating admission, schema validation and validating admission before reaching etcd. A Deployment missing required labels is rejected by a validating admission policy before it is ever stored.

docs.title: 8.3 Pods, Init and Sidecar Containers, and Probes
docs.text:
A Pod is the smallest thing Kubernetes runs: one or more containers that are always scheduled together on the same node, share one IP address and can share files. Kubernetes checks each container's health with probes and restarts or isolates containers that stop working.

A Pod's life from creation to termination. Traffic arrives only after readiness passes, and stops (eventually) after SIGTERM — design for both edges.

Think of it like…

A Pod is like a shared flat: the flatmates (containers) share one street address and the kitchen (network and volumes), move in and out together, and the landlord (kubelet) checks regularly that everyone is still alive and answering the door.

Real-world example

Kofi's checkout service needs a database schema migration before start-up and ships logs to a central store. His Pod uses an init container for the migration, a native sidecar container for the log shipper, and the main app container with a startup probe (slow Java boot), a readiness probe on /ready and a liveness probe on /healthz.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The scheduler binds the Pod to a node; the kubelet pulls images and creates a sandbox holding the Pod's network namespace.
  2. Init containers run one at a time, each to completion; a failure restarts the sequence.
  3. Sidecar containers (init containers with restartPolicy: Always) start and keep running alongside the app.
  4. App containers start; the startup probe must pass before liveness and readiness probes begin.
  5. Only Ready Pods are added to Service endpoints; failing liveness probes cause container restarts.
  6. On deletion the Pod gets SIGTERM, runs any preStop hook, and is killed after terminationGracePeriodSeconds (30 s default).

Who uses it

Every developer deploying to Kubernetes writes Pod specs; SREs tune probes and termination behaviour to avoid outages during rollouts.

Key takeaway

Know the three probes cold: startup = 'has it finished booting?', readiness = 'should it get traffic now?', liveness = 'is it stuck and needs a restart?'.

Going deeper

  • All containers in a Pod share one network namespace (one IP, talk via localhost) and can share volumes; a tiny 'pause' sandbox container holds the namespaces so app containers can restart without losing the IP.
  • Probe defaults: periodSeconds 10, timeoutSeconds 1, failureThreshold 3, successThreshold 1; handlers can be httpGet, tcpSocket, exec or gRPC, and 2xx-3xx HTTP codes count as success.
  • CrashLoopBackOff is not an error in itself but a waiting state: restart delays double from 10 s up to a 5-minute cap and reset after a container runs successfully for 10 minutes.
  • Removal from Service endpoints and SIGTERM happen in parallel, so a short preStop sleep (native sleep action, or a sleep command) prevents a few seconds of 502 errors during rollouts.
  • In-place Pod resize graduated to stable in v1.35: CPU and memory requests and limits can change through the resize subresource without recreating the Pod, subject to each container's resizePolicy.
  • Ephemeral containers (kubectl debug -it pod/web --image=busybox --target=app) attach a temporary troubleshooting container that shares the target's process namespace, ideal for distroless images with no shell.
  • OCI image volumes, stable in v1.36, mount the contents of an OCI image or artifact read-only into a Pod — handy for shipping ML model files or static data separately from the app image.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Pointing the liveness probe at a dependency such as the database: a database blip then restarts every app Pod at once. Liveness should check only the process itself.
  • Using a liveness probe instead of a startup probe for slow starters, so the app is killed before it ever finishes booting.
  • Creating bare Pods in production: nothing recreates them if the node dies. Use a Deployment, StatefulSet, DaemonSet or Job.

docs.title: Try it: A Pod with init container, native sidecar and all three probes
docs.text:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: checkout
  labels: {app: checkout}
spec:
  initContainers:
  - name: migrate
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sh", "-c", "echo running migrations; sleep 3"]
  - name: log-shipper            # native sidecar (GA in v1.33)
    image: busybox:1.36
    restartPolicy: Always
    command: ["sh", "-c", "tail -F /logs/app.log"]
    volumeMounts: [{name: logs, mountPath: /logs}]
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx:1.27
    ports: [{containerPort: 80}]
    volumeMounts: [{name: logs, mountPath: /logs}]
    startupProbe:   {httpGet: {path: /, port: 80}, failureThreshold: 30, periodSeconds: 2}
    readinessProbe: {httpGet: {path: /, port: 80}, periodSeconds: 5}
    livenessProbe:  {httpGet: {path: /, port: 80}, periodSeconds: 10, failureThreshold: 3}
    lifecycle:
      preStop: {sleep: {seconds: 5}}   # let load balancers drain first
    resources:
      requests: {cpu: 100m, memory: 64Mi}
      limits:   {memory: 128Mi}
  volumes:
  - name: logs
    emptyDir: {}
# kubectl apply -f pod.yaml && kubectl get pod checkout -w
# kubectl describe pod checkout    # see probe results and events

docs.text: Name What it does Example PodKubernetes core/v1 · Object · Current · Beginner Smallest deployable unit: one or more containers with a shared IP, shared volumes and a common lifecycle on one node. A Pod holds an nginx container and a metrics exporter; the exporter scrapes nginx at localhost:8080/status. Pod phases and conditionsKubernetes core/v1 PodStatus · Concept · Current · Beginner Phase is Pending, Running, Succeeded, Failed or Unknown; conditions like PodScheduled, Initialized and Ready give finer detail. kubectl get pod shows Running but READY 0/1 because the Ready condition is False while the readiness probe fails. Init containersKubernetes core/v1 · Concept · Current · Beginner Containers that run sequentially to completion before app containers start, for setup work like migrations or waiting for dependencies. An init container runs until nslookup postgres succeeds, so the app never starts before its database Service exists. Native sidecar containersKEP-753, stable in v1.33 · Concept · Current · Intermediate Init containers with restartPolicy: Always that start before and stop after app containers, fixing old sidecar ordering problems. A Job's log-shipping sidecar no longer keeps the Job running forever, because Kubernetes stops it once the main container finishes. Liveness probeKubernetes core/v1 Probe · Concept · Current · Beginner Periodic check that the container is still healthy; after failureThreshold consecutive failures the kubelet restarts the container. A Go service that deadlocks stops answering /healthz; after three failed checks 10 s apart the kubelet restarts it. Readiness probeKubernetes core/v1 Probe · Concept · Current · Beginner Check that decides whether a Pod should receive Service traffic; failing it removes the Pod from endpoints without restarting it. During a cache warm-up of 40 s, /ready returns 503, so users are never routed to the cold Pod. Startup probeKubernetes core/v1 Probe (GA v1.20) · Concept · Current · Intermediate Check that must succeed once before liveness and readiness probes start, protecting slow-booting applications. failureThreshold: 30 with periodSeconds: 10 gives a legacy Java app up to 300 s to boot before any restart. restartPolicy and CrashLoopBackOffKubernetes core/v1 · Concept · Current · Beginner restartPolicy is Always, OnFailure or Never; repeated crashes put the container into exponential back-off capped at five minutes. kubectl get pods shows CrashLoopBackOff with 7 restarts; kubectl logs web --previous reveals a missing DATABASE_URL variable. Graceful termination and preStop hooksKubernetes core/v1 Lifecycle · Concept · Current · Intermediate On deletion containers receive SIGTERM, preStop hooks run, and SIGKILL follows after terminationGracePeriodSeconds (default 30). A payment worker sets terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 60 so in-flight card transactions finish before the Pod stops. Ephemeral containers (kubectl debug)Kubernetes SIG Node (GA v1.25) · Command · Current · Intermediate Temporary containers added to a running Pod for troubleshooting; they have no ports or probes and are never restarted. kubectl debug -it pod/api --image=nicolaka/netshoot --target=api lets Mia run tcpdump inside a distroless Pod. In-place Pod resizeKEP-1287, stable in v1.35 · Concept · Current · Intermediate Changing a running container's CPU and memory requests and limits without recreating the Pod, via the resize subresource. kubectl patch pod api --subresource resize -p '{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"api","resources":{"limits":{"cpu":"2"}}}]}}' raises CPU with no restart. Pod-level resourcesKEP-2837, beta since v1.34 · Concept · Emerging · Advanced Setting one CPU and memory budget for the whole Pod, which its containers share, instead of only per-container values. A Pod with an app and two sidecars gets spec.resources.limits.memory: 1Gi shared by all three containers. Downward APIKubernetes core/v1 · Concept · Current · Intermediate Exposes Pod facts — name, namespace, labels, node, resource limits — to containers as environment variables or files. env POD_NAME from fieldRef metadata.name lets each replica tag its log lines with its own Pod name. imagePullPolicyKubernetes core/v1 · Concept · Current · Beginner Controls image pulls: Always, IfNotPresent or Never; the default is Always for :latest tags and IfNotPresent otherwise. A team pins image: shop/api:2.4.1@sha256:... so every node runs the identical image whatever the policy. OCI image volumesKEP-4639, stable in v1.36 · Concept · Emerging · Advanced Volume type that mounts an OCI image or artifact's files read-only into a Pod, without running it as a container. An inference Pod mounts registry.example/models/llama-small:v3 at /models while the server image stays small.

docs.title: 8.4 Workload Controllers: From Deployments to CronJobs
docs.text:
You rarely create Pods directly. Instead you create a workload controller that creates and replaces Pods for you: Deployments for stateless apps, StatefulSets for databases that need stable names and disks, DaemonSets for one agent per node, and Jobs and CronJobs for tasks that run to completion.

Deployment vs StatefulSet vs DaemonSet

Deployment StatefulSet DaemonSet Pod names random hash (web-7d9f-x2k) ordinal (db-0, db-1) one per node Storage usually shared or none own PVC per replica often hostPath Scaling any order, in parallel ordered by default follows node count Network identity via Service only stable DNS per Pod node-local Typical use web APIs, workers databases, Kafka, etcd log/metrics agents, CNI

Pick by what each replica needs: nothing special, a stable identity and disk, or one copy per node.

Think of it like…

Workload controllers are like different kinds of managers: a shift supervisor keeps five interchangeable cashiers on the tills (Deployment), a librarian keeps named, numbered shelves in order (StatefulSet), a building manager puts one smoke alarm in every room (DaemonSet), and a project lead hires temps until a task is done (Job).

Real-world example

Greenfield Bank's mobile API runs as a Deployment with 12 replicas and a rolling update of 25% surge; its Redis cache runs as a three-member StatefulSet (redis-0, redis-1, redis-2) each with its own 20 GiB disk; a DaemonSet runs a log collector on all 40 nodes; and a CronJob builds the end-of-day statement report at 02:00 Europe/London time.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Choose the controller by behaviour: stateless (Deployment), stable identity and storage (StatefulSet), per-node (DaemonSet), finite work (Job, CronJob).
  2. Write a Pod template inside the controller's spec plus a label selector matching it.
  3. The controller creates Pods (a Deployment does it through a ReplicaSet) and keeps their count and version right.
  4. Changing the Pod template triggers a rollout: new Pods are created and old ones removed according to the update strategy.
  5. Watch progress with kubectl rollout status and roll back with kubectl rollout undo if needed.

Who uses it

Application developers and DevOps engineers choose and configure these controllers for every service; database and platform teams specialise in StatefulSets and DaemonSets.

Key takeaway

If the app writes nothing important to local disk and any replica can serve any request, use a Deployment; reach for a StatefulSet only when identity or per-replica storage really matters.

Going deeper

  • A Deployment manages ReplicaSets, each labelled with a pod-template-hash; a rollout scales the new ReplicaSet up and the old one down, keeping up to revisionHistoryLimit (default 10) old ReplicaSets for rollback.
  • Rolling-update defaults are maxSurge 25% and maxUnavailable 25%; progressDeadlineSeconds (default 600) marks a rollout as failed if it makes no progress, which CI pipelines can detect with kubectl rollout status.
  • StatefulSets need a headless Service for per-Pod DNS (db-0.db.prod.svc.cluster.local); volumeClaimTemplates create one PVC per ordinal, and by default PVCs survive scale-down so data is not lost.
  • StatefulSet rollouts proceed from the highest ordinal down; setting rollingUpdate.partition: 2 updates only db-2 and above, a simple canary. v1.37 added an alpha Recreate strategy for StatefulSets.
  • Jobs default to backoffLimit 6; completions and parallelism control batch size, Indexed Jobs give each Pod a JOB_COMPLETION_INDEX, and podFailurePolicy can fail fast on non-retryable exit codes.
  • CronJobs use standard five-field cron syntax with an optional timeZone field; concurrencyPolicy Allow, Forbid or Replace decides what happens when a run is still going at the next schedule.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Running a single-replica database as a Deployment with a shared disk: two Pods may briefly mount it during a rollout and corrupt data. Use a StatefulSet or a database operator.
  • Rolling updates with no readiness probe: Kubernetes considers new Pods ready instantly and may remove all old Pods before the new ones work.
  • Forgetting a PodDisruptionBudget: a node drain during an upgrade can evict every replica of a service at once.

docs.title: Try it: A Deployment with a careful rolling update, then roll it forward and back
docs.text:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: {name: web}
spec:
  replicas: 4
  revisionHistoryLimit: 5
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate: {maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0}   # never drop below 4 ready
  selector: {matchLabels: {app: web}}
  template:
    metadata: {labels: {app: web}}
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: web
        image: nginx:1.27
        readinessProbe: {httpGet: {path: /, port: 80}}
---
# kubectl apply -f web.yaml
# kubectl set image deploy/web web=nginx:1.28 && kubectl rollout status deploy/web
# kubectl rollout history deploy/web
# kubectl rollout undo deploy/web --to-revision=1
# kubectl create cronjob report --image=busybox:1.36 --schedule='0 2 * * *' -- date

docs.title: Key kernels, commands, tools, standards & concepts
docs.text: Name What it does Example ReplicaSetKubernetes apps/v1 · Object · Current · Beginner Keeps a specified number of identical Pods running; normally created and managed by a Deployment rather than by hand. kubectl get rs shows web-6c8f (4/4 ready, current) and web-5b7d (0 replicas, kept for rollback). DeploymentKubernetes apps/v1 · Object · Current · Beginner Declarative manager for stateless Pods that handles rolling updates, rollbacks, scaling and revision history through ReplicaSets. Changing the image tag from 2.3 to 2.4 makes the Deployment roll Pods over, one surge Pod at a time. RollingUpdate and Recreate strategiesKubernetes apps/v1 DeploymentStrategy · Concept · Current · Beginner RollingUpdate replaces Pods gradually within maxSurge/maxUnavailable limits; Recreate kills all old Pods first, accepting downtime. A legacy app that cannot run two versions at once uses strategy type: Recreate during a Sunday maintenance window. kubectl rolloutKubernetes SIG CLI · Command · Current · Beginner Subcommands to watch, pause, resume, restart, inspect history of and undo rollouts of Deployments, StatefulSets and DaemonSets. kubectl rollout restart deploy/api reloads changed ConfigMap values by recreating Pods with zero downtime. StatefulSetKubernetes apps/v1 · Object · Current · Intermediate Manages Pods with stable ordinal names, stable DNS and a dedicated persistent volume each, created and updated in order. A three-node Kafka cluster runs as kafka-0..2; if kafka-1 is rescheduled it keeps its name and reattaches its own disk. volumeClaimTemplatesKubernetes apps/v1 StatefulSetSpec · Concept · Current · Intermediate Template inside a StatefulSet that creates one PersistentVolumeClaim per replica, named after the template and Pod. Template data in StatefulSet pg creates PVCs data-pg-0, data-pg-1 and data-pg-2, each 50 Gi on gp3. DaemonSetKubernetes apps/v1 · Object · Current · Beginner Ensures one copy of a Pod runs on every node, or on nodes matching a selector, including nodes added later. Fluent Bit runs as a DaemonSet; when Karpenter adds node 41, a log collector starts there automatically. JobKubernetes batch/v1 · Object · Current · Beginner Runs Pods until a set number complete successfully, retrying failures up to backoffLimit. A Job with completions: 50 and parallelism: 10 resizes 50 image batches, ten at a time. Indexed Jobs and pod failure policyKubernetes batch/v1 (Indexed GA v1.24, podFailurePolicy GA v1.31) · Concept · Current · Advanced Indexed Jobs give each Pod a unique index; podFailurePolicy decides which exit codes or disruptions should retry, ignore or fail. Exit code 42 means 'bad input', so podFailurePolicy action FailJob stops wasting retries on a hopeless run. CronJobKubernetes batch/v1 (GA v1.21) · Object · Current · Beginner Creates Jobs on a cron schedule, with time zones, concurrency rules and limits on kept job history. schedule: '0 2 * * *' with timeZone: Europe/London runs the statement report at 02:00 UK time, summer or winter. PodDisruptionBudget (PDB)Kubernetes policy/v1 · Object · Current · Intermediate Limits how many Pods of an app may be voluntarily evicted at once, for example during node drains and upgrades. minAvailable: 2 on a three-replica API means kubectl drain waits rather than evicting two replicas together. Headless Service for stable identityKubernetes core/v1 (clusterIP: None) · Concept · Current · Intermediate A Service without a virtual IP whose DNS returns individual Pod addresses, giving each StatefulSet Pod its own name. Replica pg-1 reaches the primary at pg-0.pg.db.svc.cluster.local for streaming replication. Job pod replacement policyKEP-3939, stable in v1.34 · Concept · Current · Advanced Lets a Job wait until a terminating Pod has fully stopped before creating its replacement, avoiding double resource use. A GPU training Job sets podReplacementPolicy: Failed so a new Pod never competes with a dying one for the only GPU. StatefulSet Recreate strategyKEP, alpha in v1.37 (StatefulSetRecreateStrategy) · Concept · Emerging · Advanced New alpha update strategy that replaces all StatefulSet Pods together rather than one ordinal at a time. A test cluster enables the feature gate to upgrade a database whose versions cannot run side by side.

docs.title: 8.5 Services, DNS, Ingress and the Gateway API
docs.text:
Pods come and go and change IP addresses, so clients need a stable address. A Service gives a group of Pods one fixed virtual IP and DNS name and spreads traffic across them. To let users outside the cluster in, you use a LoadBalancer Service, the older Ingress API, or its modern successor, the Gateway API.

Path of an outside request. Gateway API splits responsibility: platform teams own the Gateway, app teams own their Routes.

Think of it like…

A Service is like a company's switchboard number: callers always dial the same number, and the switchboard forwards each call to whichever staff member is at a desk today; the Gateway is the reception desk at the front door that sends visitors to the right department.

Real-world example

Mosaic Travel exposes shop.mosaic.example through one Gateway on a cloud load balancer. An HTTPRoute sends /api to Service api (six Pods) and everything else to Service web, while a second HTTPRoute sends 10% of /api traffic to api-v2 for a canary test. Inside the cluster, the api Pods reach Postgres simply as postgres.db.svc.cluster.local.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. A Service selects Pods by label; the EndpointSlice controller lists the IPs of those Pods that are Ready.
  2. kube-proxy (or Cilium's eBPF) on every node translates the Service's virtual ClusterIP to one of those Pod IPs.
  3. CoreDNS answers name lookups such as api.shop.svc.cluster.local with the ClusterIP.
  4. For outside access, a LoadBalancer Service asks the cloud for a load balancer pointing at the nodes.
  5. For HTTP routing, a Gateway (listeners, ports, TLS) plus HTTPRoutes (hosts, paths, headers, weights) send requests to Services.

Who uses it

Developers wire microservices together with Services and DNS; platform and network engineers run the Gateway or Ingress layer, TLS and load balancers.

Key takeaway

Ingress NGINX was retired on 24 March 2026 and the Ingress API is feature-frozen; for new work learn the Gateway API (GatewayClass, Gateway, HTTPRoute).

Going deeper

  • A ClusterIP is virtual: no interface owns it; packets are rewritten by iptables, nftables or eBPF rules on the sending node. The kubeadm default Service range is 10.96.0.0/12 and NodePorts use 30000-32767.
  • Service DNS names follow service.namespace.svc.cluster.local; Pods get ndots:5 in resolv.conf, so a name like api.example.com may first try several cluster suffixes — add a trailing dot or tune ndots for heavy external lookups.
  • kube-proxy's nftables mode became stable in v1.33 and scales better than iptables; IPVS mode was deprecated in v1.37, with plans to disable it by default around v1.40 and remove it around v1.43.
  • EndpointSlices hold up to 100 endpoints each by default and replaced the old Endpoints API, which was deprecated in v1.33; kube-dns was deprecated in v1.37 in favour of CoreDNS.
  • Gateway API is shipped as CRDs, not built into Kubernetes: v1.0 arrived in October 2023, v1.5 (February 2026) moved TLSRoute and ListenerSet to Standard, and v1.6 (June 2026) made TCPRoute and UDPRoute GA.
  • Service spec.externalIPs was deprecated in v1.36 (removal planned for v1.43) because of CVE-2020-8554, which let users intercept traffic; prefer LoadBalancer Services or a Gateway.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Expecting to ping a ClusterIP: ICMP usually fails because only the defined TCP/UDP ports are translated. Test with curl or nc on the Service port.
  • A Service selector that does not match the Pod labels exactly gives an empty EndpointSlice and 'connection refused'; check kubectl get endpointslices first.
  • Treating ingress-nginx as maintained: it received no fixes after March 2026. Plan a migration to a Gateway API implementation or a supported controller.

docs.title: Try it: A Service plus a Gateway API route with a 90/10 canary split
docs.text:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: {name: api, namespace: shop}
spec:
  selector: {app: api}
  ports: [{name: http, port: 80, targetPort: 8080}]
---
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata: {name: api, namespace: shop}
spec:
  parentRefs: [{name: public-gw, namespace: infra}]
  hostnames: ["shop.mosaic.example"]
  rules:
  - matches: [{path: {type: PathPrefix, value: /api}}]
    backendRefs:
    - {name: api,    port: 80, weight: 90}
    - {name: api-v2, port: 80, weight: 10}
---
# Test DNS and the Service from inside the cluster:
# kubectl run t --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never -- \
#   sh -c 'nslookup api.shop.svc.cluster.local; wget -qO- http://api.shop/healthz'
# kubectl get endpointslices -n shop -l kubernetes.io/service-name=api

docs.text: Name What it does Example ServiceKubernetes core/v1 · Object · Current · Beginner Stable virtual IP and DNS name in front of a changing set of Pods chosen by a label selector, with load-balancing. Service cart on port 80 forwards to targetPort 8080 on whichever of five cart Pods are Ready. ClusterIPKubernetes core/v1 ServiceSpec · Concept · Current · Beginner Default Service type: a virtual IP reachable only inside the cluster. Frontend Pods call http://cart.shop:80; the name resolves to ClusterIP 10.96.44.12, never exposed to the internet. NodePortKubernetes core/v1 ServiceSpec · Concept · Current · Beginner Opens the same port (30000-32767) on every node and forwards it to the Service; the building block under most cloud load balancers. On a home-lab cluster, http://192.168.1.20:31080 reaches Grafana through a NodePort Service. LoadBalancer ServiceKubernetes core/v1 + cloud-controller-manager · Concept · Current · Beginner Service type that asks the cloud (or MetalLB on bare metal) to provision an external load balancer for it. type: LoadBalancer on EKS creates an AWS Network Load Balancer whose DNS name the team puts behind a CNAME record. Headless and ExternalName ServicesKubernetes core/v1 ServiceSpec · Concept · Current · Intermediate Headless (clusterIP: None) returns Pod IPs directly in DNS; ExternalName returns a CNAME to an outside hostname. ExternalName billing-db pointing to db.legacy.example lets Pods use one internal name while the database stays outside. EndpointSliceKubernetes discovery.k8s.io/v1 · Object · Current · Intermediate Scalable lists of the addresses, ports and readiness of a Service's backends; replaces the deprecated Endpoints API. kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=cart shows three ready addresses and one terminating. kube-proxy modes: iptables, nftables, IPVSKubernetes SIG Network · Concept · Current · Advanced How nodes implement Services: iptables is the long-time default, nftables is stable since v1.33, IPVS is deprecated since v1.37. A 2,000-Service cluster switches kube-proxy to mode: nftables to cut rule-sync times on each endpoint change. Pods' /etc/resolv.conf points to nameserver 10.96.0.10, the kube-dns Service in front of CoreDNS. IngressKubernetes networking.k8s.io/v1 · Object · Legacy · Beginner Older API for HTTP host and path routing into the cluster; still supported but feature-frozen, relying on controller-specific annotations. An Ingress maps blog.example.com/ to Service blog, with a cert-manager annotation requesting a Let's Encrypt certificate. Mosaic Travel's audit flags ingress-nginx as unmaintained, so the team schedules migration to Envoy Gateway before its next PCI review. Gateway APIKubernetes SIG Network (v1.0 Oct 2023; v1.6 Jun 2026) · Specification · Current · Intermediate Role-oriented, CRD-based successor to Ingress: GatewayClass, Gateway and Routes for HTTP, gRPC, TLS, TCP and UDP traffic. The platform team owns Gateway public-gw in namespace infra; app teams attach their own HTTPRoutes without touching TLS settings. HTTPRoute and GRPCRouteGateway API gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1 · Object · Current · Intermediate Routing rules matching host, path, headers or methods, with filters for redirects and rewrites and weighted backends. An HTTPRoute sends requests with header x-beta: true to Service api-v2 and everything else to api.
