On GKE, gatewayClassName: gke-l7-global-external-managed creates a Google global HTTP(S) load balancer. ingress2gatewayKubernetes SIG Network (kubernetes-sigs) · Tool · Current · Intermediate Converter that reads Ingress objects and provider annotations and writes equivalent Gateway API resources for review. ingress2gateway print --providers=ingress-nginx --all-namespaces > gw.yaml produces HTTPRoutes the team then tests in staging. externalTrafficPolicy and internalTrafficPolicyKubernetes core/v1 ServiceSpec · Concept · Current · Advanced Local keeps traffic on the receiving node's own Pods, preserving client source IPs and avoiding an extra hop. externalTrafficPolicy: Local lets the web Pods log real customer IPs instead of node addresses.

docs.title: 8.6 Pod Networking, CNI Plugins and NetworkPolicy
docs.text:
Kubernetes promises that every Pod gets its own IP address and can reach every other Pod without address translation, but it does not build that network itself. A Container Network Interface (CNI) plugin such as Calico, Cilium or Flannel does. NetworkPolicy objects then act as a firewall between Pods — if your plugin enforces them.

Pod-to-Pod across two nodes. Each node owns a slice of the Pod CIDR; the CNI either tunnels between nodes or routes natively.

Think of it like…

The CNI plugin is the company that lays the roads between houses (Pods); NetworkPolicy is the set of gate rules saying which visitors each house will let in.

Real-world example

Helix Health must prove that only the billing Pods can reach the patient-records database. With Cilium as CNI, the team applies a default-deny policy in namespace records, then one policy allowing TCP 5432 only from Pods labelled app: billing. Hubble's flow logs show blocked attempts from other namespaces, which they attach to their HIPAA evidence pack.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. When a Pod is created, the container runtime calls the configured CNI plugin binary (from /opt/cni/bin, config in /etc/cni/net.d).
  2. The plugin creates the Pod's network interface (often a veth pair), assigns an IP from the node's Pod CIDR (IPAM) and sets routes.
  3. Traffic between nodes flows through an overlay (VXLAN, Geneve) or native routing (BGP, cloud VPC routes).
  4. NetworkPolicies select Pods by label and list allowed ingress and egress peers and ports.
  5. The plugin's agent on each node turns policies into iptables, nftables or eBPF rules and enforces them.

Who uses it

Platform and network engineers choose and run the CNI; security engineers write NetworkPolicies to segment workloads for zero-trust and compliance.

Key takeaway

NetworkPolicy is allow-list based and only works if the CNI enforces it — plain Flannel does not. Start every sensitive namespace with a default-deny policy.

Going deeper

  • The CNI specification (currently v1.1) defines a tiny contract: the runtime runs a plugin binary with ADD, DEL, CHECK, STATUS, GC or VERSION, passing JSON config on stdin and environment variables like CNI_NETNS.
  • VXLAN overlays add about 50 bytes of headers per packet, so Pod MTU is often 1450 on a 1500-byte network; mismatched MTUs cause mysterious hangs on large transfers while small requests work.
  • A Pod becomes isolated for ingress as soon as any policy selects it for ingress; all policies are additive allows, and there is no 'deny' rule in the core NetworkPolicy API.
  • Every namespace automatically gets the label kubernetes.io/metadata.name, which makes namespaceSelector rules reliable without hand-labelling namespaces.
  • Cilium (CNCF graduated October 2023; its creator Isovalent was acquired by Cisco in 2024) uses eBPF and can fully replace kube-proxy; GKE Dataplane V2 is built on Cilium.
  • SIG Network's AdminNetworkPolicy and BaselineAdminNetworkPolicy CRDs (still alpha, v1alpha1) add cluster-wide, priority-ordered rules with explicit Deny that namespace owners cannot override.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Writing a default-deny egress policy and forgetting DNS: every Pod then fails name lookups. Always allow UDP and TCP port 53 to CoreDNS.
  • Assuming NetworkPolicies work on any cluster: with a non-enforcing CNI they are accepted by the API server but silently do nothing.
  • Choosing overlapping Pod, Service and VPC CIDRs at cluster creation; these are painful or impossible to change later.

docs.title: Try it: Default-deny for a namespace, then allow only billing to reach Postgres (and DNS out)
docs.text:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: {name: default-deny, namespace: records}
spec:
  podSelector: {}            # every Pod in the namespace
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: {name: allow-billing-to-db, namespace: records}
spec:
  podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: postgres}}
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
  - from:
    - namespaceSelector: {matchLabels: {kubernetes.io/metadata.name: billing}}
      podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: billing}}
    ports: [{protocol: TCP, port: 5432}]
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: {name: allow-dns-egress, namespace: records}
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Egress]
  egress:
  - ports: [{protocol: UDP, port: 53}, {protocol: TCP, port: 53}]
# kubectl get netpol -n records

docs.title: Key kernels, commands, tools, standards & concepts
docs.text: Name What it does Example Kubernetes network modelKubernetes SIG Network · Concept · Current · Beginner Every Pod gets a unique cluster-wide IP and can reach every other Pod and node without NAT, unless policy blocks it. Pod 10.244.1.7 on node 1 opens a TCP connection straight to 10.244.2.9 on node 2 and sees its real address. Container Network Interface (CNI)CNCF containernetworking project (spec v1.1) · Specification · Current · Intermediate Standard contract between container runtimes and network plugins: a plugin binary plus JSON config that sets up Pod networking. containerd reads /etc/cni/net.d/10-calico.conflist and calls the calico and portmap binaries for each new Pod. IPAM and Pod CIDRsKubernetes and CNI IPAM plugins · Concept · Current · Intermediate IP address management: carving the cluster Pod range into per-node blocks and handing each Pod an address. With --pod-network-cidr=10.244.0.0/16 and /24 per node, a cluster supports 256 nodes of up to 254 Pods each. Overlay vs native routingCNI implementations (VXLAN, Geneve, BGP) · Concept · Current · Intermediate Overlays tunnel Pod traffic inside node-to-node packets; native routing makes the underlying network route Pod CIDRs directly. On-prem, Calico peers with top-of-rack routers via BGP so Pod IPs are routable with no tunnelling overhead. CalicoTigera (Project Calico, open source) · Software · Current · Intermediate Widely used CNI and policy engine offering BGP or overlay networking and iptables, nftables or eBPF data planes. A telco uses Calico GlobalNetworkPolicy to block all Pods from the metadata IP 169.254.169.254 cluster-wide. CiliumCNCF graduated; created by Isovalent (Cisco) · Software · Current · Intermediate eBPF-based CNI providing networking, kube-proxy replacement, L3-L7 policy, encryption, load balancing and Hubble observability. Cilium's kube-proxy replacement lets a 900-node cluster drop thousands of iptables rules and cut Service latency. Flannelflannel-io (originally CoreOS) · Software · Current · Beginner Simple overlay CNI giving each node a subnet, usually over VXLAN; it does not enforce NetworkPolicy on its own. k3s ships Flannel by default, plus a small embedded policy controller to enforce NetworkPolicies. Cloud VPC CNIsAmazon VPC CNI, Azure CNI, GKE Dataplane V2 · Software · Current · Intermediate Cloud plugins that give Pods real VPC addresses, so cloud firewalls, load balancers and flow logs see Pod IPs directly. On EKS, each Pod gets an IP from the subnet via the VPC CNI, so subnet size limits how many Pods fit. Multus CNIk8snetworkplumbingwg · Software · Current · Advanced Meta-plugin that attaches several network interfaces to a Pod, common in telecom and high-performance networking. A 5G user-plane Pod gets eth0 for management plus two SR-IOV interfaces for line-rate packet traffic. NetworkPolicyKubernetes networking.k8s.io/v1 · Object · Current · Intermediate Label-based firewall rules listing which Pods, namespaces or IP blocks may send traffic to or receive it from selected Pods. Policy allow-frontend lets only app: web Pods reach app: api on TCP 8080; everything else is dropped. Default-deny policyKubernetes NetworkPolicy pattern · Concept · Current · Intermediate A policy with an empty podSelector and no rules, isolating every Pod in a namespace until explicit allows are added. Each new team namespace is created with default-deny ingress and egress by the platform's namespace template. CiliumNetworkPolicy and Calico policiesCilium and Calico CRDs · Object · Current · Advanced Vendor policy resources adding L7 HTTP rules, DNS-name egress rules, explicit deny and cluster-wide scope. toFQDNs: matchName api.stripe.com lets checkout Pods call Stripe while blocking all other internet egress. AdminNetworkPolicyKubernetes SIG Network (policy.networking.k8s.io/v1alpha1 CRD) · Object · Emerging · Advanced Cluster-admin policies with priorities and explicit Allow, Deny or Pass actions that override namespace NetworkPolicies. A platform team denies all traffic into namespace kube-system from tenant namespaces, whatever tenants write themselves. HubbleCilium project · Tool · Current · Intermediate Network observability for Cilium: shows Pod-to-Pod flows, DNS queries, HTTP calls and policy verdicts. hubble observe --namespace records --verdict DROPPED shows exactly which Pod tried to reach Postgres and was blocked. Dual-stack networkingKubernetes SIG Network (GA v1.23) · Concept · Current · Advanced Pods and Services receive both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses, chosen with ipFamilyPolicy and ipFamilies. A mobile operator's Service uses ipFamilyPolicy: PreferDualStack so IPv6-only handsets reach it natively.

docs.title: 8.7 Storage, ConfigMaps and Secrets
docs.text:
Containers lose their files when they restart, so Kubernetes attaches volumes. Persistent data uses a PersistentVolumeClaim (a request for storage) that a StorageClass fulfils by creating a real disk through a CSI driver. Settings and passwords are kept out of images in ConfigMaps and Secrets, which Pods read as environment variables or files.

Dynamic provisioning with CSI. WaitForFirstConsumer delays disk creation until the Pod is scheduled, so the disk lands in the Pod's zone.

Think of it like…

A PersistentVolumeClaim is like booking a storage locker by size and type; the StorageClass is the storage company's price list, the CSI driver is the van that delivers the actual locker, and ConfigMaps are the instruction sheet taped to the door.

Real-world example

Nadia deploys a WordPress site for the fictional Corner Café. MySQL runs in a StatefulSet with a 20 GiB claim on StorageClass gp3-encrypted, which the AWS EBS CSI driver turns into an encrypted EBS volume in the same zone as the Pod. Site settings live in a ConfigMap, the database password in a Secret, and a nightly VolumeSnapshot protects the data.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. An administrator (or the cloud) defines StorageClasses naming a CSI provisioner and parameters such as disk type and encryption.
  2. A developer creates a PersistentVolumeClaim asking for a size, access mode and StorageClass.
  3. The CSI driver's provisioner creates a disk and a matching PersistentVolume, which is bound to the claim.
  4. When a Pod using the claim is scheduled, the CSI driver attaches the disk to that node and mounts it into the container.
  5. ConfigMaps and Secrets are created separately and referenced by the Pod as env vars or mounted files.

Who uses it

Developers request storage and configuration; platform and storage engineers run CSI drivers, StorageClasses, backups and snapshot policies.

Key takeaway

Remember the chain PVC → StorageClass → CSI driver → PV, and that ReadWriteOnce means one node, not one Pod.

Going deeper

  • A CSI driver has a controller part (CreateVolume, ControllerPublishVolume, snapshots, resize) helped by sidecars such as external-provisioner and external-attacher, plus a node DaemonSet doing NodeStageVolume and NodePublishVolume mounts.
  • Access modes: ReadWriteOnce (one node), ReadOnlyMany, ReadWriteMany (needs shared storage such as NFS, CephFS or EFS) and ReadWriteOncePod (exactly one Pod, stable since v1.29).
  • Reclaim policy Delete removes the cloud disk with the PVC; Retain keeps it for manual recovery. Dynamic provisioning uses the class default, which is usually Delete.
  • VolumeAttributesClass, stable in v1.34, lets you change IOPS or throughput of a live volume; VolumeGroupSnapshot, stable in v1.36, takes crash-consistent snapshots across several PVCs at once.
  • ConfigMaps and Secrets are capped at 1 MiB each; mounted files update automatically (after the kubelet's sync delay) but environment variables and subPath mounts do not change until the Pod restarts.
  • Secrets are only base64-encoded in the API and stored unencrypted in etcd unless encryption at rest is configured; marking a ConfigMap or Secret immutable: true reduces API server watch load and accidental edits.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Using hostPath for application data: it ties the Pod to one node's disk and can expose the host filesystem. Use PVCs instead.
  • Assuming kubectl delete pvc keeps the disk: with reclaimPolicy Delete the cloud volume and its data are destroyed.
  • Believing base64 hides secrets: anyone who can read the Secret, or create a Pod that mounts it, can decode it in seconds.

docs.title: Try it: StorageClass, claim, config and secret consumed by one Pod
docs.text:
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata: {name: fast}
provisioner: ebs.csi.aws.com          # or your cluster's CSI driver
parameters: {type: gp3, encrypted: "true"}
volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer
allowVolumeExpansion: true
reclaimPolicy: Delete
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata: {name: data}
spec:
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
  storageClassName: fast
  resources: {requests: {storage: 20Gi}}
---
# kubectl create configmap site --from-literal=SITE_NAME='Corner Cafe'
# kubectl create secret generic db --from-literal=password='change-me'
# kubectl get secret db -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d   # encoding, NOT encryption
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: app}
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sh", "-c", "echo $SITE_NAME; ls /data; sleep 3600"]
    envFrom: [{configMapRef: {name: site}}]
    volumeMounts:
    - {name: data, mountPath: /data}
    - {name: creds, mountPath: /etc/creds, readOnly: true}
  volumes:
  - {name: data, persistentVolumeClaim: {claimName: data}}
  - {name: creds, secret: {secretName: db}}

docs.title: Key kernels, commands, tools, standards & concepts
docs.text: Name What it does Example Volumes and emptyDirKubernetes core/v1 · Concept · Current · Beginner A volume is storage mounted into a Pod; emptyDir is scratch space that lives exactly as long as the Pod. An image-resizer Pod writes temporary thumbnails to an emptyDir with medium: Memory for RAM-speed scratch space. hostPathKubernetes core/v1 · Concept · Current · Intermediate Mounts a file or directory from the node into the Pod; needed by some system agents but risky for normal apps. A log-collector DaemonSet mounts /var/log read-only via hostPath; restricted Pod Security forbids it for app teams. PersistentVolume (PV)Kubernetes core/v1 · Object · Current · Beginner Cluster-level object representing a real piece of storage — cloud disk, NFS share or local SSD — with capacity and access modes. kubectl get pv shows pvc-3f2a…, 20Gi, RWO, Bound to default/data, class fast. PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC)Kubernetes core/v1 · Object · Current · Beginner A namespaced request for storage of a size, access mode and class, which Pods reference by name. Pod spec volume persistentVolumeClaim: claimName: data mounts the 20 GiB disk at /var/lib/mysql. StorageClassKubernetes storage.k8s.io/v1 · Object · Current · Beginner Named storage profile giving the CSI provisioner, parameters, reclaim policy, binding mode and whether volumes can expand. Classes standard (HDD) and fast (gp3, 6000 IOPS) let teams choose cost versus speed per claim. Access modesKubernetes core/v1 (RWO, ROX, RWX, RWOP) · Concept · Current · Intermediate Declare how a volume may be mounted: read-write by one node, read-only by many, read-write by many, or by one Pod. A shared uploads folder for six web Pods on different nodes needs RWX storage such as Amazon EFS, not EBS. Container Storage Interface (CSI)CSI spec (Kubernetes, Mesos, Cloud Foundry communities) · Specification · Current · Intermediate Standard gRPC interface letting any storage vendor write one driver that Kubernetes uses for provisioning, attaching and snapshots. Installing the Azure Disk CSI driver lets PVCs with provisioner disk.csi.azure.com create managed disks. Dynamic provisioning and WaitForFirstConsumerKubernetes storage.k8s.io/v1 · Concept · Current · Intermediate PVCs automatically create volumes on demand; WaitForFirstConsumer waits for scheduling so the disk matches the Pod's zone. Without it, a disk created in zone a strands a Pod scheduled in zone b with a 'volume node affinity conflict'. VolumeSnapshotKubernetes snapshot.storage.k8s.io/v1 (GA v1.20) · Object · Current · Intermediate Point-in-time copy of a PVC through the CSI driver; new PVCs can be restored from a snapshot via dataSource. Before a schema migration, Nadia snapshots data, then restores it into PVC data-restore when the migration fails. Volume expansion and VolumeAttributesClassKubernetes storage (VAC stable v1.34) · Concept · Current · Advanced Grow a PVC by editing its size, and change performance attributes like IOPS through a VolumeAttributesClass without recreating it. Editing spec.resources.requests.storage from 20Gi to 50Gi grows the EBS volume and filesystem online. Rook-Ceph and LonghornRook (CNCF graduated), Longhorn (CNCF incubating, created by Rancher) · Software · Current · Advanced In-cluster storage systems that pool node disks into replicated block, file and object storage for bare-metal clusters. An on-prem lab runs Longhorn with three replicas per volume so a failed node loses no PVC data. ConfigMapKubernetes core/v1 · Object · Current · Beginner Stores non-secret configuration as key-value pairs or files, consumed as environment variables, command arguments or mounted files. Same image, different ConfigMaps: LOG_LEVEL=debug in staging and LOG_LEVEL=warn in production. SecretKubernetes core/v1 · Object · Current · Beginner Holds small sensitive values — passwords, tokens, TLS keys — base64-encoded and access-controlled separately from ConfigMaps. kubectl create secret tls web-tls --cert=tls.crt --key=tls.key gives the Gateway its HTTPS certificate. Secret typesKubernetes core/v1 · Concept · Current · Intermediate Built-in types such as Opaque, kubernetes.io/tls, kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson and basic-auth validate required keys. A dockerconfigjson Secret listed in imagePullSecrets lets Pods pull from a private Harbor registry. Immutable ConfigMaps and SecretsKubernetes core/v1 (GA v1.21) · Concept · Current · Intermediate Setting immutable: true blocks edits and lets kubelets stop watching the object, reducing API server load in big clusters. Teams publish app-config-v7 as immutable and roll out by pointing the Deployment at app-config-v8. Projected volumesKubernetes core/v1 · Concept · Current · Advanced Combine Secrets, ConfigMaps, Downward API data and short-lived ServiceAccount tokens into one mounted directory. A Pod mounts a projected volume with a token for audience vault plus a CA bundle, all under /var/run/creds.

docs.title: 8.8 Scheduling and Resource Management
docs.text:
Every container should say how much CPU and memory it needs (requests) and the most it may use (limits). The scheduler uses requests to place Pods on nodes with room, and rules such as affinity, taints and topology spread let you steer Pods towards or away from particular nodes, zones or each other.

One scheduling cycle. Filtering decides where a Pod can go; scoring decides where it should go.

Think of it like…

Scheduling is like seating guests at a wedding: each guest has a size of chair they need (requests), some must sit near family (affinity), some tables are reserved for VIPs only (taints), and you spread friends across tables so one spill does not ruin everyone's evening (topology spread).

Real-world example

Orbit Games runs game servers that need 4 CPUs and 8 GiB each. They taint their high-CPU node pool so only game servers tolerate it, spread replicas evenly across three zones, and give matchmaking a higher PriorityClass so that when the cluster is full, low-priority batch analytics Pods are preempted first.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. New Pods enter the scheduling queue, ordered by priority.
  2. Filter: nodes without enough unrequested CPU/memory, with untolerated taints, or failing affinity rules are removed.
  3. Score: remaining nodes are ranked, for example by spreading, image locality and balanced resource use.
  4. The Pod is bound to the best node; if none fit, a higher-priority Pod may preempt lower-priority ones.
  5. At run time the kubelet enforces limits through cgroups: CPU over limit is throttled, memory over limit is OOM-killed.

Who uses it

Developers set requests and limits; platform engineers design node pools, taints, quotas and priorities to balance cost, reliability and fairness.

Key takeaway

The scheduler places Pods by requests, not real usage; a Pod with no requests can land on an overloaded node, so always set them.

Going deeper

  • CPU is measured in cores (1 = one vCPU, 250m = a quarter); memory in bytes with binary suffixes (Mi, Gi). CPU limits use the CFS quota over 100 ms periods, so a busy Pod is throttled rather than killed.
  • QoS class is derived automatically: Guaranteed (requests = limits for every container's CPU and memory), Burstable (some requests), BestEffort (none); under node memory pressure BestEffort Pods are evicted first.
  • Node allocatable = capacity minus kube-reserved, system-reserved and the hard eviction threshold (memory.available<100Mi by default), so a 16 GiB node never offers all 16 GiB to Pods.
  • Built-in PriorityClasses system-cluster-critical (2,000,000,000) and system-node-critical (2,000,001,000) protect DNS, CNI and other core add-ons; user classes can go up to 1,000,000,000.
  • The scheduling framework exposes extension points (PreFilter, Filter, Score, Reserve, Permit, Bind); v1.36-v1.37 added workload-aware and gang scheduling so groups of Pods can be placed all-or-nothing.
  • Taint effects are NoSchedule, PreferNoSchedule and NoExecute; NoExecute also evicts running Pods that lack a matching toleration, optionally after tolerationSeconds.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Setting memory limits far above requests across many Pods: the node is overcommitted and the kernel OOM-kills containers when they all get busy.
  • Using taints alone to dedicate nodes: a taint keeps other Pods off but does not pull your Pods on; combine it with a nodeSelector or affinity.
  • Copying 'required' anti-affinity onto large Deployments: with more replicas than nodes, extra Pods stay Pending forever. Prefer topology spread or 'preferred' rules.

docs.title: Try it: Requests/limits, a toleration, zone spreading and anti-affinity in one Deployment
docs.text:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: {name: game}
spec:
  replicas: 6
  selector: {matchLabels: {app: game}}
  template:
    metadata: {labels: {app: game}}
    spec:
      priorityClassName: high-priority      # create the PriorityClass first
      tolerations:
      - {key: dedicated, operator: Equal, value: game, effect: NoSchedule}
      nodeSelector: {pool: high-cpu}
      topologySpreadConstraints:
      - maxSkew: 1
        topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
        whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
        labelSelector: {matchLabels: {app: game}}
      affinity:
        podAntiAffinity:
          preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
          - weight: 100
            podAffinityTerm:
              topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
              labelSelector: {matchLabels: {app: game}}
      containers:
      - name: server
        image: nginx:1.27
        resources:
          requests: {cpu: "4", memory: 8Gi}
          limits:   {memory: 8Gi}            # memory limit = request
# kubectl taint nodes node-7 dedicated=game:NoSchedule
# kubectl describe node node-7 | grep -A8 'Allocated resources'

docs.title: Key kernels, commands, tools, standards & concepts
docs.text: Name What it does Example Resource requestsKubernetes core/v1 ResourceRequirements · Concept · Current · Beginner Guaranteed minimum CPU and memory a container asks for; the scheduler sums requests to decide whether a node has room. Three Pods requesting 1 CPU each fit on a 4-CPU node with 3.5 allocatable; a fourth waits Pending. Resource limitsKubernetes core/v1 ResourceRequirements · Concept · Current · Beginner Upper bounds enforced by cgroups: exceeding the CPU limit throttles; exceeding the memory limit gets the container OOM-killed. A leaky service with limits.memory: 512Mi restarts with Last State: OOMKilled, exit code 137. QoS classesKubernetes SIG Node · Concept · Current · Intermediate Guaranteed, Burstable or BestEffort, assigned from requests and limits; decides eviction order and kernel OOM priority. The payments Pod sets requests equal to limits, earning Guaranteed QoS so it is evicted last under pressure. LimitRangeKubernetes core/v1 · Object · Current · Intermediate Per-namespace defaults and minimum or maximum values for container requests and limits. A LimitRange gives every container without settings a default request of 100m CPU and 128Mi memory. ResourceQuotaKubernetes core/v1 · Object · Current · Intermediate Caps the total CPU, memory, storage and object counts a namespace may consume. Team search's namespace is capped at requests.cpu: 40, 100 Pods and services.loadbalancers: 2, enforced at admission. nodeSelector and node affinityKubernetes core/v1 · Concept · Current · Beginner Constrain Pods to nodes with certain labels; affinity adds required versus preferred rules and richer operators. nodeAffinity requiring kubernetes.io/arch In [arm64] lands the service on cheaper Graviton nodes. Pod affinity and anti-affinityKubernetes core/v1 · Concept · Current · Intermediate Place Pods near or away from other Pods matching a selector within a topology such as a node or zone. Anti-affinity on kubernetes.io/hostname keeps the three Redis replicas on three different nodes. Taints and tolerationsKubernetes core/v1 · Concept · Current · Intermediate Taints on nodes repel Pods; only Pods with a matching toleration may schedule there (or keep running, for NoExecute). GPU nodes carry nvidia.com/gpu=present:NoSchedule so ordinary web Pods never occupy expensive GPU machines. Topology spread constraintsKubernetes core/v1 (GA v1.19) · Concept · Current · Intermediate Spread replicas evenly across zones, nodes or other topology domains, limited by a maximum allowed skew. maxSkew: 1 across three zones places six replicas as 2-2-2, so losing one zone removes only a third. PriorityClass and preemptionKubernetes scheduling.k8s.io/v1 · Object · Current · Intermediate Gives Pods an integer priority; when resources are short, the scheduler may evict lower-priority Pods to fit higher ones. Checkout runs at priority 100000 and nightly reports at 1000, so reports are preempted during a Black Friday spike. Node-pressure evictionKubernetes SIG Node (kubelet) · Concept · Current · Intermediate The kubelet evicts Pods when node memory, disk or PIDs fall below thresholds, starting with those exceeding their requests. When nodefs.available drops below 10%, the kubelet evicts BestEffort Pods filling the disk with logs. kube-scheduler framework and profilesKubernetes SIG Scheduling · Concept · Current · Advanced Plugin-based scheduler design; profiles let one scheduler binary run differently configured schedulers by name. A profile with NodeResourcesFit set to MostAllocated packs batch Pods tightly to free whole nodes for scale-down. DeschedulerKubernetes SIG Scheduling (kubernetes-sigs) · Tool · Current · Advanced Add-on that evicts Pods breaking current policies, such as spread or affinity, so the scheduler can place them better. After a zone recovers, the descheduler rebalances Pods that had piled into the two healthy zones. Allocatable and system reservationsKubernetes SIG Node (kubelet config) · Concept · Current · Advanced Node capacity minus resources reserved for the OS, kubelet and eviction headroom; the scheduler only offers allocatable. kubectl describe node shows capacity 8 CPUs but allocatable 7.91, because kube-reserved and system-reserved are set.

docs.title: 8.9 Autoscaling Pods and Nodes
docs.text:
Kubernetes can grow and shrink applications automatically. The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler adds or removes Pod replicas based on metrics, the Vertical Pod Autoscaler adjusts how much CPU and memory each Pod gets, and node autoscalers such as Cluster Autoscaler and Karpenter add or remove machines so the Pods have somewhere to run. KEDA scales on events like queue length, even down to zero.

A traffic spike, end to end. Pod autoscaling and node autoscaling are separate loops that cooperate through Pending Pods.

Think of it like…

Autoscaling is like a supermarket opening more tills when queues grow (HPA), giving a slow cashier a faster scanner (VPA), and calling in extra staff from home when every till is busy (node autoscaling).

Real-world example

Fern & Finch, a fictional online florist, sees traffic jump tenfold on Valentine's morning. The HPA scales the shop from 4 to 40 Pods at 70% CPU; 20 of the new Pods stay Pending, so Karpenter launches five larger spot instances within about a minute. At midnight, KEDA scales the order-email worker to zero once the queue is empty, and Karpenter consolidates nodes to cut cost.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. metrics-server (or a Prometheus adapter) exposes Pod metrics through the Kubernetes metrics APIs.
  2. The HPA controller checks every 15 seconds and computes desired replicas from current versus target metric.
  3. It updates the Deployment's replica count; new Pods that do not fit stay Pending.
  4. Cluster Autoscaler or Karpenter sees Pending Pods and adds nodes; later it removes empty or underused nodes.
  5. VPA, run separately, recommends or applies better requests so each Pod is sized correctly.

Who uses it

SREs and platform engineers tune autoscaling for reliability and cloud cost; FinOps teams rely on it to avoid paying for idle capacity.

Key takeaway

HPA utilisation targets are percentages of requests, so an HPA on CPU does nothing useful unless the Pods have CPU requests.

Going deeper

  • The HPA formula is desiredReplicas = ceil(currentReplicas × currentMetric / targetMetric); a default 10% tolerance prevents flapping, and v1.37 made that tolerance configurable per HPA as a stable feature.
  • Scale-up reacts immediately while scale-down uses a 300-second stabilisation window by default; behavior policies can cap change rates, for example at most 20% of Pods removed per minute.
  • HPA scale-to-zero for Object and External metrics arrived as alpha in v1.36 and became beta, enabled by default, in v1.37; before that, KEDA was the usual way to reach zero replicas.
  • Cluster Autoscaler works on predefined node groups (for example AWS Auto Scaling groups); Karpenter, now a kubernetes-sigs project at v1, chooses instance types per batch of Pending Pods and consolidates underused nodes.
  • VPA has update modes Off (recommend only), Initial, Recreate and InPlaceOrRecreate, which uses in-place Pod resize; never let VPA and HPA both act on the same CPU or memory metric.
  • KEDA (CNCF graduated) offers dozens of scalers — Kafka lag, SQS depth, Prometheus queries, cron — and handles 0↔1 activation while driving an HPA for 1↔N.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Scaling on CPU for an I/O-bound or queue-driven service: CPU stays low while users wait. Scale on request rate, latency or queue length instead.
  • Setting maxReplicas without capacity behind it: the HPA asks for 40 Pods, but node quotas or cloud limits leave half Pending.
  • Forgetting PodDisruptionBudgets and safe-to-evict settings, so node consolidation interrupts long-running jobs or drops a quorum.

docs.title: Try it: An autoscaling/v2 HPA with a gentle scale-down policy
docs.text:
# quick version: kubectl autoscale deploy shop --cpu-percent=70 --min=4 --max=40
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata: {name: shop}
spec:
  scaleTargetRef: {apiVersion: apps/v1, kind: Deployment, name: shop}
  minReplicas: 4
  maxReplicas: 40
  metrics:
  - type: Resource
    resource:
      name: cpu
      target: {type: Utilization, averageUtilization: 70}
  behavior:
    scaleDown:
      stabilizationWindowSeconds: 300      # wait 5 min before shrinking
      policies: [{type: Percent, value: 20, periodSeconds: 60}]
# kubectl get hpa shop -w
# kubectl describe hpa shop    # shows events and current metrics

docs.title: Key kernels, commands, tools, standards & concepts
docs.text: Name What it does Example HorizontalPodAutoscaler (HPA)Kubernetes autoscaling/v2 · Object · Current · Beginner Controller that changes a workload's replica count to keep a metric — CPU, memory, custom or external — near a target. An HPA keeps average CPU at 70% of requests, scaling the API between 4 and 40 replicas. Resource, custom and external metrics APIsKubernetes metrics.k8s.io, custom.metrics.k8s.io, external.metrics.k8s.io · API · Current · Advanced Aggregated APIs the HPA reads: Pod CPU/memory, per-object app metrics, and metrics from outside the cluster. Prometheus Adapter publishes http_requests_per_second so the HPA targets 100 requests per second per Pod. HPA behavior policiesKubernetes autoscaling/v2 · Concept · Current · Intermediate Per-direction rules — stabilisation windows, percent or Pod-count policies — that control how fast scaling happens. scaleUp allows doubling every 15 s for flash sales; scaleDown removes at most 10% per minute to stay safe. HPA scale to zeroKEP-2021 (HPAScaleToZero; beta, on by default, v1.37) · Concept · Emerging · Advanced Lets minReplicas be 0 when scaling on Object or External metrics, so idle workloads use no Pods at all. A PDF-export worker scales to zero overnight and back to two Pods when the external queue metric rises above zero. Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA)Kubernetes SIG Autoscaling (kubernetes/autoscaler) · Software · Current · Intermediate Watches real usage and recommends or applies right-sized CPU and memory requests for each container. VPA in Off mode shows the API requests 2 CPUs but uses 300m, so the team cuts requests and frees four nodes. Cluster AutoscalerKubernetes SIG Autoscaling · Software · Current · Intermediate Adds nodes to node groups when Pods are Pending for lack of room and removes nodes that stay underused. On AKS, enabling the cluster autoscaler with min 3 and max 20 nodes lets the node pool follow demand. Karpenterkubernetes-sigs (created by AWS; v1.0 in 2024) · Software · Current · Intermediate Node autoscaler that launches right-sized instances directly for Pending Pods and continuously consolidates to cut cost. A NodePool allowing spot c7g and m7g instances lets Karpenter pick the cheapest type fitting 12 Pending Pods. Karpenter NodePool and NodeClaimKarpenter karpenter.sh/v1 CRDs · Object · Current · Advanced NodePool sets constraints and limits on nodes Karpenter may create; NodeClaim represents each node it requests. NodePool limits cpu: 1000 and expireAfter: 720h, so nodes are refreshed every 30 days for patching. KEDACNCF graduated project (created by Microsoft and Red Hat) · Software · Current · Intermediate Event-driven autoscaler that scales workloads, including to zero, from sources like Kafka, RabbitMQ, SQS, cron or Prometheus. A ScaledObject runs one consumer per 50 Kafka messages of lag, from 0 up to 30 Pods. ScaledObject and ScaledJobKEDA keda.sh/v1alpha1 CRDs · Object · Current · Advanced KEDA resources linking a Deployment or Job template to triggers, thresholds and minimum or maximum replicas. A ScaledJob starts one video-transcode Job per message waiting in the queue. Node consolidation and disruption budgetsKarpenter / Cluster Autoscaler · Concept · Current · Advanced Removing or replacing underused nodes to save money, limited by PDBs and node-disruption budgets. Karpenter replaces three half-empty m7i.2xlarge nodes with one m7i.4xlarge, honouring each app's PDB. Overprovisioning with placeholder PodsKubernetes autoscaling pattern · Concept · Current · Advanced Low-priority 'pause' Pods reserve headroom; real Pods preempt them instantly while new nodes boot in the background. Two spare nodes' worth of placeholder Pods hide the 60-90 s node start time during sudden spikes. A large 400-Pod service sets a 5% tolerance on scaleUp so it reacts sooner to traffic growth.

docs.title: 8.10 Cluster Security: RBAC, Pod Security, Admission and Secrets
docs.text:
Kubernetes security has layers. RBAC decides who may do what through the API. Pod Security Standards and security contexts limit what containers may do on the node. Admission policies (built-in CEL policies, OPA Gatekeeper or Kyverno) reject or fix risky objects before they are stored. Secrets need encryption at rest and, ideally, an external secrets manager.

Every API write passes these gates. Mutation happens before validation, so validators see the final object.

Think of it like…

Cluster security is like an office building: ID badges prove who you are (authentication), badge rules decide which floors you can enter (RBAC), the safety inspector refuses dangerous equipment at the loading dock (admission control), and valuables go in a bank vault rather than a desk drawer (external secret managers).

Real-world example

Northwind Insurance gives developers edit rights only in their own namespaces, and CI uses a ServiceAccount that can update Deployments in one namespace only. Every application namespace enforces the restricted Pod Security Standard. A Kyverno policy blocks images not signed by the build pipeline, and database passwords are synced from HashiCorp Vault by the External Secrets Operator rather than stored in Git.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Authentication: the API server identifies the caller from a client certificate, an OIDC token or a ServiceAccount token.
  2. Authorisation: RBAC (plus the Node authoriser for kubelets) checks whether that identity may perform the verb on the resource.
  3. Mutating admission: webhooks or MutatingAdmissionPolicies may add defaults such as labels or sidecars.
  4. Validating admission: Pod Security Admission, ValidatingAdmissionPolicies, Gatekeeper or Kyverno can reject the object.
  5. The object is stored; at run time securityContext settings, seccomp, user namespaces and NetworkPolicies limit what Pods can do.

Who uses it

Platform security engineers, DevSecOps teams and cluster administrators design these controls; auditors check them against CIS and NSA/CISA guidance; the CKS exam tests them hands-on.

Key takeaway

RBAC is allow-only — there are no deny rules — so least privilege means granting the narrowest verbs and resources, and checking with kubectl auth can-i.

Going deeper

  • Kubernetes has no User object: humans are identified by certificates or OIDC tokens from an identity provider; members of the group system:masters bypass RBAC entirely, so never issue such certificates for daily use.
  • Since v1.24 ServiceAccounts no longer get long-lived token Secrets automatically; Pods receive projected, audience-bound tokens that expire (one hour by default) and are rotated by the kubelet.
  • Pod Security Admission (stable v1.25, the year PodSecurityPolicy was removed) applies privileged, baseline or restricted levels per namespace in enforce, audit or warn mode, optionally pinned to a version.
  • ValidatingAdmissionPolicy (stable v1.30) and MutatingAdmissionPolicy (stable v1.36) run CEL expressions inside the API server — no webhook network hop — while webhooks default to a 10-second timeout and a failurePolicy of Fail.
  • Encryption at rest is set with an EncryptionConfiguration; the KMS v2 provider (stable v1.29) wraps data keys with a key in a cloud KMS or HSM, so an etcd backup alone cannot reveal Secrets.
  • User namespaces in Pods (hostUsers: false) became stable in v1.36: root inside the container maps to an unprivileged UID on the host, blunting many container-escape vulnerabilities.
  • Enable API audit logging with a policy that records metadata for Secrets (never request bodies) and full requests for RBAC changes; audit trails are key evidence after an incident.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Binding cluster-admin to CI pipelines or default ServiceAccounts 'to make it work': one leaked token then owns the whole cluster.
  • Granting 'create pods' and assuming Secrets are safe: anyone who can create a Pod in a namespace can mount and read every Secret there.
  • Forgetting that RBAC verbs like escalate, bind, impersonate and wildcard '*' resources allow privilege escalation; review them first in audits.

docs.title: Try it: Least-privilege CI identity, verified with auth can-i, plus restricted Pod Security
docs.text:
kubectl create namespace shop
kubectl label namespace shop pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version=latest
kubectl create serviceaccount deployer -n shop
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata: {name: deploy-updater, namespace: shop}
rules:
- apiGroups: ["apps"]
  resources: ["deployments"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch", "patch", "update"]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata: {name: deployer-can-update, namespace: shop}
subjects: [{kind: ServiceAccount, name: deployer, namespace: shop}]
roleRef: {apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io, kind: Role, name: deploy-updater}
---
# kubectl auth can-i patch deployments -n shop --as=system:serviceaccount:shop:deployer  # yes
# kubectl auth can-i get secrets -n shop --as=system:serviceaccount:shop:deployer        # no
# kubectl run bad -n shop --image=nginx --privileged   # rejected by Pod Security

docs.title: 8.11 Extending Kubernetes: CRDs, Controllers and Operators
docs.text:
Kubernetes can learn new object types. A CustomResourceDefinition (CRD) adds a new kind — say, PostgresCluster or Certificate — to the API, and a controller that you or a vendor writes watches those objects and does the work. A controller that encodes the expert knowledge needed to run a complex application is called an operator.

Inside a controller. Informers cache objects locally; the work queue ensures each object is reconciled by key, idempotently.

Think of it like…

A CRD is like adding a new form to a government office's set of official forms; the operator is the trained clerk who knows exactly what to do whenever that form is filed — including the tricky cases.

Real-world example

Tara's team needs PostgreSQL with automatic failover and backups. They install the CloudNativePG operator, then create a 12-line Cluster object asking for three instances and daily backups to object storage. The operator creates the Pods, Services and PVCs, promotes a replica within seconds when the primary's node fails, and reports progress in the object's status.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Apply a CRD defining the new kind's group, versions, OpenAPI schema and scope.
  2. The API server now serves the new resource: kubectl get, RBAC, watch and admission all work as for built-in kinds.
  3. Deploy a controller (usually as a Deployment with a ServiceAccount) that watches the custom resources.
  4. Its reconcile function compares each object's spec with reality and creates or updates the needed Pods, Services or cloud resources.
  5. It writes progress into status.conditions and uses finalizers to clean up external resources on deletion.

Who uses it

Platform engineers build internal APIs with CRDs; vendors ship operators for databases, messaging and monitoring; Go developers write controllers with Kubebuilder or Operator SDK.

Key takeaway

An operator is not magic — it is just a controller with domain knowledge. Interviewers like the answer 'CRD = the API, controller = the behaviour'.

Going deeper

  • apiextensions.k8s.io/v1 CRDs require a structural OpenAPI v3 schema; unknown fields are pruned, and x-kubernetes-validations rules written in CEL (stable since v1.29) enforce cross-field checks inside the API server.
  • A CRD can serve several versions but stores one; a conversion webhook translates between them, and the StorageVersionMigration API, moved in-tree and stable in v1.37, rewrites stored objects to the new version.
  • Reconcile functions must be idempotent and level-based: they may run many times for one change, after restarts, or on periodic resyncs, and must converge to the same result.
  • Owner references on child objects give automatic garbage collection; finalizers such as backup.lab.example.com/cleanup keep a parent from disappearing until external resources (buckets, DNS records) are removed.
  • The Operator Framework describes five capability levels: basic install, seamless upgrades, full lifecycle (backup, recovery), deep insights (metrics, alerts) and auto pilot (auto-scaling, auto-tuning).
  • The API aggregation layer is the heavier alternative to CRDs: you run your own API server registered by an APIService, as metrics-server does for metrics.k8s.io.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Storing large or fast-changing data in custom resources: every object lives in etcd (1.5 MiB limit) and floods watchers. Keep CRDs small and declarative.
  • Writing edge-triggered logic ('on create, do X once'): missed events or restarts then leave work undone. Always reconcile full desired state.
  • Deleting a CRD casually: it deletes every custom resource of that kind in the cluster, and operators may then delete real databases.

docs.title: Try it: Define a tiny CRD with schema and CEL validation, then use it like a built-in kind
docs.text:
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata: {name: backups.lab.example.com}
spec:
  group: lab.example.com
  scope: Namespaced
  names: {plural: backups, singular: backup, kind: Backup, shortNames: [bk]}
  versions:
  - name: v1
    served: true
    storage: true
    subresources: {status: {}}
    additionalPrinterColumns:
    - {name: Schedule, type: string, jsonPath: .spec.schedule}
    schema:
      openAPIV3Schema:
        type: object
        properties:
          spec:
            type: object
            required: [schedule, retainDays]
            properties:
              schedule:   {type: string}
              retainDays: {type: integer}
            x-kubernetes-validations:
            - rule: "self.retainDays >= 1 && self.retainDays <= 365"
              message: retainDays must be 1-365
---
apiVersion: lab.example.com/v1
kind: Backup
metadata: {name: nightly}
spec: {schedule: "0 1 * * *", retainDays: 30}
# kubectl get bk ; kubectl explain backup.spec ; kubectl api-resources | grep lab

docs.title: 8.12 Packaging and GitOps: Helm, Kustomize, Argo CD and Flux
docs.text:
Real applications need dozens of YAML files that differ slightly between development, staging and production. Helm packages them into reusable, versioned charts with settings; Kustomize patches plain YAML for each environment. GitOps tools such as Argo CD and Flux then keep the cluster in sync with what is in Git, so Git becomes the single source of truth.

A GitOps change from pull request to cluster. Nobody runs kubectl against production; the agent pulls from Git and repairs drift.

Think of it like…

Helm is a recipe with blanks for quantities, Kustomize is a printed recipe with sticky-note edits per kitchen, and GitOps is a head chef who checks every few minutes that each kitchen is cooking exactly what the master recipe book says.

Real-world example

Quill Media runs 30 microservices in three environments. Each service has a Helm chart; environment differences live in values files in a Git repository. Argo CD watches the repo: a merged pull request changing image.tag to 3.8.1 rolls out to staging within minutes, and when someone hand-edits production, Argo CD flags the drift and self-heals it back.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Package manifests as a Helm chart (templates + values) or as a Kustomize base with per-environment overlays.
  2. Store the desired state for every environment in Git; changes go through pull requests and review.
  3. A GitOps agent inside the cluster (Argo CD or Flux) pulls the repo, renders Helm or Kustomize, and compares it with live objects.
  4. It applies differences, waits for health checks, and reports Synced/Healthy or the exact drift.
  5. Rollback is a git revert; progressive delivery tools can shift traffic gradually and abort on bad metrics.

Who uses it

DevOps and platform engineers build the pipelines; developers change apps by pull request; auditors like GitOps because every change is reviewed and recorded in Git.

Key takeaway

Know the four OpenGitOps principles — declarative, versioned and immutable, pulled automatically, continuously reconciled — and that 'pull' means credentials stay inside the cluster.

Going deeper

  • Helm 4.0 shipped in November 2025, the first major version in six years; Helm 3's final feature release (3.22) came in September 2026 and its security fixes are scheduled to end on 10 February 2027.
  • Helm stores each release revision as a Secret (sh.helm.release.v1.<name>.v<N>) in the release's namespace, which is how helm history and helm rollback work without any server component.
  • Charts can be pushed to and pulled from OCI registries (helm push shop-1.2.0.tgz oci://registry.example/charts), so the same registry and signing tools serve both images and charts.
  • Kustomize has been built into kubectl since v1.14 (kubectl apply -k); it never uses templates, only overlays, patches, generators and transformers on valid YAML.
  • Argo CD checks Git every three minutes by default (or immediately on a webhook) and models apps as Application objects; ApplicationSets generate many Applications from lists, clusters or Git folders.
  • Flux is a set of controllers (source, kustomize, helm, notification, image automation) using CRDs such as GitRepository, OCIRepository, Kustomization and HelmRelease; Argo and Flux both graduated in the CNCF in 2022.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Putting plain Secrets in Git: base64 is not encryption. Use Sealed Secrets, SOPS or an External Secrets Operator reference instead.
  • Pinning charts or images to 'latest': GitOps then cannot tell what changed and rollbacks are impossible. Pin versions and image digests.
  • Relying on free Bitnami images without checking: many moved to an unmaintained legacy repository in 2025, so charts may pull stale, unpatched images.

docs.title: Try it: Helm and Kustomize side by side
docs.text:
# Helm: scaffold, render, install, upgrade, roll back
helm create shop && helm lint shop
helm template shop ./shop --set image.tag=1.27 | less
helm install shop ./shop -n shop --create-namespace
helm upgrade shop ./shop -n shop --set replicaCount=3
helm history shop -n shop && helm rollback shop 1 -n shop

# Kustomize: overlays/prod/kustomization.yaml
#   apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
#   kind: Kustomization
#   resources: [../../base]
#   namespace: shop-prod
#   images: [{name: shop, newTag: 3.8.1}]
#   patches: [{path: replicas.yaml}]
kubectl kustomize overlays/prod      # preview
kubectl apply -k overlays/prod       # apply
kubectl diff -k overlays/prod        # what would change?

A team finds its Redis chart pulling an outdated bitnamilegacy image, so it switches to a maintained image source.

docs.title: 8.13 Observability and Service Mesh
docs.text:
Observability means being able to tell what your cluster and apps are doing from the outside: metrics (numbers over time), logs (text events) and traces (the path of one request through many services). A service mesh adds a layer that encrypts and observes traffic between services and controls retries, timeouts and traffic splits, without changing application code.

A typical Kubernetes observability stack. Data flows upward: sources emit, collectors gather, stores keep, dashboards and alerts explain.

Think of it like…

Observability is a car's dashboard, trip log and dash-cam together; a service mesh is a city's managed road network with traffic lights, speed cameras and armoured lanes between every building.

Real-world example

At Harbour Ticketing, checkout latency spikes every evening. Grafana dashboards from Prometheus show the payment service at 95% CPU; an OpenTelemetry trace reveals 600 ms spent in a fraud-check call; Loki logs show retries timing out. Istio ambient mode already encrypts all service-to-service traffic with mTLS and its metrics confirm the fraud service's error rate is 4%.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. metrics-server feeds kubectl top and autoscalers; kube-state-metrics turns object state into metrics for Prometheus.
  2. Prometheus scrapes /metrics endpoints from apps, kubelets and exporters every 15-60 seconds and evaluates alert rules.
  3. A node-level agent (Fluent Bit or the OpenTelemetry Collector) ships container logs to a store such as Loki or Elasticsearch.
  4. Instrumented apps send traces via OTLP to a Collector and on to Jaeger or Tempo.
  5. A mesh (Istio, Linkerd, Cilium) adds mTLS identity, golden-signal metrics and traffic policy for every service call.

Who uses it

SREs, platform engineers and on-call developers live in these tools; observability and mesh skills are core to SRE and platform-engineering job descriptions.

Key takeaway

Know the difference: metrics tell you something is wrong, traces tell you where, and logs tell you why.

Going deeper

  • metrics-server keeps only the latest CPU and memory samples in memory (no history) for the metrics.k8s.io API, whose definition became stable in v1.37; use Prometheus for history and alerting.
  • Prometheus pulls metrics over HTTP in a text format and stores time series locally; Prometheus 3.0 (November 2024) added a new UI, native OTLP ingestion and UTF-8 metric names. Kubernetes' own native-histogram metrics reached beta in v1.37.
  • Container logs written to stdout and stderr land in /var/log/pods on the node, rotated by the kubelet (containerLogMaxSize defaults to 10 Mi); anything not shipped elsewhere disappears with the Pod or node.
  • OpenTelemetry (CNCF) standardises APIs, SDKs and the OTLP protocol for traces, metrics and logs; its Collector receives, processes and exports data to almost any backend, avoiding vendor lock-in.
  • Istio's ambient mode, generally available since Istio 1.24 (November 2024), replaces per-Pod sidecars with a per-node ztunnel for L4 mTLS plus optional waypoint proxies for L7, cutting memory use sharply.
  • Meshes give each workload a SPIFFE identity (spiffe://cluster.local/ns/shop/sa/api) in a short-lived X.509 certificate, enabling mutual TLS and identity-based authorisation policies between services.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Using high-cardinality labels such as user IDs or request IDs on Prometheus metrics: series counts explode and Prometheus runs out of memory.
  • Relying on kubectl logs for incident forensics: logs vanish when Pods are deleted or nodes are replaced. Ship logs centrally.
  • Adding a service mesh before you need it: it is another critical system to upgrade and debug. Start with clear needs such as mTLS or traffic splitting.

docs.title: Try it: First-look commands, then install a monitoring stack on a lab cluster
docs.text:
kubectl top nodes && kubectl top pods -A --sort-by=memory   # needs metrics-server
kubectl get events -A --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | tail -20
kubectl logs deploy/web --since=10m -f
kubectl logs pod/web-7d9f --previous           # the crashed container's logs

helm repo add prometheus-community https://prometheus-community.github.io/helm-charts
helm install mon prometheus-community/kube-prometheus-stack -n monitoring --create-namespace
kubectl -n monitoring port-forward svc/mon-grafana 3000:80    # open http://localhost:3000

docs.title: 8.14 AI and GPU Workloads on Kubernetes
docs.text:
Kubernetes has become a common platform for training and serving AI models. GPUs and other accelerators are made visible to the scheduler through device plugins or the newer Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) API, and add-ons such as Kueue, JobSet and LeaderWorkerSet manage queues of expensive training jobs and multi-node inference servers.

Layers of an AI platform on Kubernetes. Each layer is a separate open-source project; the Kubernetes core supplies scheduling and DRA.

Think of it like…

Running AI on Kubernetes is like running a film studio's sound stages: there are only a few expensive stages (GPUs), so a booking office (Kueue) queues productions fairly, a whole crew must be booked together or not at all (gang scheduling), and each stage's equipment list (DRA) says exactly what is inside.

Real-world example

Lyra Labs, a fictional AI start-up, owns 64 H100 GPUs on 8 nodes. Kueue gives research a guaranteed 32 GPUs that can borrow idle production quota at night. A 4-node training run is a JobSet that starts only when all 32 GPUs are free. Their chatbot serves a large model with LeaderWorkerSet groups of two nodes each, behind a Gateway API inference extension that routes by model.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The NVIDIA GPU Operator (or a cloud's managed setup) installs drivers, the container toolkit and the device plugin or DRA driver on GPU nodes.
  2. Nodes advertise accelerators: as a count such as nvidia.com/gpu: 8 (device plugin) or as detailed ResourceSlices (DRA).
  3. Pods request GPUs through resource limits or a ResourceClaim, often with tolerations for tainted GPU nodes.
  4. Batch jobs are submitted to a Kueue LocalQueue, which admits them when quota is free and supports gang admission.
  5. Inference servers (vLLM, KServe) scale with HPA or KEDA on queue depth and are exposed through a Gateway.

Who uses it

ML platform engineers, MLOps engineers and AI infrastructure teams at labs, clouds and enterprises build these platforms; GPU efficiency is one of the hottest Kubernetes skills in 2026.

Key takeaway

Know both paths: the device plugin gives whole GPUs as an opaque count, while DRA (stable since v1.34) lets Pods claim devices by attributes, share them and describe topology.

Going deeper

  • Device plugins (introduced in v1.8, stable since v1.26) register extended resources over a gRPC socket with the kubelet; they can only count identical devices, so GPU sharing and attribute matching need workarounds.
  • Dynamic Resource Allocation reached GA in v1.34 with the resource.k8s.io/v1 API: drivers publish ResourceSlices, admins define DeviceClasses, and Pods use ResourceClaims selected with CEL over device attributes.
  • DRA kept growing: v1.36 made prioritised alternatives and admin access stable, and v1.37 made device taints and tolerations, a standard numaNode attribute and extended-resource requests via DRA drivers stable.
  • Gang scheduling and workload-aware scheduling arrived as alpha in v1.36 and moved to beta in v1.37, so a group of Pods is scheduled all-or-nothing instead of deadlocking with half a job placed.
  • NVIDIA GPUs can be shared through Multi-Instance GPU (MIG: up to seven hardware-isolated slices on A100/H100-class GPUs), time-slicing, or MPS; the GPU Operator configures these per node.
  • The CNCF launched the Certified Kubernetes AI Conformance programme on 11 November 2025, defining a tested baseline of capabilities that platforms must offer so AI and ML frameworks run portably; a v2.0 roadmap followed.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Letting an ordinary Pod land on a GPU node and block it: taint GPU nodes and give only GPU workloads the toleration.
  • Starting distributed training Pods one by one: half a job holds GPUs while waiting forever. Use Kueue or gang scheduling for all-or-nothing admission.
  • Assuming a GPU limit means a share: with the device plugin, nvidia.com/gpu: 1 is a whole physical GPU unless MIG or time-slicing is configured.

docs.title: Try it: Requesting a GPU: classic device plugin vs Dynamic Resource Allocation
docs.text:
# 1) Device plugin style (whole GPU, counted resource)
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: cuda-test}
spec:
  restartPolicy: Never
  tolerations: [{key: nvidia.com/gpu, operator: Exists, effect: NoSchedule}]
  containers:
  - name: cuda
    image: nvcr.io/nvidia/cuda:12.4.1-base-ubuntu22.04
    command: ["nvidia-smi"]
    resources: {limits: {nvidia.com/gpu: 1}}
---
# 2) DRA style (resource.k8s.io/v1): claim a device from a DeviceClass
apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1
kind: ResourceClaimTemplate
metadata: {name: one-gpu}
spec:
  spec:
    devices:
      requests:
      - name: gpu
        exactly: {deviceClassName: gpu.nvidia.com}
# Pod spec then uses:
#   resourceClaims: [{name: gpu, resourceClaimTemplateName: one-gpu}]
#   containers[].resources.claims: [{name: gpu}]
# kubectl get deviceclasses,resourceslices

docs.title: 8.15 Distributions, Managed Services and the Release Cycle
docs.text:
You can run upstream Kubernetes yourself, use a distribution that packages it (OpenShift, RKE2, k3s, Talos), or rent a managed service where the cloud runs the control plane (EKS, AKS, GKE). Whatever you choose, Kubernetes ships three minor versions a year and each is supported for about 14 months, so upgrading is a routine, never-ending job.

Kubernetes minor releases, 2025-2026. Three releases a year; v1.38 is expected around December 2026.

Think of it like…

Kubernetes is like a car engine: you can build the car yourself, buy a complete model from a manufacturer (a distribution), or lease one with servicing included (a managed service) — and every few months the engine gets a new model year you must move to before support runs out.

Real-world example

In October 2026, Pinewood Retail's EKS clusters run v1.34, whose upstream end of life is 27 October 2026. The platform team reads the v1.35 deprecation notes, fixes two Helm charts still relying on cgroup v1 nodes, upgrades staging first, then production one minor version at a time — 1.35, then 1.36 — with node groups replaced after each control-plane step.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Track the upstream schedule: a new minor about every four months and patch releases roughly monthly.
  2. Before upgrading, read the release notes' deprecations and removals and scan manifests for removed APIs.
  3. Upgrade the control plane one minor version at a time (1.35 → 1.36, never skipping).
  4. Then upgrade nodes, by draining and replacing them or with kubeadm upgrade node, respecting PodDisruptionBudgets.
  5. Update add-ons (CNI, CoreDNS, CSI drivers, ingress) to versions supporting the new release, and test.

Who uses it

Platform and cluster operations teams own upgrades; architects choose between managed services and distributions; vendors and consultancies build careers around specific platforms.

Key takeaway

Memorise the numbers: three releases per year, roughly 14 months of support, the newest three minors maintained, kubelet up to three minors older than the API server, and never skip a control-plane minor.

Going deeper

  • Since 2021 (v1.22) Kubernetes ships three minor releases per year in roughly 15-week cycles; each minor gets about 12 months of patches plus a 2-month maintenance period, so v1.37 (26 August 2026) reaches end of life on 28 October 2027.
  • Features move alpha (off by default, may change or vanish) → beta (usually on by default for non-API features) → GA (stable, cannot be disabled). Each change is tracked as a Kubernetes Enhancement Proposal (KEP).
  • Version skew policy: API servers in an HA cluster may differ by one minor; kubelets and kube-proxy may be up to three minors older than the API server but never newer; kubectl is supported one minor either side.
  • v1.35 made the kubelet refuse to start on cgroup v1 hosts by default (failCgroupV1: true); v1.37 deprecated kube-proxy IPVS mode and kube-dns and announced future removal of cgroup v1 support.
  • Managed services extend upstream support: EKS offers 14 months of standard support plus 12 months of paid extended support, GKE has an extended channel, and AKS offers two-year long-term support on its Premium tier.
  • The CNCF's Certified Kubernetes programme runs the upstream conformance test suite (often via Sonobuoy or Hydrophone), so workloads written for one certified distribution behave the same on another.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Skipping minor versions on the control plane (1.34 → 1.36): it is unsupported and can corrupt storage migrations. Step through each minor.
  • Upgrading the cluster but not add-ons: an old CNI or CSI driver may not support the new version, breaking networking or storage.
  • Ignoring 'deprecated API' warnings until upgrade day: manifests using removed API versions fail to apply after the upgrade.

docs.title: Try it: Check versions and plan an upgrade on a kubeadm cluster
docs.text:
kubectl version                          # client and server versions
kubectl get nodes -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,KUBELET:.status.nodeInfo.kubeletVersion

# On the first control-plane node (after upgrading the kubeadm package):
sudo kubeadm upgrade plan               # shows target versions and add-on changes
sudo kubeadm upgrade apply v1.37.1

# For each node, one at a time:
kubectl drain worker-1 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data
#   (on worker-1) upgrade kubeadm, run: sudo kubeadm upgrade node
#   then upgrade the kubelet and kubectl packages and restart the kubelet
kubectl uncordon worker-1

docs.title: Chapter 4: Linux in Depth
docs.text: Linux runs most of the world's servers, clouds, containers, phones and supercomputers, so it is the operating system you are most likely to manage in a job. This chapter tours the 2026 distribution landscape, the filesystem hierarchy, users, permissions, sudo and capabilities, package managers, systemd and the boot chain, shell scripting and the classic text tools. It then covers process and network administration, /proc, /sys and kernel modules, eBPF observability, performance analysis, and how the kernel itself is developed and released.

docs.title: 4.1 Linux Distributions & Families in 2026
docs.text:
Linux itself is only a kernel. A distribution ('distro') bundles that kernel with tools, libraries, a package manager, an installer, default settings and a support policy. Most distros belong to a few families — Red Hat, Debian and SUSE — plus independent ones such as Arch, Alpine and NixOS, and the family decides which commands and package formats you use.

The big distribution families. Arrows show where code flows; Arch, Alpine and NixOS are independent.

Think of it like…

The kernel is a car engine; distributions are finished cars from different makers — a reliable saloon with a 10-year warranty (RHEL, Ubuntu LTS), a test car with the newest parts (Fedora, Arch), or a tiny city car (Alpine).

Real-world example

Leila joins fictional Meridian Bank's platform team. Production databases run RHEL 10 under a 10-year support contract, the CI runners use Ubuntu 26.04 LTS, containers are built on Alpine and Debian slim images, developers use Fedora 44 laptops, and a dev team trials NixOS for reproducible build machines. She learns dnf, apt and apk in her first week.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Upstream projects (kernel, systemd, GNOME, OpenSSL...) release source code.
  2. A distribution packages, patches and tests them together, choosing versions and defaults.
  3. Releases are fixed (point releases with long support) or rolling (continuous updates).
  4. Security teams backport fixes into the shipped versions for the support period.
  5. Users install from images and keep systems current through the distro's repositories.

Who uses it

Every Linux administrator, DevOps engineer, cloud engineer and developer must pick and support distributions; job adverts often name RHEL or Ubuntu specifically.

Key takeaway

Learn one distro from each big family — RHEL-like (dnf, SELinux) and Debian/Ubuntu (apt, AppArmor) — because certifications (RHCSA) and most jobs assume one of them.

Going deeper

  • RHEL 10 shipped in May 2025 on Linux 6.12 and requires x86-64-v3 CPUs (roughly Intel Haswell or newer); RHEL 10.2 and 9.8 followed on 20 May 2026, and each major RHEL release gets 10 years of maintenance.
  • Since June 2023 Red Hat publishes RHEL sources mainly through CentOS Stream; AlmaLinux now aims for ABI compatibility, and CIQ, Oracle and SUSE formed the OpenELA project to share enterprise Linux sources.
  • Debian 13 'Trixie' (August 2025) is current stable, with point release 13.7 in September 2026 and LTS until June 2030; Debian 14 'Forky' is in testing.
  • Ubuntu 26.04 LTS 'Resolute Raccoon' (23 April 2026) ships Linux 7.0, uses Rust-based sudo-rs and uutils coreutils by default, and gets 5 years of standard support, extended to 10 years with Ubuntu Pro.
  • SUSE Linux Enterprise Server 16.0 (November 2025) and openSUSE Leap 16.0 introduced the web-based Agama installer and switched the default security module from AppArmor to SELinux.
  • Fedora releases roughly every six months with about 13 months of support; Fedora 44 arrived in spring 2026 and Fedora 45, targeted for late October 2026, uses Linux 7.2.
  • Alpine uses musl libc and BusyBox instead of glibc and GNU coreutils, so its base container image is only a few megabytes but some glibc-only binaries will not run on it.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Saying 'CentOS' for a new server: CentOS Linux 7 ended in June 2024; choose Rocky, AlmaLinux, CentOS Stream or RHEL itself.
  • Running interim (non-LTS) Ubuntu releases in production: they get only 9 months of support; servers should use LTS releases.
  • Assuming every distro has the same tools: package managers, firewalls, network config and security modules differ between families.

docs.title: 4.2 The Filesystem Hierarchy & 'Everything Is a File'
docs.text:
Linux has one directory tree starting at / (root), with no drive letters. The Filesystem Hierarchy Standard (FHS) says what belongs where: programs in /usr, settings in /etc, changing data in /var, users' files in /home. Linux also follows the Unix idea that 'everything is a file': disks, terminals, processes and kernel settings all appear as files you can read and write.

Key top-level directories. One tree for everything; each directory has one job.

Think of it like…

The tree is like a well-organised office building: reception (/), the policy binders (/etc), the warehouse of tools (/usr), the mail room that fills and empties daily (/var) and private offices (/home).

Real-world example

Oliver, a new support engineer at fictional Tidewater Telecom, must find why a web server will not start. He knows where to look without searching: configuration in /etc/nginx, logs in /var/log/nginx, the binary in /usr/sbin/nginx, the service unit in /usr/lib/systemd/system, and its runtime PID file in /run/nginx.pid.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The kernel mounts the root file system at / during boot.
  2. Other file systems (/boot, /home, USB drives) are mounted onto directories in that tree.
  3. Virtual file systems are mounted too: /proc (processes), /sys (devices), /dev (device nodes), /run (runtime tmpfs).
  4. Programs find their files using standard paths, so packages and admins agree where things live.
  5. Ordinary tools — cat, echo, ls — work on all of it because everything is presented as files.

Who uses it

All Linux users, administrators and developers; packagers and container image builders follow FHS closely.

Key takeaway

Remember the three big ones: /etc = configuration, /var = variable data (logs, caches, spools, databases), /usr = installed, read-only software.

Going deeper

  • FHS 3.0 was published by the Linux Foundation in 2015; distributions follow it closely but not perfectly, and man 7 hier and man 7 file-hierarchy describe each system's actual layout.
  • Most distributions have completed the '/usr merge': /bin, /sbin and /lib are symlinks into /usr, so the whole OS can live on one read-only /usr volume (Fedora since 17, Debian since 12).
  • /run is a tmpfs created at every boot for PID files, sockets and lock files; it replaced /var/run, which is now a symlink to it.
  • /tmp may be a tmpfs in RAM (the default on Fedora, Arch and since Debian 13) and is often cleaned at boot, while /var/tmp is meant to survive reboots.
  • Device files in /dev are character or block nodes with major and minor numbers, created dynamically by devtmpfs and udev; /dev/null, /dev/zero and /dev/urandom are pseudo-devices.
  • Image-based and container systems lean on FHS: /usr is the read-only OS image, while /etc and /var hold the machine's own state.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Storing important data in /tmp: it may be in RAM or wiped at boot; use /var/lib/<app> or /srv.
  • Editing files under /usr/lib (for example systemd units) directly: package updates overwrite them; put overrides in /etc.
  • Thinking /root and / are the same: / is the top of the tree, /root is the root user's home directory.

docs.title: Try it: Explore the hierarchy and 'everything is a file'

ls /
man hier                      # the hierarchy explained
ls -l /bin                    # a symlink to usr/bin on merged-/usr systems
cat /proc/cpuinfo | head -5   # CPU details as a file
echo $$ ; ls /proc/$$          # your shell as a directory

docs.title: 4.3 Users, Groups, Permissions & ACLs
docs.text:
Linux is multi-user: every process runs as a user, and every file has an owner, a group and permission bits saying who may read (r), write (w) or execute (x) it. Permissions are checked separately for the owner, the group and everyone else. Access control lists (ACLs) add finer rules when three categories are not enough.

What r, w and x mean on files vs directories

On a file On a directory r (4) Read contents List names (ls) w (2) Modify contents Create, delete, rename entries x (1) Run as program Enter (cd) and access entries setgid (2000) Run with file's group New files inherit group sticky (1000) (ignored on Linux) Only owner may delete (/tmp)

On a directory, x means 'may enter', and w lets you delete other people's files unless the sticky bit is set.

Think of it like…

Each file is a room with three keyholes: one for its owner, one for members of a team, and one for visitors; ACLs are a guest list pinned on the door naming extra people.

Real-world example

At fictional Quarry Design, Ana creates a shared folder /srv/projects owned by group 'design' with mode 2770, so only the team can enter and new files inherit the group. A contractor, Ben, needs read-only access to one subfolder, so she adds an ACL: setfacl -m u:ben:rx /srv/projects/brochure — no group changes needed.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Each account has a numeric UID and a primary GID, defined in /etc/passwd and /etc/group (or a directory such as LDAP/FreeIPA).
  2. When a process opens a file, the kernel compares the process's UID and groups with the file's owner and group.
  3. It applies the first matching class — owner, then group, then others — and checks the r, w or x bit for that class.
  4. If the file has an ACL, named-user and named-group entries are checked too, limited by the ACL mask.
  5. Root (UID 0) bypasses most checks, which is why administrators avoid working as root.

Who uses it

Every Linux administrator, DevOps engineer and security analyst; permission problems are among the most common support tickets.

Key takeaway

Know octal by heart: r=4, w=2, x=1, so 644 = rw-r--r-- (files), 755 = rwxr-xr-x (programs, directories), 600 = rw------- (private keys).

Going deeper

  • Account data lives in /etc/passwd (name, UID, GID, home, shell), /etc/shadow (password hashes, readable only by root) and /etc/group; getent passwd also queries LDAP or SSSD sources through NSS.
  • Modern distributions hash passwords with yescrypt (shadow entries starting $y$) or SHA-512 ($6$); older MD5 ($1$) hashes are weak and should be replaced.
  • Regular users typically start at UID 1000; UIDs below that are reserved for system accounts that run services and usually have /usr/sbin/nologin as their shell.
  • The umask removes permissions from newly created files: with umask 022 new files get 644 and directories 755; 027 makes new files 640.
  • POSIX ACLs (getfacl/setfacl) add named users and groups plus a mask; default ACLs on directories are inherited by new files, and ls -l shows a '+' after the mode.
  • Enterprise systems usually keep users in a central directory — FreeIPA/IdM, Active Directory via SSSD or Samba winbind — instead of local files.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Using chmod 777 to 'fix' access: it lets anyone modify or replace the file; find the correct owner, group or ACL instead.
  • Forgetting x on directories: a readable file inside a directory without x for you is still inaccessible.
  • Editing /etc/passwd or /etc/sudoers with a normal editor: use vipw, vigr and visudo, which lock and syntax-check the files.

docs.title: Try it: Practise permissions safely in a temporary folder

cd "$(mktemp -d)"
touch notes.txt; ls -l notes.txt
chmod 640 notes.txt; ls -l notes.txt     # rw-r-----
chmod u+x,o-r notes.txt; stat -c '%A %a %U:%G' notes.txt
id; umask
getfacl notes.txt
