docs.title: 4.4 Root, sudo, setuid & Linux Capabilities
docs.text:
The root account (UID 0) can do almost anything, so day-to-day work happens as a normal user who borrows power only when needed. sudo runs a single command as root after checking rules in /etc/sudoers; setuid programs run with their owner's rights; and Linux capabilities split root's power into about 40 smaller privileges that can be granted one at a time.

What happens when you type sudo. Every step is a control point: policy, authentication, logging, then a single privileged command.

Think of it like…

Root is the master key to the whole building. sudo is a front desk that lends you the master key for one task and writes it in a logbook; capabilities are individual keys — one for the server room, one for the post room — so nobody needs the master key at all.

Real-world example

Dev at fictional Cobalt Games wants a Node.js game server to listen on port 443, which normally needs root. Rather than running it as root, he grants one capability: sudo setcap cap_net_bind_service=+ep /usr/local/bin/gameserver — or AmbientCapabilities=CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE in its systemd unit. If the server is hacked, the attacker gets an ordinary user, not root.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. A user runs sudo <command>; sudo checks /etc/sudoers and /etc/sudoers.d for a matching rule.
  2. It authenticates the user (their own password, cached for a few minutes) via PAM.
  3. It logs the command (journal or /var/log/auth.log / secure) and runs it as root or another user.
  4. For setuid binaries, the kernel sets the effective UID to the file's owner when the program starts.
  5. With capabilities, the kernel checks for a specific capability (for example CAP_NET_ADMIN) instead of UID 0.

Who uses it

System administrators, security engineers, DevOps teams writing service units, and container engineers dropping privileges.

Key takeaway

Always edit sudo rules with visudo (it syntax-checks), and grant the narrowest command list possible instead of ALL.

Going deeper

  • Linux defines around 40 capabilities, such as CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE (ports below 1024), CAP_NET_ADMIN, CAP_SYS_PTRACE and CAP_SYS_ADMIN, which is so broad it is often called 'the new root'.
  • Each process has permitted, effective, inheritable, bounding and ambient capability sets; systemd exposes them as CapabilityBoundingSet= and AmbientCapabilities= in unit files.
  • Ubuntu 25.10 and 26.04 LTS use sudo-rs, a memory-safe Rust reimplementation, by default; systemd 256 added run0, which starts privileged commands via the service manager instead of a setuid binary.
  • Serious bugs show why setuid code is risky: Baron Samedit (CVE-2021-3156) in sudo, PwnKit (CVE-2021-4034) in polkit's pkexec, and a 2025 sudo --chroot flaw (CVE-2025-32463) all gave local root.
  • Setting the no_new_privs flag (NoNewPrivileges=yes in systemd) prevents a process and its children from gaining privileges through setuid binaries or file capabilities.
  • Distros grant administrative sudo through a group: 'sudo' on Debian and Ubuntu, 'wheel' on Fedora, RHEL and Arch.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Granting 'ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL' to service accounts or many users: any compromise becomes full root with no friction.
  • Allowing sudo for editors, pagers or interpreters (vi, less, python): they can spawn a root shell; GTFOBins lists such escapes.
  • Running containers or services as root 'because it is easier': drop to a normal user and add only the capabilities required.

docs.text:
sudo -l                            # what you may run with sudo
grep Cap /proc/$$/status           # your shell's capability sets
capsh --decode=$(grep CapBnd /proc/$$/status | awk '{print $2}')
find /usr/bin -perm -4000 2>/dev/null   # setuid programs
getcap -r /usr/bin 2>/dev/null

docs.title: 4.5 Package Management: apt, dnf, zypper, pacman, Snap & Flatpak
docs.text:
Linux installs software from packages: archives containing the program, its metadata and a list of what else it needs. A package manager downloads packages from trusted repositories, checks their signatures, resolves dependencies and keeps everything updated. Each family has its own tools, and universal formats like Flatpak and Snap work across distros.

Package tools by family

Debian / Ubuntu Fedora / RHEL Arch Format .deb .rpm .pkg.tar.zst Low-level tool dpkg rpm pacman High-level tool apt dnf (dnf5 on Fedora) pacman Install apt install nginx dnf install nginx pacman -S nginx Which package owns a file dpkg -S /usr/bin/ls rpm -qf /usr/bin/ls pacman -Qo /usr/bin/ls Community extras PPAs EPEL, COPR AUR

Same ideas, different commands and formats.

Think of it like…

A package manager is an app store and a careful librarian in one: it fetches the book you ask for, the other books it refers to, checks they are genuine editions and records exactly what is on your shelves.

Real-world example

Hana administers 40 servers at fictional Juniper Logistics: Ubuntu web servers and Rocky Linux databases. A critical OpenSSL fix is announced, so she runs apt update && apt upgrade on Ubuntu and dnf upgrade --security on Rocky through Ansible. Both package managers verify signatures, restart affected services and log the change for the audit.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The package manager downloads repository metadata (package lists, versions, dependencies) and checks its signature.
  2. You ask for a package; the solver calculates every dependency that must be installed or upgraded.
  3. Packages are downloaded and their cryptographic signatures verified against trusted keys.
  4. Files are unpacked into place, and maintainer scripts run (create users, restart services).
  5. The database of installed packages is updated so later upgrades and removals are exact.

Who uses it

Every Linux administrator and developer, DevOps engineers writing Dockerfiles and Ansible playbooks, and packagers who build software for distros.

Key takeaway

Know the low-level and high-level pairs: dpkg + apt (Debian/Ubuntu), rpm + dnf (Fedora/RHEL), rpm + zypper (SUSE), and pacman (Arch) which does both.

Going deeper

  • Debian 13 ships APT 3.0, which added a clearer columnar output and uses Sequoia-based OpenPGP verification; repository sources are moving to the structured deb822 '.sources' format.
  • Fedora 41 (October 2024) replaced dnf with the faster C++ rewrite dnf5; RHEL 10 and its clones still use the dnf 4 code base with the same command syntax.
  • EPEL (Extra Packages for Enterprise Linux) is the Fedora-maintained add-on repository most RHEL, Rocky and AlmaLinux servers use for extra tools such as htop.
  • Flatpak apps run in a bubblewrap sandbox with shared runtimes, mostly from Flathub; Snap packages are confined by AppArmor and served from Canonical's Snap Store.
  • Package signatures are the key supply-chain control: apt checks signed Release files and dnf checks RPM GPG signatures, so a tampered mirror cannot serve modified packages.
  • Automatic patching is common on servers: unattended-upgrades on Debian/Ubuntu and dnf-automatic on Fedora and RHEL clones apply security updates on a schedule.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Running 'curl ... | sudo bash' installers from random sites: they bypass signatures and the package database; prefer official repositories.
  • Mixing repositories from different releases (Debian testing on stable, Fedora repos on RHEL): this creates broken dependencies ('FrankenDebian').
  • Using pip install --user or sudo pip into the system Python: modern distros block it (PEP 668); use venvs, pipx or distro packages.

docs.title: Try it: The same task in four package managers
docs.text:
# Debian / Ubuntu
sudo apt update && apt list --upgradable && sudo apt install htop
# Fedora / RHEL / Rocky / Alma
sudo dnf check-update; sudo dnf install htop; dnf history
# openSUSE / SLES
sudo zypper refresh && sudo zypper install htop
# Arch
sudo pacman -Syu htop

docs.title: 4.6 systemd, the Linux Boot Chain, journald & Timers
docs.text:
After the boot loader starts the Linux kernel, the kernel launches one program — PID 1 — which starts everything else. On almost every major distro that program is systemd. It starts services in parallel from small configuration files called units, groups them into targets (like 'multi-user' or 'graphical'), restarts them if they crash, collects their logs in the journal and can replace cron with timers.

The Linux boot chain. Each stage verifies or loads the next; systemd takes over once the kernel is running.

Think of it like…

systemd is a theatre stage manager: it knows which actors (services) must be ready before others, calls them on stage in the right order, replaces anyone who collapses, and keeps a complete logbook of the show.

Real-world example

Kwame at fictional Ironbridge Analytics deploys a Python API. He writes /etc/systemd/system/api.service with Restart=on-failure, MemoryMax=1G and User=api, enables it, and adds api-report.timer to run a report every night at 02:00. When it crashes he reads journalctl -u api --since '1 hour ago' and sees the stack trace immediately.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. UEFI firmware loads the boot loader (shim + GRUB 2, or systemd-boot) from the EFI System Partition.
  2. The boot loader loads the kernel and the initramfs, passing the kernel command line.
  3. The initramfs finds and unlocks the real root file system (LVM, LUKS, RAID), then switches to it.
  4. The kernel runs /sbin/init — systemd — as PID 1, which builds a dependency graph of units.
  5. systemd activates units in parallel until default.target (multi-user or graphical) is reached, then shows a login.

Who uses it

Every Linux administrator, DevOps engineer and SRE; writing and debugging unit files is a core RHCSA and LFCS skill.

Key takeaway

Learn the daily five: systemctl status, systemctl restart, systemctl enable --now, journalctl -u <unit> -f, and systemctl list-timers.

Going deeper

  • Unit types include service, socket, timer, target, mount, automount, path, slice and scope; vendor units live in /usr/lib/systemd/system and admin overrides in /etc/systemd/system.
  • Dependencies combine requirement (Wants=, Requires=) with ordering (After=, Before=); they are independent, so a unit usually needs both Wants= and After= on its dependency.
  • journald stores structured, indexed binary logs; they are kept only in RAM (/run/log/journal) unless /var/log/journal exists or Storage=persistent is set.
  • Timers support calendar expressions like OnCalendar=Mon..Fri 02:00, catch up missed runs with Persistent=true, and add RandomizedDelaySec= so fleets do not all run at once.
  • systemd 258 (2025) removed cgroup v1 support entirely, and since systemd 260 legacy SysV init scripts are no longer supported; v262 was released in September 2026.
  • Unified Kernel Images (UKIs) bundle the kernel, initramfs and command line into one signed EFI file, simplifying Secure Boot and measured boot with systemd-boot.
  • Alternatives remain: Alpine and Gentoo use OpenRC, Void uses runit, and some embedded systems use BusyBox init or s6.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Editing vendor unit files in /usr/lib/systemd/system: updates overwrite them; use systemctl edit to create a drop-in override in /etc.
  • Forgetting systemctl daemon-reload after changing unit files by hand, so systemd keeps using the old definition.
  • Assuming 'enable' starts a service: it only sets it to start at boot; use 'enable --now' or 'start' as well.

docs.title: Try it: Explore systemd on your machine
docs.text:
systemctl get-default                 # graphical.target or multi-user.target
systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running | head
systemd-analyze blame | head         # slowest units at boot
journalctl -b -p warning | tail      # warnings from this boot
systemctl list-timers

On Alpine, rc-update add sshd default enables SSH at boot under OpenRC.

docs.title: 4.7 Shells, Pipes, Redirection & Bash Scripting
docs.text:
The shell is the program that reads your commands. Its superpower is plumbing: pipes (|) send one program's output into another, and redirection (>, >>, 2>, <) connects commands to files. Put commands in a file with a shebang line and you have a script that automates work, with variables, conditions, loops and functions.

A pipeline: the top five IP addresses in a web log. Each program does one job; the pipe streams data between them without temporary files.

Think of it like…

Commands are kitchen appliances that each do one job; pipes are conveyor belts between them, redirection is choosing which bowl the result lands in, and a script is a written recipe anyone can follow exactly.

Real-world example

Every morning Sofia at fictional Larkspur Retail checked disk space on 30 servers by hand. She writes a 20-line bash script with set -euo pipefail that loops over a host list, runs df through ssh, and emails any file system above 85%. ShellCheck catches two quoting bugs before she schedules it with a systemd timer.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The shell reads a line and splits it into words, expanding variables ($HOME), globs (*.log) and command substitution $(...).
  2. It sets up redirections and pipes, connecting file descriptors 0, 1 and 2.
  3. It finds the program via $PATH (or runs a built-in), then forks and executes it.
  4. Each command returns an exit status ($?): 0 means success, anything else means failure.
  5. Scripts combine these with if, case, for, while and functions; the shebang (#!/usr/bin/env bash) chooses the interpreter.

Who uses it

Linux administrators, DevOps and SRE engineers, data engineers and security analysts — shell scripting appears in almost every operations job description.

Key takeaway

Start scripts with #!/usr/bin/env bash and set -euo pipefail, quote every variable ("$file"), and run ShellCheck before trusting a script.

Going deeper

  • Bash is the default interactive shell on most Linux distributions; macOS switched its default to zsh in 10.15 Catalina (2019), and Debian and Ubuntu use the small, fast dash as /bin/sh for scripts.
  • Redirection works on file descriptors: > or 1> replaces stdout, >> appends, 2> redirects stderr, 2>&1 merges stderr into stdout (order matters), and &> sends both in bash.
  • set -e exits on errors, set -u treats unset variables as errors and set -o pipefail makes a pipeline fail if any part fails — together they prevent many silent failures.
  • Exit status conventions: 0 success, 1 general error, 2 misuse, 126 not executable, 127 command not found, and 128+N when killed by signal N (130 for Ctrl-C).
  • Write POSIX sh when scripts must run anywhere (Alpine, BusyBox, dash); use bash features such as arrays, [[ ]] and ${var//a/b} only with a bash shebang.
  • Configuration loads from startup files: ~/.bashrc for interactive shells, ~/.bash_profile or ~/.profile for login shells, ~/.zshrc for zsh; environment variables are inherited by child processes only if exported.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Leaving variables unquoted: a filename with spaces turns rm $file into deleting several wrong files; always write "$file".
  • Parsing ls output in scripts: use globs (for f in *.log) or find -print0 with xargs -0 instead.
  • Writing 'cmd > out.txt 2>&1' as 'cmd 2>&1 > out.txt': the second form still sends errors to the terminal.

docs.title: Try it: Pipes, redirection and a tiny safe script
docs.text:
ls /usr/bin | wc -l                       # pipe: count programs
ls /nonexistent 2> errors.txt; cat errors.txt
cat > hello.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
for name in "$@"; do
  echo "Hello, ${name}!"
done
EOF
chmod +x hello.sh && ./hello.sh Ada Linus; echo "exit: $?"

docs.title: 4.8 Finding & Processing Text: grep, sed, awk, find & Friends
docs.text:
Linux stores most configuration and logs as plain text, so a small set of tools does a huge amount of work: grep finds lines, sed edits streams of text, awk works with columns, find locates files, and sort, uniq, cut and xargs glue them together. Combined with pipes, they answer questions about thousands of files or millions of log lines in seconds.

The text toolkit. Small tools that each do one thing well, joined by pipes.

Think of it like…

These tools are a workshop of hand tools: grep is a magnifying glass, sed is a find-and-replace pen, awk is a spreadsheet calculator, find is a metal detector, and xargs is an assistant who passes each item to the right tool.

Real-world example

During an incident at fictional Sterling Hotels, Raj must know which customers saw errors. In one pipeline he finds all of today's gzipped logs with find, searches them with zgrep for ' 503 ', extracts the user ID column with awk, removes duplicates with sort -u and counts them with wc -l: 1,284 affected customers, answered in 40 seconds.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Locate files: find by name, size, age or type, or list them with globs.
  2. Filter lines: grep with a regular expression keeps only what matters.
  3. Transform: sed substitutes text; awk splits lines into fields and computes.
  4. Aggregate: sort, uniq -c, wc and head turn lines into answers.
  5. Act: xargs or find -exec runs commands on each result.

Who uses it

Administrators, SREs, security analysts hunting through logs, data engineers and developers — these commands appear in nearly every Linux interview.

Key takeaway

Learn regular expressions once and reuse them everywhere: grep -E, sed -E, awk, find -regex, vim and most programming languages.

Going deeper

  • grep supports basic (BRE), extended (-E) and, in GNU grep, Perl-compatible (-P) regular expressions; useful flags are -r recursive, -i ignore case, -v invert, -n line numbers, -o only the match and -C 3 for context.
  • sed applies scripts line by line: s/old/new/g substitutes, -n with p prints selected lines, and -i edits in place (GNU sed accepts -i alone; BSD/macOS sed needs -i '').
  • awk splits each line into fields $1...$NF using -F as separator and supports patterns, variables, associative arrays and printf, making it a tiny report language.
  • find tests can be combined (-name, -type f, -size +100M, -mtime -7, -user) and acted on with -delete, -exec cmd {} + or -print0 | xargs -0 for filenames containing spaces.
  • Modern alternatives are popular: ripgrep (rg) and fd are much faster on large source trees and respect .gitignore, and jq is the standard tool for JSON from APIs and kubectl.
  • Ubuntu 26.04 uses the Rust uutils coreutils for commands like sort, cut and wc; behaviour aims to match GNU, but scripts relying on rare GNU options should be tested.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Running sed -i or find -delete without testing: first run without -i or with -print to see what would change.
  • Using grep on structured JSON or YAML: field order and nesting change; use jq or yq for reliable results.
  • Forgetting that uniq only collapses adjacent duplicates: always sort before uniq.

docs.title: Try it: Text-processing practice on files every Linux system has
docs.text:
grep -c '/bin/bash$' /etc/passwd              # accounts using bash
awk -F: '$3 >= 1000 {print $1, $6}' /etc/passwd   # regular users and homes
find /etc -name '*.conf' -mtime -30 2>/dev/null | head
sed -n '1,5p' /etc/os-release
cut -d: -f7 /etc/passwd | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

David Peter) · Tool · Current · Intermediate Fast modern replacements for grep -r and find that skip ignored files by default. rg -n 'TODO' src/ searches a large codebase in a fraction of grep's time.

docs.title: 4.9 Managing Processes & Resources: ps, top, kill, nice & ulimit
docs.text:
Linux gives administrators tools to see every running process, how much CPU and memory each uses, and to control them: ps takes a snapshot, top and htop show a live view, kill sends signals to stop or reload programs, nice changes priority, and ulimit sets per-process limits such as the number of open files.

Stopping a service gracefully, then forcefully. systemd sends SIGTERM, waits (TimeoutStopSec, 90 s by default), then sends SIGKILL.

Think of it like…

These tools are the control room of a factory: ps is the staff list, top is the live CCTV wall, kill is the intercom to tell a worker to stop or restart, nice decides who gets the machines first, and ulimit is the rule on how many tools each worker may borrow.

Real-world example

Late on Friday, the build server at fictional Oakridge Software slows to a crawl. Elena opens htop and sees a stuck test runner at 100% CPU on all cores. She tries kill -TERM 8812 so it can clean up; when it ignores that after 30 seconds, kill -KILL 8812 ends it. She then runs future test jobs with nice -n 10 so interactive users stay responsive.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Find the process: ps aux, pgrep or the top/htop view sorted by CPU or memory.
  2. Inspect it: its user, state (R, S, D, Z), parent, start time, CPU% and RSS.
  3. Adjust it: renice to lower priority, taskset to pin CPUs, or ionice for disk priority.
  4. Signal it: SIGTERM asks politely, SIGHUP often means reload, SIGKILL forces termination.
  5. Prevent repeats: set limits with ulimit, /etc/security/limits.conf or systemd unit directives.

Who uses it

System administrators, SREs on call, developers debugging hung programs and anyone preparing for RHCSA, LFCS or Linux+.

Key takeaway

Use SIGTERM (15) first and SIGKILL (9) only as a last resort — SIGKILL cannot be caught, so the program cannot flush data or remove lock files.

Going deeper

  • Load average (uptime, /proc/loadavg) is the 1-, 5- and 15-minute exponentially smoothed count of tasks running, runnable or in uninterruptible D state — on Linux it reflects I/O waits too, so compare it with the number of CPUs.
  • Nice values range from -20 (highest priority) to 19 (lowest), default 0; only root can lower a nice value. ionice classes are realtime, best-effort (levels 0-7) and idle.
  • Common signals: 1 SIGHUP (reload/hang-up), 2 SIGINT (Ctrl-C), 9 SIGKILL, 15 SIGTERM (default for kill), 18/19 SIGCONT/SIGSTOP on x86; kill -l lists them all.
  • A zombie is an exited process whose parent has not collected its exit status; it uses no memory, but many zombies point to a buggy parent, and killing the parent lets init reap them.
  • ulimit sets soft and hard per-process limits (open files, processes, core size, stack); systemd services ignore limits.conf and use LimitNOFILE= and similar directives instead.
  • htop and btop add colour, tree views and mouse support; atop records history so you can replay what happened during last night's slowdown.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Reaching for kill -9 first: it skips cleanup, may corrupt data and leaves stale lock files; send SIGTERM and wait a little.
  • Reading a load average of 8 as 'overloaded' without checking CPU count: on a 32-core server it is light load.
  • Raising nofile in /etc/security/limits.conf for a systemd service and wondering why nothing changed: set LimitNOFILE= in the unit.

renice -n 5 -p $!                   # lower its priority
kill -TERM $!; sleep 1; ps -p $! || echo 'gone'

ulimit -n                           # max open files for this shell

docs.title: 4.10 Linux Networking Configuration: ip, NetworkManager, netplan & nftables
docs.text:
Linux networking has two layers of tools: low-level commands that show and change the kernel's live network state (ip, ss), and configuration managers that make settings permanent (NetworkManager, netplan, systemd-networkd). On top sits the firewall — nftables in the kernel, usually driven by firewalld or ufw — plus DNS resolution through systemd-resolved and /etc/resolv.conf.

Who configures what in Linux networking. High-level tools write configuration; the kernel holds the live state.

Think of it like…

ip is like adjusting the furniture in a room right now; NetworkManager or netplan is the floor plan that puts everything back after a reboot; the firewall is the doorman who checks every visitor against a list.

Real-world example

Chen sets up a new Ubuntu 26.04 web server at fictional Willowbrook Media. He writes a netplan YAML file with a static IP, gateway and DNS, tests it with netplan try (which rolls back automatically if he loses SSH), then allows only ports 22, 80 and 443 with ufw. ss -tlnp confirms nginx is listening, and dig confirms DNS works.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The kernel exposes interfaces (eth0, enp3s0, wlan0), addresses, routes and neighbour tables.
  2. A configuration service (NetworkManager, systemd-networkd, or netplan rendering to one of them) applies settings at boot and on changes.
  3. DNS resolution goes through glibc's NSS (/etc/nsswitch.conf), /etc/hosts and a resolver such as systemd-resolved.
  4. Packets pass through netfilter hooks, where nftables rules (via firewalld or ufw) accept, drop or NAT them.
  5. Tools like ip, ss, ping, dig and tcpdump verify each layer when troubleshooting.

Who uses it

Linux and network administrators, cloud and DevOps engineers, and Kubernetes engineers whose CNI plugins build on the same kernel features.

Key takeaway

Retire net-tools habits: use ip a (not ifconfig), ip r (not route), ss -tulpn (not netstat) — they are what current distros install and what exams expect.

Going deeper

  • iproute2 (ip, ss, tc, bridge) replaced the old net-tools package; changes made with ip are immediate but lost at reboot unless saved in a configuration manager.
  • Interfaces get predictable names such as enp3s0 (PCI bus 3, slot 0) or wlp2s0 from systemd-udevd, replacing eth0-style names whose order could change between boots.
  • NetworkManager stores connections as keyfiles in /etc/NetworkManager/system-connections; RHEL 9 and later use keyfiles by default instead of the old ifcfg files.
  • Netplan, Ubuntu's default since 17.10, reads YAML from /etc/netplan and renders it for systemd-networkd (servers) or NetworkManager (desktops); netplan try reverts after 120 seconds unless confirmed.
  • nftables (Linux 3.13+) replaced iptables as the kernel firewall framework; the modern iptables command is usually iptables-nft, translating rules to nftables, while firewalld uses nftables as its backend.
  • systemd-resolved runs a local stub resolver at 127.0.0.53 and supports per-interface DNS, DNS over TLS and DNSSEC; resolvectl query example.com shows which server answered.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Changing firewall rules on a remote server without a safety net: use netplan try, firewalld's --timeout option or console access before reloading rules.
  • Editing /etc/resolv.conf directly on systems where it is a symlink managed by systemd-resolved or NetworkManager: changes are overwritten.
  • Mixing firewall front-ends (ufw, firewalld and raw nft rules) on one host: they overwrite each other; pick one.

docs.title: 4.11 /proc, /sys, sysctl & Kernel Modules
docs.text:
The Linux kernel can be inspected and tuned while it runs. /proc and /sys are virtual directories where the kernel publishes information and settings as files; sysctl is the tool for kernel tunables under /proc/sys; and kernel modules are pieces of kernel code — mostly drivers — that can be loaded and unloaded without rebooting.

Windows into the running kernel. Most kernel inspection and tuning happens through files and a few small tools.

Think of it like…

/proc and /sys are the dashboard and the fuse box of a car you can open while driving; sysctl adjusts settings on the dashboard, and modules are plug-in parts you can fit or remove without stopping the engine.

Real-world example

Imani turns an Ubuntu VM at fictional Saltmarsh Networks into a router for a lab. She enables forwarding with sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1, makes it permanent in /etc/sysctl.d/99-router.conf, loads the WireGuard module with modprobe wireguard, and checks the NIC driver and firmware with ethtool -i and modinfo. No reboot is needed at any step.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The kernel exposes process data in /proc/<pid> and system data in files such as /proc/cpuinfo and /proc/interrupts.
  2. Tunables live under /proc/sys (for example net/ipv4/ip_forward); sysctl reads and writes them with dotted names.
  3. Devices and drivers appear as an object tree in /sys, with one value per file.
  4. When hardware appears, udev or modprobe loads the matching module (.ko file) and its dependencies.
  5. Persistent settings go into /etc/sysctl.d/*.conf and /etc/modules-load.d or /etc/modprobe.d.

Who uses it

Linux administrators, performance and network engineers, embedded developers and security teams hardening kernels.

Key takeaway

sysctl -w changes last only until reboot; make them permanent in /etc/sysctl.d/ and apply with sysctl --system.

Going deeper

  • Each process has /proc/<pid>/ with cmdline, environ, status, fd/, maps, limits, cgroup and ns/; tools like ps, top and lsof simply read these files.
  • Common tunables include net.ipv4.ip_forward, net.core.somaxconn, fs.file-max, kernel.pid_max, vm.max_map_count (Elasticsearch needs 262144) and kernel.kptr_restrict for hardening.
  • Modules are .ko files in /lib/modules/$(uname -r); modprobe resolves dependencies from modules.dep, while insmod loads a single file without dependency handling.
  • With Secure Boot, many distributions enable kernel lockdown and require signed modules, so unsigned third-party modules (such as some GPU drivers) need a Machine Owner Key enrolled with mokutil.
  • DKMS (originally from Dell, 2003) rebuilds out-of-tree modules like NVIDIA, VirtualBox or ZFS automatically whenever a new kernel is installed.
  • Unloading modules on production systems is risky and sometimes blocked; blacklisting in /etc/modprobe.d is the clean way to stop a module loading at boot.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Copying sysctl 'performance tweaks' from old blog posts: many are obsolete or harmful on modern kernels; change one setting at a time and measure.
  • Forgetting to rebuild the initramfs after blacklisting a module needed early in boot, so it still loads.
  • Loading unsigned or unknown kernel modules: they run with full kernel privilege and taint the kernel for support purposes.

docs.title: Try it: Read kernel information and settings safely
docs.text:
uname -a
cat /proc/cmdline
sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward kernel.pid_max vm.swappiness
lsmod | head
modinfo -F description ext4 2>/dev/null || modinfo ext4 | head -5
sudo dmesg --level=err,warn | tail

docs.title: 4.12 eBPF & Modern Linux Observability
docs.text:
eBPF lets you run small, safety-checked programs inside the Linux kernel without writing a kernel module or rebooting. The programs attach to events — a system call, a function, a network packet — and collect data or make decisions at full kernel speed. It powers modern observability, networking (Cilium) and security monitoring (Falco, Tetragon).

Life of an eBPF program. The verifier is what makes it safe to run user-supplied code in the kernel.

Think of it like…

eBPF is like being allowed to fit tiny, inspected sensors onto any pipe in a running factory: an inspector checks each sensor is harmless before it goes on, and the sensors report back without stopping production.

Real-world example

Aisha's payment API at fictional Northgate Bank has random 200 ms slowdowns. Instead of adding logging and redeploying, she runs a bpftrace one-liner measuring disk I/O latency and an execsnoop trace. Within minutes she sees a cron job launching a log compressor that saturates the disk every 15 minutes, and moves it to off-peak hours.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. A tool writes an eBPF program (in C, Rust or a high-level language like bpftrace) and compiles it to eBPF bytecode.
  2. The bpf() system call loads it; the in-kernel verifier proves it terminates and only touches memory safely.
  3. A JIT compiler translates the bytecode into native machine code.
  4. The program attaches to a hook: kprobe, tracepoint, uprobe, perf event, XDP, tc, cgroup or LSM.
  5. It stores results in eBPF maps, which user-space tools read to print histograms, metrics or alerts.

Who uses it

SREs and performance engineers, Kubernetes networking and security teams, observability vendors and kernel developers.

Key takeaway

Start with ready-made tools — bpftrace one-liners and BCC/libbpf-tools such as execsnoop, opensnoop and biolatency — before writing your own programs.

Going deeper

  • eBPF extends the classic Berkeley Packet Filter (1992); the extended version arrived in Linux 3.18 (2014) with 64-bit registers, maps and helper functions.
  • The verifier explores every program path; since Linux 5.2 it accepts programs up to one million verified instructions, and bounded loops are allowed.
  • BTF type information and CO-RE ('compile once, run everywhere') let one compiled eBPF program run across kernel versions without recompiling on each host.
  • XDP programs run in the network driver before the kernel allocates packet buffers, letting load balancers and DDoS filters drop millions of packets per second per core.
  • The eBPF Foundation (Linux Foundation, 2021) hosts the ecosystem; Microsoft maintains eBPF for Windows, and sched_ext uses eBPF to write CPU schedulers.
  • Cilium (CNI and service mesh) and Falco are CNCF graduated projects built on eBPF; Tetragon adds kernel-level security enforcement from the Cilium community.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming eBPF tracing is free: high-frequency probes (every packet or every function call) add measurable overhead; prefer tracepoints and sampling.
  • Running tools on old kernels without BTF: many modern tools need kernel 5.8+ with BTF enabled (check for /sys/kernel/btf/vmlinux).
  • Granting containers CAP_BPF or CAP_SYS_ADMIN casually: loading eBPF programs is a powerful privilege that attackers can abuse.

docs.title: Try it: First eBPF one-liners (needs root and bpftrace installed)
docs.text:
# which programs are being started, system-wide
sudo bpftrace -e 'tracepoint:syscalls:sys_enter_execve { printf("%s -> %s\n", comm, str(args.filename)); }'
# count system calls by process for 5 seconds
sudo bpftrace -e 'tracepoint:raw_syscalls:sys_enter { @[comm] = count(); } interval:s:5 { exit(); }'
sudo bpftool prog list | head

docs.title: 4.13 Performance Analysis Tools: perf, vmstat, iostat, sar & strace
docs.text:
When a Linux system is slow, a standard toolkit tells you why: vmstat and mpstat for CPU and memory, iostat for disks, sar for history, pidstat for per-process use, strace for system calls, and perf for profiling exactly which code burns CPU. Good engineers check CPU, memory, disk and network systematically rather than guessing.

Which tool looks at which part of the system. Pick the tool for the layer you suspect; work from the top down.

Think of it like…

It is like a doctor's examination: pulse and temperature first (uptime, vmstat), then specific tests (iostat, pidstat), then a scan (perf, flame graphs) only once you know where to look.

Real-world example

A report at fictional Copperfield Media takes 40 minutes instead of 10. Luca runs vmstat 1 (high 'wa' I/O wait), then iostat -xz 1 (one disk at 100% utilisation with 30 ms waits), then pidstat -d 1 (the culprit is a backup). A perf flame graph of the report itself shows nothing unusual. Moving the backup window fixes it.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Get the overview: uptime (load), dmesg (errors), vmstat 1 (run queue, memory, swap, I/O wait).
  2. Check each resource for utilisation, saturation and errors: mpstat (CPUs), free (memory), iostat -xz (disks), sar -n DEV (network).
  3. Find the process responsible with pidstat or top.
  4. Look inside it: strace for system calls, perf record/report or a flame graph for CPU hot spots, eBPF tools for latency.
  5. Change one thing, then measure again with the same tools to confirm the improvement.

Who uses it

SREs, performance engineers, Linux administrators, database administrators and developers optimising code.

Key takeaway

Memorise Brendan Gregg's 60-second checklist: uptime, dmesg | tail, vmstat 1, mpstat -P ALL 1, pidstat 1, iostat -xz 1, free -m, sar -n DEV 1, sar -n TCP,ETCP 1, top.

Going deeper

  • vmstat columns to know: r (runnable tasks; more than CPU count means CPU saturation), si/so (swap in/out), us/sy/id/wa/st (user, system, idle, I/O wait, stolen by the hypervisor).
  • iostat -x reports r/s, w/s, average wait (r_await, w_await in ms), queue size (aqu-sz) and %util; on SSDs and NVMe, 100% util does not necessarily mean saturation because they serve many requests in parallel.
  • sar, from the sysstat package, records metrics every 10 minutes by default (via a systemd timer) so you can look at yesterday's CPU, memory, disk and network data.
  • perf uses CPU hardware counters and kernel events: perf stat counts cycles, instructions, cache and branch misses; perf record -g samples stacks (often at 99 Hz) for perf report or flame graphs.
  • Flame graphs, invented by Brendan Gregg in 2011, show sampled stack traces as stacked boxes whose width is proportional to time spent, making hot code paths obvious.
  • strace uses ptrace and can slow a program dramatically; for production, prefer perf trace or eBPF-based tools with far lower overhead.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Tuning before measuring: changing sysctls or hardware without data often makes things worse; establish a baseline first.
  • Reading high I/O wait (wa) as a CPU problem: it means CPUs are idle while waiting for storage; investigate the disks.
  • Leaving strace attached to a busy production process: it can slow it by orders of magnitude; use short, filtered traces.

docs.title: 4.14 How the Linux Kernel Is Developed & Released
docs.text:
The Linux kernel is one of the largest collaborative software projects in the world: thousands of developers from hundreds of companies send changes by email to subsystem maintainers, who pass them up to Linus Torvalds. A new mainline version appears roughly every nine to ten weeks, stable updates follow weekly, and some versions are kept as long-term support (LTS) kernels for years.

From patch to your distribution. Features enter only in the merge window; afterwards only fixes are accepted.

Think of it like…

It works like a big newspaper: reporters (developers) file stories to section editors (subsystem maintainers), who send the best to the editor-in-chief (Linus) during a short window; after that, only corrections are accepted until the edition is printed.

Real-world example

Zoe, an engineer at a fictional NIC maker, Tern Semiconductor, adds support for a new card. She posts her patch series to the netdev mailing list, revises it twice after review, and the networking maintainers queue it. It is merged during the 7.3 merge window, appears in 7.3-rc1 and should ship in Linux 7.3; distributions pick it up later.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. A developer writes a patch with a clear description and a Signed-off-by line, then emails it to the right list and maintainers.
  2. Reviewers comment publicly; the developer posts revised versions (v2, v3...) until maintainers accept it into their tree.
  3. Maintainer trees are merged daily into linux-next for integration testing.
  4. After a release, Linus opens a two-week merge window and pulls the maintainers' trees, then tags rc1.
  5. Weekly release candidates (rc2...rc7, sometimes rc8) fix bugs; then the final version is released and the stable team takes over.

Who uses it

Kernel developers, hardware vendors, distribution kernel maintainers, embedded engineers and anyone who needs to know which kernel version contains a feature or fix.

Key takeaway

Know the version facts for 2026: Linux 7.0 (April), 7.1 (June) and 7.2 (August) are released, 7.3 is due in October, and 6.18 is the newest LTS kernel.

Going deeper

  • After 6.19 (February 2026) Linus Torvalds renumbered to 7.0 simply because minor numbers were getting large; 7.0 was released on 12 April 2026, 7.1 on 14 June and 7.2 on 16 August.
  • As of October 2026, kernel.org lists longterm kernels 6.18 and 6.12 (until December 2028), 6.6 and 6.1 (December 2027), and 5.15 and 5.10 (December 2026); stable and LTS releases are maintained by Greg Kroah-Hartman and Sasha Levin.
  • Each release typically contains around 12,000-15,000 changes from roughly 2,000 developers; companies such as Intel, Google, AMD, Red Hat, Linaro, Meta and Huawei contribute heavily.
  • Distribution kernels differ from mainline: RHEL 10 is based on 6.12 with years of backported fixes, Debian 13 also uses 6.12, and Ubuntu 26.04 LTS ships 7.0.
  • The kernel project became a CVE Numbering Authority in February 2024 and now assigns CVEs to most fixed bugs, so it publishes thousands per year; the advice is simply to run current stable or LTS updates.
  • Rust support was merged in Linux 6.1 (December 2022); by late 2025 maintainers agreed it was no longer experimental, and new drivers such as Nova (NVIDIA GPUs) are written in Rust.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Thinking a bigger major number means a big change: 7.0 was a routine release with a renumbered version, not a redesign.
  • Comparing distro kernel version numbers with mainline directly: a RHEL '6.12' kernel contains many features backported from later releases.
  • Running an end-of-life kernel because 'it works': it no longer receives security fixes; move to a supported stable or LTS line.

docs.title: Chapter 3: Memory Management, File Systems & I/O
docs.text: This chapter follows data through the machine: how every program gets its own virtual address space, how pages, page tables and the TLB translate addresses, and what the kernel does when memory runs short — page faults, replacement, swap, compression and the OOM killer. It then moves to storage: the VFS, inodes and file descriptors, the page cache, the major file systems of Linux, Windows and macOS, the block layer and I/O schedulers, device drivers with DMA and the IOMMU, and finally power management with ACPI sleep states and CPU frequency scaling.

docs.title: 3.1 Address Spaces & Virtual Memory
docs.text:
Every running program believes it owns a huge, private, tidy block of memory starting near zero — its virtual address space. Behind the scenes the CPU's memory management unit (MMU) and the OS translate each virtual address to a real location in RAM. This keeps programs apart, lets the OS move memory around freely and allows programs to reserve more memory than the machine physically has.

A Linux x86-64 process address space. High addresses at the top; the heap grows up and the stack grows down towards each other.

Think of it like…

It is like a hotel where every guest's key card says 'Room 1': the front desk privately maps each guest's 'Room 1' to a different real room, so nobody can walk into anyone else's room.

Real-world example

Amara, a developer at the fictional Kestrel Analytics, opens two copies of the same Python script. Both store a counter in their own heap, yet changing it in one never affects the other, because the MMU maps each process's pages to different physical RAM. On her 16 GB laptop, 40 processes together reserve over 200 GB of virtual memory but occupy only about 9 GB of real RAM.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The loader lays out the program's code, data, heap, shared libraries and stack at virtual addresses.
  2. The kernel gives each process its own page tables and points the MMU at them (CR3 on x86, TTBR0 on Arm) at every context switch.
  3. On each memory access the MMU translates virtual to physical and checks read, write, execute and user/kernel permissions.
  4. Accesses to unmapped or forbidden addresses raise a fault; the kernel either fixes it (loads a page) or kills the program with a segmentation fault.
  5. The top part of every address space is reserved for the kernel and is unreachable from user mode.

Who uses it

Systems programmers, performance engineers, SREs investigating memory use, and security researchers studying exploits all work with address spaces daily.

Key takeaway

Memorise the difference between virtual size (VSZ/VIRT, address ranges reserved) and resident set size (RSS, pages actually in RAM) — a classic interview question is why a process shows 30 GB VIRT but 200 MB RSS.

Going deeper

  • x86-64 with 4-level paging uses 48-bit virtual addresses: 128 TiB for user space (up to 0x00007fffffffffff) and 128 TiB for the kernel; 5-level paging (LA57) extends this to 57 bits and 128 PiB in total.
  • Addresses between the two halves are non-canonical; touching one raises a general-protection fault, which conveniently catches many corrupted-pointer bugs.
  • 64-bit Linux maps all physical RAM into the kernel half (the 'direct map'), so kernel code can reach any page frame by adding a fixed offset to its physical address.
  • With ASLR enabled (/proc/sys/kernel/randomize_va_space = 2) the stack, heap, mmap base and position-independent executables land at random addresses on each run.
  • A 32-bit process can address only 4 GiB in total — typically 3 GiB user and 1 GiB kernel on Linux, 2 GiB/2 GiB on Windows by default — a major reason servers moved to 64-bit.
  • Linux's default overcommit policy (vm.overcommit_memory = 0) lets processes reserve far more than RAM plus swap, betting that many reserved pages are never touched.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Reading VIRT or VSZ as real memory use: it counts reserved address ranges; RSS, or better PSS, shows RAM actually consumed.
  • Thinking 'virtual memory' just means using the disk: it is the address-translation mechanism; swapping is only one optional feature built on it.
  • Assuming pointers printed by a program are physical addresses: user programs only ever see virtual addresses, and they change between runs with ASLR.

docs.title: Try it: See your shell's memory map and its virtual vs resident size (Linux)
docs.text:
cat /proc/self/maps | head -20       # regions of the 'cat' process itself
ps -o pid,vsz,rss,comm -p $$          # VSZ and RSS in KiB for your shell
grep -E 'VmSize|VmRSS' /proc/$$/status

docs.title: Key kernels, commands, tools, standards & concepts
docs.text: Name What it does Example Virtual address spaceEvery modern OS (Linux, Windows, macOS) · Concept · Current · Beginner The private range of addresses a process sees; the OS maps pieces of it to RAM, files or nothing at all. Two browser tabs each run in separate processes, so a crash or exploit in one cannot directly read the other's memory. Physical address and page frameCPU and memory controller · Concept · Beginner The real location in RAM; physical memory is divided into fixed-size frames (usually 4 KiB) that virtual pages map onto. A server with 64 GiB of RAM has about 16.7 million 4 KiB page frames for the kernel to hand out. Memory management unit (MMU)Part of every modern CPU core · Component · Current · Beginner Hardware that translates each virtual address into a physical one using page tables, enforcing permissions on every access. Writing to a read-only code page makes the MMU raise a fault, which Linux reports as 'Segmentation fault (core dumped)'. Text, data and BSS segmentsELF (Linux) and PE (Windows) executable formats · Concept · Beginner The loaded program's machine code (text), initialised globals (data) and zero-initialised globals (BSS, which takes no file space). size /usr/bin/ls prints the text, data and bss byte counts of the ls program. Heap (brk/sbrk)C runtime + kernel · Concept · Beginner The region for dynamically allocated memory; malloc grows it with the brk system call or by mapping new regions with mmap. strace -e trace=brk,mmap python3 -c 'x=[0]*10**7' shows the interpreter asking the kernel for more heap. Stack and guard pageOS + compiler ABI · Concept · Beginner Per-thread memory for function calls and local variables, growing downward; an unmapped guard page below catches overflows. Infinite recursion hits the guard page and dies with a stack overflow; on Linux the default main-thread stack limit is 8 MiB (ulimit -s). Kernel/user address splitOS design · Concept · Intermediate The upper part of every address space belongs to the kernel and is only accessible in privileged mode. A system call does not switch address spaces; the CPU simply raises privilege so kernel addresses become accessible. Canonical addressesx86-64 architecture (Intel, AMD) · Concept · Advanced On 64-bit x86, unused upper address bits must copy bit 47 (or 56); other addresses are invalid and fault immediately. A corrupted pointer like 0x4141414141414141 from a buffer overflow is non-canonical, so dereferencing it crashes instantly. RSS, PSS and USSLinux /proc accounting · Concept · Intermediate Resident set size counts all pages in RAM; proportional set size divides shared pages among users; unique set size counts only private pages. Twenty PHP workers share a 30 MB library: each RSS includes all 30 MB, but each PSS includes only 1.5 MB of it. /proc/<pid>/maps and smapsLinux kernel procfs · Tool · Current · Intermediate Text files listing every memory region of a process with addresses, permissions and backing file; smaps adds per-region RSS and PSS. grep -A3 heap /proc/1234/smaps shows how much of process 1234's heap is actually resident. pmapprocps-ng · Command · Current · Beginner Prints a readable memory map of a process, with region sizes and the files backing them. pmap -x $(pgrep -n nginx) lists nginx's libraries, heap and stack with RSS and dirty kilobytes. ASLR (address space layout randomization)Linux, Windows (Vista+), macOS · Concept · Current · Intermediate Places stack, heap, libraries and executables at random addresses each run so attackers cannot predict where code lives. Running cat /proc/self/maps twice shows the libc base address changing between runs. Memory overcommitLinux vm.overcommit_memory (0, 1, 2) · Concept · Intermediate Allowing processes to reserve more virtual memory than RAM plus swap; 0 = heuristic, 1 = always allow, 2 = strict limit. A database vendor recommends vm.overcommit_memory=2 so allocations fail cleanly instead of the OOM killer striking later. Reserve vs commit (VirtualAlloc)Microsoft Win32 API · API · Current · Intermediate Windows separates reserving address ranges from committing them; committed memory counts against RAM plus page file. A game reserves 8 GB of address space at start-up but commits pages only as levels load, keeping the system commit charge low.

docs.title: 3.2 Paging, Page Tables, the TLB & Huge Pages
docs.text:
Paging chops both virtual and physical memory into equal-sized pieces called pages (usually 4 KiB). A page table — really a tree of tables — records which virtual page lives in which physical frame. Because walking that tree on every access would be slow, the CPU caches recent translations in a small, very fast Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB), and huge pages (2 MiB or 1 GiB) let one TLB entry cover far more memory.

Translating a virtual address on x86-64. A TLB hit skips every step after the first; a miss costs several memory reads.

Think of it like…

A page table is like a multi-volume street directory: volume, then page, then line gives you the house; the TLB is the sticky note on your fridge with the ten addresses you visit most, and a huge page is listing a whole street instead of every house.

Real-world example

Daniel, a database engineer at fictional Northwind Freight, runs PostgreSQL with 64 GB of shared buffers. With 4 KiB pages that is 16.7 million mappings and frequent TLB misses. After reserving 2 MiB huge pages (vm.nr_hugepages=33000, huge_pages=on), only about 32,800 mappings are needed and his query throughput rises by several percent with lower CPU time spent on page walks.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The CPU splits a virtual address into table indexes (9 bits per level on x86-64) plus a 12-bit offset within the page.
  2. It first checks the TLB; a hit gives the physical frame in about a cycle.
  3. On a miss, the hardware page walker reads up to four (or five) levels of tables from cache or RAM.
  4. The final page-table entry gives the frame number plus flags (present, writable, user, no-execute, accessed, dirty).
  5. The translation is cached in the TLB; when the kernel changes mappings it must flush stale entries, even on other CPUs.
  6. Huge pages stop the walk one or two levels early, so a single entry maps 2 MiB or 1 GiB.

Who uses it

Kernel developers, database and JVM tuners, HPC and AI infrastructure engineers, and virtualisation engineers who care about TLB efficiency.

Key takeaway

Remember the x86-64 numbers: 4 KiB pages, 512 entries per table, 4 levels (PGD, PUD, PMD, PTE) for 48-bit addresses, and huge pages of 2 MiB (PMD level) and 1 GiB (PUD level).

Going deeper

  • Each x86-64 page table is exactly one 4 KiB page holding 512 eight-byte entries, so each level consumes 9 address bits: 4 levels × 9 bits + 12 offset bits = 48 bits.
  • Modern cores have a small first-level data TLB (often around 64-96 entries) backed by a unified second-level TLB of roughly 1,500-3,000 entries; exact sizes vary by microarchitecture.
  • Process-context identifiers (PCID on x86, ASID on Arm) tag TLB entries with an address-space ID so a context switch does not have to flush the whole TLB.
  • When one CPU changes a mapping that other CPUs may cache, the kernel sends inter-processor interrupts to make them invalidate it — a 'TLB shootdown' that can hurt many-core performance.
  • Arm64 supports 4 KiB, 16 KiB and 64 KiB base pages; Apple Silicon uses 16 KiB, and Android 15 added support for 16 KiB-page devices, so apps must not hard-code 4096.
  • Explicit huge pages (hugetlbfs) are reserved up front via vm.nr_hugepages and never swapped; Transparent Huge Pages (THP) are created automatically by the kernel and khugepaged.
  • Multi-size THP (mTHP), added in Linux 6.8, allows intermediate sizes such as 16-64 KiB folios, and Linux 7.2 taught khugepaged to collapse memory into these sizes.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming THP always helps: some databases (for example Redis and older MongoDB guidance) recommend disabling it because compaction and khugepaged can cause latency spikes.
  • Forgetting that hugetlbfs pages are reserved permanently: setting nr_hugepages too high starves the rest of the system of RAM.
  • Hard-coding a 4096-byte page size in code; use sysconf(_SC_PAGESIZE) because Arm systems may use 16 KiB or 64 KiB pages.

getconf PAGESIZE                          # usually 4096
grep -i huge /proc/meminfo                # huge page pools and THP usage
cat /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled
sudo dmesg | grep -i 'level paging'       # 4-level or 5-level

docs.text: Name What it does Example PageOS memory unit · Concept · Beginner A fixed-size block of virtual memory, normally 4 KiB on x86 and most Arm Linux systems, mapped as a unit. A 10 KiB array occupies parts of three 4 KiB pages, and each page can be in RAM, swapped out or not yet created. Page tableKernel data structure walked by the MMU · Concept · Beginner A per-process tree of tables mapping virtual page numbers to physical frames, plus permission and status bits. When Firefox opens a new tab process, the kernel builds a fresh page-table tree for it. Page-table entry (PTE) flagsx86-64 and Arm64 architectures · Concept · Intermediate Bits in each entry: present, writable, user-accessible, no-execute, accessed and dirty, which the kernel uses for protection and reclaim. The kernel clears the writable bit on shared pages after fork, so the first write triggers copy-on-write. Multi-level paging (4- and 5-level)Intel/AMD x86-64; Linux PGD/P4D/PUD/PMD/PTE · Concept · Current · Advanced Splitting the page table into a tree so empty regions need no tables; 5-level paging supports 57-bit addresses for huge-memory servers. A small process touching 50 MB needs only a handful of 4 KiB tables instead of one gigantic flat table. Translation lookaside buffer (TLB)CPU cache for translations · Component · Current · Intermediate A tiny, fast cache of recent virtual-to-physical translations; a miss forces a page-table walk costing tens to hundreds of cycles. perf stat -e dTLB-load-misses ./app counts how often an application misses in the data TLB. TLB reachPerformance metric · Concept · Advanced The amount of memory the TLB can map at once: entries × page size; larger pages greatly increase reach. 1,536 entries × 4 KiB covers only 6 MiB, but the same entries holding 2 MiB pages cover 3 GiB. PCID / ASIDIntel/AMD PCID; Arm ASID · Concept · Current · Advanced Address-space tags on TLB entries so translations of several processes can coexist and context switches avoid full flushes. After Meltdown, Linux's KPTI relied on PCID to keep the cost of switching between user and kernel page tables acceptable. TLB shootdownSMP kernels · Concept · Advanced Interrupting other CPUs so they discard stale translations after a mapping is changed or freed. A program calling munmap in a tight loop on a 128-core server shows high time in flush_tlb functions in perf. Huge pages (hugetlbfs)Linux vm.nr_hugepages; x86 2 MiB / 1 GiB · Concept · Current · Intermediate Pre-reserved large pages that applications request explicitly; never swapped, giving predictable TLB-friendly memory. An Oracle Database host reserves 40,000 × 2 MiB huge pages for the SGA at boot. Transparent Huge Pages (THP)Linux kernel (since 2.6.38) · Concept · Current · Intermediate The kernel automatically backs suitable anonymous memory with 2 MiB pages; modes are always, madvise or never. echo madvise | sudo tee /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled limits THP to programs that request it. khugepagedLinux kernel thread · Component · Advanced Background kernel thread that scans memory and collapses runs of small pages into huge pages. A JVM heap gradually gains huge pages after start-up as khugepaged merges its 4 KiB pages. Multi-size THP (mTHP) and foliosLinux 6.8+ memory management · Concept · Emerging · Advanced Folios group contiguous pages into one unit; mTHP lets the kernel use intermediate sizes like 16, 32 or 64 KiB. On an Arm64 laptop, enabling 64 KiB mTHP lets the CPU's contiguous-PTE feature cut TLB misses for apps. 16 KiB and 64 KiB base pagesArm64 (Apple Silicon, Android 15+, some servers) · Concept · Emerging · Intermediate Arm64 supports larger base pages, trading some memory waste for fewer TLB misses and smaller page tables. Android 15 requires apps with native code to be built 16 KB-aligned so they run on 16 KiB-page devices. Large pages (Windows)Microsoft Win32 VirtualAlloc MEM_LARGE_PAGES · API · Current · Advanced Windows' huge-page equivalent; needs the 'Lock pages in memory' privilege and allocates non-pageable 2 MiB pages. SQL Server uses large pages for its buffer pool when the service account holds the Lock Pages in Memory right.

docs.title: 3.3 Page Faults, Demand Paging & Copy-on-Write
docs.text:
A page fault is the CPU telling the kernel 'this page is not ready'. Most faults are normal: the OS loads pages only when they are first touched (demand paging) and shares pages between processes until one of them writes (copy-on-write). Only faults on truly invalid addresses crash a program.

A copy-on-write fault after fork(). The page is copied only at the first write, not when the child is created.

Think of it like…

Demand paging is like a library that only fetches a book from the warehouse when you ask for it, and copy-on-write is like two students sharing one textbook until one wants to scribble in it — then they get their own photocopy.

Real-world example

When Lina at fictional Brightwater Labs starts a 200 MB data tool, it opens in under a second because Linux maps the binary but reads in only the pages actually executed. Her Python server then forks 8 workers: they share the parent's 300 MB of memory, and only the pages each worker modifies are copied, so total RAM grows by about 60 MB rather than 2.4 GB.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. A process touches an address whose page-table entry is missing or forbids the access; the MMU raises a page-fault exception.
  2. The CPU records the faulting address (CR2 on x86) and jumps to the kernel's fault handler.
  3. The kernel looks up the virtual memory area (VMA): no VMA or a permission violation means SIGSEGV.
  4. For a valid area it allocates a zeroed page, reads the page from a file or swap, or copies a shared page (copy-on-write).
  5. It updates the page table and restarts the instruction, which now succeeds — the program never notices.

Who uses it

Performance engineers reading fault counters, kernel and runtime developers, and anyone explaining why fork is fast or why a program crashed with a segfault.

Key takeaway

Know the three fault kinds: minor (page already in RAM, just map it), major (must read from disk or swap — slow), and invalid (segmentation fault).

Going deeper

  • A minor fault typically costs around a microsecond or less; a major fault that waits for an NVMe SSD costs tens of microseconds, and one that waits for a spinning disk costs several milliseconds.
  • Linux tracks each mapped range as a virtual memory area (VMA); since Linux 6.1 VMAs are stored in a maple tree, and per-VMA locking reduces contention during faults in multithreaded programs.
  • Anonymous memory is first mapped to a shared zero page on read; a real page is allocated only on the first write, so huge calloc'd arrays cost nothing until used.
  • Copy-on-write makes fork nearly free, but a parent with a huge, busy heap can see a burst of COW faults — which is why Redis snapshots may double memory use under heavy writes.
  • File-backed faults read ahead: Linux fetches neighbouring pages (readahead, often 128 KiB by default) because programs usually read sequentially.
  • The Dirty COW bug (CVE-2016-5195) was a race in Linux's copy-on-write path that let ordinary users write to read-only files, showing how security-critical this code is.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Treating all page faults as errors: millions of minor faults are normal; only major faults and invalid accesses deserve attention.
  • Expecting malloc to fail when memory is short: on Linux the allocation usually succeeds and the trouble starts later, at first touch.
  • Benchmarking without warm-up: the first run pays demand-paging faults and cold caches, so measure after the working set is loaded.

docs.title: Try it: Count minor and major page faults for a command (Linux)
docs.text:
/usr/bin/time -v python3 -c 'x = bytearray(200_000_000)' 2>&1 | grep -i fault
ps -o min_flt,maj_flt,comm -p $$

docs.title: 3.4 Page Replacement Algorithms
docs.text:
When RAM is full and a new page is needed, the OS must evict an existing page. A page replacement algorithm chooses the victim, aiming to evict the page least likely to be needed soon. Real kernels approximate the ideal using cheap hardware 'accessed' bits.

Page faults for one reference string (3 frames). String 7,0,1,2,0,3,0,4,2,3,0,3,2: smarter algorithms evict fewer useful pages.

Think of it like…

It is like a small desk with room for eight books: when you need a ninth, you put back the one you have not opened for the longest time, not the one you are halfway through.

Real-world example

A teaching assistant at fictional Westbrook University shows students the reference string 7,0,1,2,0,3,0,4,2,3,0,3,2 with 3 frames. FIFO causes 10 faults, LRU 9 and the optimal algorithm 7. Students then see how Linux's multi-generational LRU sorts pages by age using the accessed bits.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Each access sets the page's hardware 'accessed' (referenced) bit; writes also set the 'dirty' bit.
  2. When free memory falls below a watermark, the reclaim code (kswapd on Linux) starts scanning candidate pages.
  3. The algorithm ranks pages by recent use (clock hand, LRU lists or generations) and picks cold ones.
  4. Clean file pages are simply dropped; dirty pages are written back first; anonymous pages go to swap.
  5. If the evicted page is touched again, a major fault brings it back — too many of these is thrashing.

Who uses it

OS students (a guaranteed exam topic), kernel memory-management developers, and engineers tuning caches, databases and CDN servers that use the same ideas.

Key takeaway

Be ready to simulate FIFO, LRU and OPT by hand on a reference string, count faults, and explain Belady's anomaly (FIFO can fault more with more frames).

Going deeper

  • Belady's optimal algorithm (OPT/MIN, 1966) evicts the page used furthest in the future; it is impossible in practice but gives the lower bound every real algorithm is measured against.
  • True LRU needs an update on every memory access, which hardware cannot afford, so kernels approximate it with accessed bits sampled by a clock hand or list scans.
  • Linux traditionally kept active and inactive lists for file and anonymous pages; the multi-generational LRU (MGLRU), merged in Linux 6.1, sorts pages into generations and is enabled by default in many distributions.
  • Reclaim balances file-backed and anonymous pages; vm.swappiness (default 60, range 0-200) biases the kernel towards swapping anonymous memory or dropping page cache.
  • Working-set models (Denning, 1968) keep in RAM the pages used in the last Δ time window; Windows trims per-process working sets when memory gets tight.
  • Kernel watermarks (min, low, high per zone) decide when kswapd wakes up and when allocating processes must perform slow 'direct reclaim' themselves.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming more frames always means fewer faults: with FIFO, Belady's anomaly can make 4 frames fault more than 3.
  • Thinking evicting a page always means disk writes: clean file-backed pages are simply discarded and re-read later if needed.
  • Setting vm.swappiness=0 to 'disable swap': it only discourages swapping anonymous pages; use swapoff to actually disable swap.

docs.title: Try it: Simulate FIFO vs LRU page replacement in Python
docs.text:
def faults(refs, frames, lru=False):
    mem, n = [], 0
    for p in refs:
        if p in mem:
            if lru: mem.remove(p); mem.append(p)
            continue
        n += 1
        if len(mem) == frames: mem.pop(0)
        mem.append(p)
    return n
refs = [7,0,1,2,0,3,0,4,2,3,0,3,2]
print('FIFO', faults(refs, 3), 'LRU', faults(refs, 3, lru=True))

docs.text: Name What it does Example FIFO replacementClassic OS algorithm · Concept · Beginner Evicts the page that has been in memory longest, regardless of how recently it was used; simple but often poor. A page holding a hot loop gets evicted just because it was loaded first, causing an immediate re-fault. Belady's anomalyLászló Bélády et al., 1969 · Concept · Intermediate The counter-intuitive case where FIFO produces more page faults when given more frames. Reference string 1,2,3,4,1,2,5,1,2,3,4,5 gives 9 faults with 3 frames but 10 with 4 frames under FIFO. Optimal (OPT/MIN) algorithmLászló Bélády, IBM, 1966 · Concept · Intermediate Evicts the page whose next use is furthest in the future; unrealisable but the benchmark for comparison. Simulators compute OPT offline from a recorded trace to show how close LRU gets. LRU (least recently used)Classic OS algorithm · Concept · Beginner Evicts the page unused for the longest time, relying on the idea that recent use predicts near-future use. Redis's allkeys-lru eviction policy applies the same idea to cached keys. Clock (second-chance)Classic OS algorithm (Multics lineage) · Concept · Intermediate Pages sit in a circle; a hand clears accessed bits and evicts the first page found with its bit already clear. A page used since the hand's last pass gets a second chance; an idle page is evicted on the next sweep. Accessed and dirty bitsMMU page-table entry flags · Concept · Intermediate Hardware sets 'accessed' on any use and 'dirty' on writes, giving the OS cheap usage and modification information. During reclaim, a dirty page must be written to disk or swap before its frame can be reused. Working set modelPeter Denning, 1968 · Concept · Intermediate A process's working set is the pages it used in a recent time window; keeping it resident prevents thrashing. Windows Task Manager's 'Working set' column shows each process's resident pages. Page fault frequency (PFF)Classic OS control scheme · Concept · Advanced Adjusts a process's frame allocation by watching its fault rate: too high adds frames, too low removes them. A batch scheduler suspends a job whose fault rate stays high instead of letting it thrash. Active/inactive LRU listsLinux memory management · Concept · Advanced Linux's two-list LRU approximation: pages are promoted to active when re-used and demoted to inactive before eviction. grep -E 'Active|Inactive' /proc/meminfo shows active and inactive file and anonymous memory. Multi-generational LRU (MGLRU)Linux 6.1+ (originally from Google) · Concept · Current · Advanced Groups pages into age generations using accessed-bit scans, improving eviction choices and lowering CPU cost. cat /sys/kernel/mm/lru_gen/enabled shows whether MGLRU is on; ChromeOS and Android adopted it to reduce jank. kswapdLinux kernel thread (one per NUMA node) · Component · Intermediate Background reclaim thread that wakes when free memory drops below the low watermark and frees pages until high. top showing kswapd0 at high CPU is a sign the machine is under memory pressure. Direct reclaimLinux memory management · Concept · Advanced When kswapd cannot keep up, the process requesting memory must reclaim pages itself, adding latency to its allocation. A latency-sensitive trading app shows millisecond stalls traced to allocstall counters in /proc/vmstat. vm.swappinessLinux sysctl (default 60, range 0-200) · Concept · Current · Intermediate Controls the relative preference for reclaiming anonymous memory (to swap) versus page cache. sudo sysctl vm.swappiness=10 on a database server keeps its anonymous buffers in RAM longer. ARC (adaptive replacement cache)IBM research (Megiddo & Modha, 2003); OpenZFS · Concept · Current · Advanced Balances recency and frequency by tracking recently and frequently used lists plus ghost entries of evicted items. OpenZFS uses its ARC to cache file-system blocks; arc_summary shows its hit ratio.

docs.title: 3.5 Swapping, zram/zswap & Thrashing
docs.text:
Swap is disk space the OS uses as overflow when RAM is full: rarely used memory pages are moved out and brought back when needed. Compressed swap (zram, zswap, Windows and macOS memory compression) squeezes pages inside RAM first, which is much faster than disk. If a system keeps swapping pages in and out it 'thrashes' and grinds almost to a halt.

Swap options compared

Disk swap zswap zram Where pages go Swap partition/file Compressed RAM cache, then disk Compressed RAM disk Needs backing disk Yes Yes No (optional writeback) Speed Slowest Fast for cached pages Fast Typical use Servers, hibernation Laptops/servers with SSD Phones, Pis, Fedora desktops Hibernation Supported Via backing swap Not on its own

Compression trades CPU time for avoiding slow disk I/O.

Think of it like…

Swap is like a storage locker across town for things that do not fit in your flat; compression is vacuum-packing your winter clothes so they fit in the wardrobe; thrashing is driving to the locker every ten minutes.

Real-world example

Tomás runs a 4 GB Raspberry Pi 5 at fictional Greenleaf Farms for sensor dashboards. Every evening the Grafana and InfluxDB containers spike and the SD card swap makes the Pi freeze. He replaces the swap file with a 2 GB zram device using zstd; pages compress roughly 3:1, the spikes fit in RAM, and the freezes stop.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Under memory pressure, reclaim chooses cold anonymous pages (pages not backed by a file).
  2. With zswap, the page is first compressed into a RAM pool; with zram, it goes to a compressed RAM block device used as swap.
  3. Otherwise the page is written to a swap partition or swap file and its PTE records the swap location.
  4. When the process touches it again, a major fault reads (and decompresses) the page back into RAM.
  5. If the working sets of running programs exceed RAM, this cycle repeats constantly — thrashing.

Who uses it

Linux administrators, desktop and embedded engineers, cloud SREs sizing instances, and Kubernetes operators deciding whether nodes should have swap.

Key takeaway

Swap is not a substitute for RAM: a small amount helps the kernel evict truly idle pages, but sustained swap-in activity (si in vmstat) means you need more memory or less load.

Going deeper

  • Fedora has enabled swap on zram by default since Fedora 33, sized from RAM and capped at 8 GiB; Android and ChromeOS also rely heavily on zram.
  • Common compressors are lz4 (fastest) and zstd (better ratio); typical desktop data compresses about 2-4×, so a zram device holds several times its RAM cost.
  • Pressure Stall Information (PSI, Linux 4.20+) in /proc/pressure/memory reports the share of time tasks were stalled waiting for memory — a better thrashing signal than free memory.
  • Windows keeps a page file (pagefile.sys) and, since Windows 10, compresses pages in the memory of a 'Memory Compression' process; macOS has used compressed memory since OS X 10.9 Mavericks.
  • Kubernetes long required swap to be off on nodes; the NodeSwap feature now lets nodes use swap for Burstable pods, but many clusters still disable it.
  • Swap space has priorities: the kernel fills higher-priority devices first, so zram is usually given a higher priority than any disk swap.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Putting swap on SD cards or cheap flash and expecting it to be fast: it is slow and wears the media; prefer zram on small devices.
  • Judging memory health by 'free' RAM: Linux uses spare RAM for cache; watch available memory, swap-in rates and PSI instead.
  • Disabling swap entirely 'for performance': the kernel then cannot evict idle anonymous pages and the OOM killer may strike sooner.

free -h
zramctl                  # zram devices and compression ratio (if any)

docs.title: 3.6 Kernel & User-Space Memory Allocators
docs.text:
Allocators hand out pieces of memory and take them back. The kernel uses a buddy allocator for whole pages and slab-style caches for small, frequently used objects. Programs use malloc/free (or new/delete), implemented by a user-space allocator such as glibc's ptmalloc, jemalloc or mimalloc, which carves big chunks from the kernel into small pieces.

Who allocates memory, top to bottom. Each layer gets big chunks from the layer below and hands out smaller pieces.

Think of it like…

The buddy allocator is a baker who only sells loaves in sizes 1, 2, 4, 8 slices and can split or rejoin halves; the slab allocator is a pre-sliced tray of sandwiches all the same size, ready to hand out instantly.

Real-world example

Ravi's chat service at fictional Lumen Messaging grows from 2 GB to 9 GB RSS over a week, although its live data stays near 2 GB. A heap profile shows glibc's per-thread arenas holding fragmented free memory. Switching to jemalloc via LD_PRELOAD keeps RSS around 3 GB, and the team adds allocator metrics to its dashboards.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. At boot the kernel's buddy allocator takes all free page frames, grouped in power-of-two blocks (orders 0 to 10 = 4 KiB to 4 MiB).
  2. Requests for 2^n pages are served by splitting larger blocks; freed blocks merge with their 'buddy' when both are free.
  3. The slab layer (SLUB on Linux) keeps caches of fixed-size objects (inodes, dentries, kmalloc-64...) carved from buddy pages.
  4. In user space, malloc keeps free lists and size classes, asking the kernel for memory with brk or mmap.
  5. Large allocations (128 KiB+ by default in glibc) get their own mmap so they return to the OS when freed.

Who uses it

Kernel developers, C/C++/Rust systems programmers, game and database engineers, and SREs chasing memory leaks and fragmentation.

Key takeaway

Interview favourite: internal fragmentation is waste inside an allocated block (asked for 33 bytes, got 64); external fragmentation is free memory split into pieces too small to use.

Going deeper

  • Linux's buddy allocator manages orders 0-10 by default (MAX_PAGE_ORDER), so the largest contiguous block it hands out on x86-64 is 4 MiB; /proc/buddyinfo shows free counts per order.
  • Linux once had three slab allocators; SLOB was removed in 6.4 and the original SLAB in 6.8, leaving SLUB as the only implementation.
  • kmalloc returns physically contiguous memory suitable for DMA; vmalloc returns memory that is only virtually contiguous, built from scattered pages, and is slower to set up.
  • glibc's ptmalloc2 uses per-thread arenas and a per-thread cache (tcache, since glibc 2.26); allocations above M_MMAP_THRESHOLD (128 KiB initially, adaptive) use mmap directly.
  • jemalloc (FreeBSD's libc allocator), Google's tcmalloc and Microsoft's mimalloc all use size classes and thread-local caches to reduce lock contention and fragmentation on many-core servers.
  • Memory-safety tools hook allocators: AddressSanitizer adds red zones around blocks, and Linux's KASAN and KFENCE do similar checks inside the kernel.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Expecting free() to shrink RSS immediately: allocators often keep freed memory for reuse, so RSS may stay high without being a leak.
  • Mixing allocators — freeing memory from one library's malloc with another's free — causes heap corruption and crashes.
  • Swapping allocators blindly: jemalloc or mimalloc can help or hurt; benchmark with your real workload and watch RSS and latency.

docs.title: Try it: Peek at the kernel's buddy and slab allocators (Linux)

sudo slabtop -o | head -15   # biggest slab caches
sudo grep -E 'dentry|inode_cache' /proc/slabinfo
