docs.title: 3.7 Memory-Mapped Files & Shared Memory
docs.text:
Memory mapping makes a file (or a chunk of anonymous memory) appear directly in a program's address space. Instead of calling read and write, the program just uses pointers, and the kernel loads and saves pages behind the scenes through the page cache. Mapping the same file or region in two processes is also the fastest way to share memory between them.

One page cache, many views. Mapped processes and read() callers all share the same cached pages of the file.

Think of it like…

Instead of photocopying pages from a reference book whenever you need them (read), you get a window that looks straight onto the book itself — and if a colleague opens the same window, you both see the same pages.

Real-world example

Mei builds a search engine at fictional Orchid Retail. Her 12 GB product index is mmapped read-only, so 20 worker processes share one copy through the page cache instead of each reading 12 GB into private buffers. After a restart the index is already 'warm' in cache, so the service is ready in seconds.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The program calls mmap(addr, length, PROT_READ, MAP_SHARED or MAP_PRIVATE, fd, offset).
  2. The kernel creates a VMA describing the region but loads nothing yet.
  3. Touching a page causes a fault; the kernel finds or reads the file page in the page cache and maps it.
  4. With MAP_SHARED, writes go into the shared page cache and reach the file at writeback or msync; MAP_PRIVATE writes are copy-on-write and never reach the file.
  5. munmap (or process exit) removes the mapping; the pages may stay in the page cache for others.

Who uses it

Database and search-engine developers (LMDB, SQLite, Lucene), game and media programmers, and anyone loading large AI model files quickly.

Key takeaway

Remember MAP_SHARED versus MAP_PRIVATE: shared mappings write through to the file and are visible to other processes; private mappings give each process its own copy-on-write view.

Going deeper

  • Executables and shared libraries are themselves memory-mapped: the dynamic loader maps libc.so once in the page cache and every process shares those physical pages.
  • Mapping avoids the extra copy that read() makes from the page cache into a user buffer, but each first touch costs a page fault, so mmap is not automatically faster for streaming reads.
  • madvise() hints such as MADV_SEQUENTIAL, MADV_RANDOM, MADV_WILLNEED and MADV_DONTNEED tune readahead and reclaim for a mapping.
  • Errors on mapped files arrive as signals: if the file is truncated or the disk fails, touching the page raises SIGBUS instead of returning an error code.
  • POSIX shared memory (shm_open) on Linux lives in tmpfs under /dev/shm; memfd_create creates anonymous memory files that can be passed between processes as file descriptors.
  • Windows offers the same idea through CreateFileMapping and MapViewOfFile; named mappings backed by the page file serve as shared memory between processes.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming writes to a MAP_SHARED mapping are on disk immediately: they are not durable until msync or fsync completes.
  • Mapping files on network file systems or removable media: a disconnect turns ordinary memory accesses into SIGBUS crashes.
  • Expecting MAP_PRIVATE changes to be saved: they are copy-on-write and vanish when the process exits.

docs.title: Try it: Memory-map a file in Python and change it in place
docs.text:
import mmap
open('demo.bin', 'wb').write(b'hello world')
with open('demo.bin', 'r+b') as f, mmap.mmap(f.fileno(), 0) as m:
    m[0:5] = b'HELLO'      # write through the mapping
print(open('demo.bin', 'rb').read())   # b'HELLO world'

docs.title: 3.8 The OOM Killer & cgroup Memory Limits
docs.text:
When Linux runs completely out of memory and cannot free any, the Out-Of-Memory (OOM) killer picks a process and kills it to save the system. Control groups (cgroups) let administrators put memory limits on groups of processes — such as a container or a service — so one misbehaving program hits its own limit instead of starving everyone.

What happens when memory runs out. Limits and early user-space killers act before the kernel's last-resort OOM killer.

Think of it like…

The OOM killer is a lifeboat officer who must throw the heaviest cargo overboard to keep the ship afloat; cgroup limits are giving each passenger a fixed luggage allowance so it never comes to that.

Real-world example

At fictional Harbor Pay, a reporting container leaks memory every night. Without limits, the host's OOM killer once killed the payments database instead. Mohammed sets memory.max=2G and memory.high=1.8G for the reporting cgroup: now it slows under reclaim at 1.8 GB and, if it keeps leaking, only that container is OOM-killed and restarted.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. An allocation fails to find free pages even after reclaim, compaction and swapping.
  2. If the failing task is inside a cgroup that hit memory.max, only that cgroup's processes are considered (a cgroup OOM).
  3. Otherwise the global OOM killer scores every process by memory use (oom_badness) adjusted by oom_score_adj (-1000 to +1000).
  4. The highest-scoring process receives SIGKILL; its memory is reaped and the event is logged in the kernel log.
  5. User-space daemons such as systemd-oomd can act earlier, killing a cgroup when memory pressure (PSI) stays high.

Who uses it

Linux and Kubernetes administrators, SREs on call, container platform teams and developers whose pods show OOMKilled.

Key takeaway

Know where to look: 'dmesg | grep -i oom' or 'journalctl -k | grep -i killed' on a host, and exit code 137 (128 + SIGKILL 9) or reason OOMKilled for containers.

Going deeper

  • cgroup v2 offers four memory knobs: memory.min and memory.low protect a group's memory, memory.high throttles and reclaims, and memory.max is the hard limit that triggers a cgroup OOM.
  • oom_score_adj ranges from -1000 (never kill) to +1000 (kill first); systemd exposes it as OOMScoreAdjust=, and Kubernetes sets it from a pod's QoS class.
  • memory.oom.group=1 makes the kernel kill every process in the cgroup together, so a container is never left half-alive after an OOM.
  • systemd-oomd (enabled by default on Fedora since 34 and Ubuntu desktop since 22.04) watches PSI and swap usage and kills whole cgroups before the system locks up.
  • Kubernetes memory limits map to memory.max on the container cgroup; a container exceeding its limit is OOM-killed and restarted, appearing as OOMKilled with exit code 137.
  • The kernel log entry lists a memory summary and a table of processes with RSS, swap and oom_score_adj, which tells you exactly why a particular victim was chosen.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Setting oom_score_adj=-1000 on many processes: the OOM killer then has nothing safe to kill and the whole system may hang.
  • Confusing an application's own OutOfMemoryError (for example a Java heap limit) with the kernel OOM killer; they have different causes and fixes.
  • Setting container limits exactly at average usage: short spikes then trigger OOM kills; size limits with headroom and watch memory.peak.

docs.title: Try it: See OOM scores and your session's memory limits (Linux)
docs.text:
cat /proc/$$/oom_score /proc/$$/oom_score_adj
cg=$(cut -d: -f3 /proc/self/cgroup)
cat /sys/fs/cgroup$cg/memory.max /sys/fs/cgroup$cg/memory.current 2>/dev/null
journalctl -k | grep -i 'out of memory' | tail -3

docs.title: 3.9 The VFS, Inodes, Directories & File Descriptors
docs.text:
Programs use the same calls — open, read, write, close — whether a file lives on ext4, NTFS, a USB stick or a network share. The Virtual File System (VFS) layer makes that possible by translating generic calls into each file system's own code. Inside, every file is described by an inode (its metadata and where its data lives), directories map names to inodes, and an open file is referred to by a small number called a file descriptor.

From a system call to the disk. The VFS gives every file system the same front door.

Think of it like…

The VFS is a universal travel adapter: your laptop plug (open/read/write) fits every country's socket (file system). An inode is the library catalogue card for a book, a directory is the index of titles, and a file descriptor is the numbered ticket the librarian hands you while you borrow it.

Real-world example

Jonas at fictional Pinecrest Hosting gets 'No space left on device' although df -h shows 40% free. df -i reveals 100% of inodes used: a mail queue created 6 million tiny files. Deleting the queue frees inodes; he later reformats with more inodes (mkfs.ext4 -i 8192) because ext4 fixes the inode count at creation.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. A program calls open("/home/jo/a.txt", O_RDONLY); the VFS walks the path one component at a time.
  2. For each component it checks the dentry cache, asking the file system to look up names that are not cached.
  3. The final dentry points to an inode; the VFS checks permissions against the inode's owner, group and mode.
  4. The kernel creates an open-file object (struct file) with the current offset and puts it in the process's descriptor table.
  5. It returns the lowest free number (e.g. 3); later read(3, ...) calls go through the file system's own read function.

Who uses it

Every developer and administrator meets file descriptors and inodes; kernel, storage and container engineers work with the VFS directly.

Key takeaway

Memorise the standard descriptors (0 stdin, 1 stdout, 2 stderr) and that a file name is not part of the inode — which is why hard links and 'deleted but still open' files work.

Going deeper

  • Linux's VFS defines four core objects — superblock (a mounted file system), inode (a file), dentry (a name in a directory) and file (an open instance with an offset) — each with operation tables a file system fills in.
  • An ext4 inode is 256 bytes by default and holds mode, owner, size, timestamps, link count and extent pointers; the inode count is fixed at mkfs time, unlike XFS and Btrfs, which allocate inodes dynamically.
  • Large directories are indexed (ext4 uses hashed B-tree 'htree' indexes, XFS and Btrfs use B+trees) so lookups stay fast with millions of entries.
  • Open-file limits: the default soft limit for a process is often 1,024 descriptors (ulimit -n), and systemd services commonly raise LimitNOFILE to tens of thousands or more.
  • Deleting a file removes a name; the inode and data are freed only when the link count reaches zero and no process still has it open; a deleted 50 GB log keeps using disk until closed.
  • Windows uses handles rather than descriptors and NTFS keeps per-file records in the Master File Table (MFT); the I/O Manager with filter drivers plays a role similar to the VFS.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Believing the file name is stored in the inode: names live in directories, which is why one inode can have several names (hard links).
  • Deleting a huge log that is still open and expecting space back; truncate it (> file) or restart the writer, and check with lsof +L1.
  • Ignoring inode exhaustion: 'No space left on device' with free blocks usually means df -i shows 100% inode use.

echo hi > a.txt && ln a.txt hard.txt && ln -s a.txt soft.txt
ls -li a.txt hard.txt soft.txt     # same inode for hard link
stat a.txt
df -i .                            # inode usage

docs.title: 3.10 The Page Cache & Writeback
docs.text:
The page cache keeps recently read and written file data in otherwise unused RAM. Reads that hit the cache need no disk access, and writes usually land in the cache first ('dirty' pages) and are written to disk a little later by background writeback. Programs that need data to be truly on disk must ask with fsync.

A buffered write and its journey to disk. write() returns long before the data is durable; fsync is what waits.

Think of it like…

The page cache is a desk drawer of frequently used files: you work from the drawer, and every so often a clerk carries the changed papers back to the archive — unless you insist they be filed right now (fsync).

Real-world example

Grace's nightly import at fictional Fernhill Insurance reads a 6 GB CSV twice. The first pass takes 40 seconds from SSD; the second takes 4 seconds because the file is in the page cache — 'free' shows buff/cache at 7 GB. When a power cut later loses the last seconds of an import, she adds fsync after each committed batch.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. read() first looks for the file's pages in the page cache; misses trigger disk reads (plus readahead).
  2. write() copies data into cache pages and marks them dirty, returning almost immediately.
  3. Background flusher threads write dirty pages after about 30 seconds, or sooner when dirty data passes thresholds.
  4. If dirty data exceeds vm.dirty_ratio, writing processes are throttled until writeback catches up.
  5. fsync or fdatasync forces a file's dirty data (and journal) to stable storage and waits; under memory pressure clean cache pages are simply dropped.

Who uses it

Database engineers, storage and backup administrators, performance engineers, and anyone puzzled that Linux 'uses all the RAM'.

Key takeaway

'Free' memory being low is normal on Linux — look at the 'available' column, which counts reclaimable cache.

Going deeper

  • Linux writeback defaults: dirty data older than 30 s (vm.dirty_expire_centisecs=3000) is written, flushers wake every 5 s (dirty_writeback_centisecs=500), background writeback starts at 10% (dirty_background_ratio) and writers are throttled at 20% (dirty_ratio).
  • On large-RAM servers those percentages mean gigabytes of dirty data, so administrators often use vm.dirty_background_bytes and vm.dirty_bytes for fixed limits.
  • fsync must also flush the drive's volatile write cache (a FLUSH/FUA command); SSDs with power-loss protection can acknowledge quickly, consumer SSDs without it may be slow.
  • O_DIRECT bypasses the page cache entirely; databases like Oracle and MySQL InnoDB (innodb_flush_method=O_DIRECT) use it because they manage their own caches.
  • The 2018 'fsyncgate' discovery showed PostgreSQL could lose data after a failed fsync because Linux marked pages clean; PostgreSQL now panics and recovers from its WAL instead of retrying.
  • Windows has an equivalent system file cache managed by the Cache Manager, and FlushFileBuffers plays the role of fsync.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming write() means the data is safe on disk: it is only in RAM until writeback or fsync completes.
  • Dropping caches (drop_caches) on production 'to free memory': it only throws away useful cache and causes a burst of disk reads.
  • Benchmarking storage with buffered I/O and small files: you measure RAM speed; use fio with direct=1 or files larger than RAM.

docs.title: Try it: Watch the page cache speed up a second read (Linux)
docs.text:
dd if=/dev/urandom of=big.bin bs=1M count=512 status=none
sync; echo 3 | sudo tee /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches   # test machines only
time cat big.bin > /dev/null    # cold: from disk
time cat big.bin > /dev/null    # warm: from page cache
free -h; grep -E 'Dirty|Writeback' /proc/meminfo

docs.title: 3.11 File Systems Compared: ext4, XFS, Btrfs, ZFS, NTFS, ReFS & APFS
docs.text:
A file system decides how files, folders and free space are laid out on a disk and how they survive crashes. Linux usually uses ext4, XFS or Btrfs; Windows uses NTFS (and ReFS on servers); Apple devices use APFS. They differ in maximum sizes, crash-safety method (journaling or copy-on-write), snapshots, checksums and speed.

Three Linux file systems at a glance

ext4 XFS Btrfs Crash safety Journal (data=ordered) Metadata journal Copy-on-write Max volume 1 EiB 8 EiB 16 EiB Data checksums No (metadata only) No (metadata CRC) Yes (crc32c+) Snapshots No (use LVM) No (use LVM) Yes, subvolumes Shrink online Offline only No shrinking Yes Typical default Debian, Ubuntu RHEL, Rocky, Alma Fedora WS, openSUSE

ext4 is the simple default, XFS scales, Btrfs adds snapshots and checksums.

Think of it like…

File systems are different filing systems for the same warehouse: one keeps a logbook of every change before making it (journaling), another never overwrites a shelf but builds a new one and switches the sign (copy-on-write).

Real-world example

Felix sets up storage at fictional Riverbend Studios. Editing workstations keep ext4 for simplicity; the 200 TB render archive uses XFS for huge parallel writes; the build server uses Btrfs so a snapshot before each upgrade allows instant rollback; the Windows file server stays on NTFS, and the Macs use APFS with snapshots for Time Machine.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. mkfs writes the on-disk structures: superblock, allocation maps or B-trees, inode tables and a journal or tree root.
  2. On a write, the file system allocates extents (contiguous block runs) and updates metadata.
  3. Journaling file systems log metadata changes first, then apply them; copy-on-write ones write new blocks and atomically switch a root pointer.
  4. After a crash, the journal is replayed (or the last consistent tree root is used), so no full scan is needed.
  5. fsck-type tools (e2fsck, xfs_repair, btrfs check, chkdsk) repair damage that crash recovery cannot.

Who uses it

Linux and Windows administrators, storage engineers, NAS and backup specialists, and digital-forensics analysts.

Key takeaway

Know the defaults: ext4 on Debian/Ubuntu, XFS on RHEL and its clones, Btrfs on Fedora Workstation and openSUSE, NTFS on Windows, APFS on Apple devices.

Going deeper

  • ext4 (stable since Linux 2.6.28, 2008) uses extents and delayed allocation; with 4 KiB blocks a single file can reach 16 TiB, and Linux 6.19 added support for block sizes larger than the page size.
  • XFS, created by SGI in 1993 and the RHEL default since RHEL 7, uses allocation groups that let many CPUs allocate in parallel; online repair arrived in Linux 6.10 and Linux 7.0 added autonomous self-healing.
  • Btrfs checksums data and metadata, supports subvolumes, snapshots, send/receive and transparent compression (zstd); its RAID 5/6 modes are still not recommended for production.
  • OpenZFS is a copy-on-write file system and volume manager with end-to-end checksums and RAID-Z; its CDDL licence keeps it out of the mainline kernel, so it ships as a separate module.
  • bcachefs was merged in Linux 6.7, marked externally maintained in 6.17 and removed from mainline in 6.18; it now lives outside the kernel tree as a separate module.
  • NTFS (1993) remains Windows' main file system; ReFS adds integrity streams and block cloning and backs Windows 11's Dev Drive; APFS (2017) brought clones, snapshots and native encryption to Apple devices.
  • Linux reads and writes NTFS through Paragon's ntfs3 driver (since 5.15) and, from Linux 7.1 (June 2026), a rewritten NTFS driver with full write support.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Treating snapshots as backups: a snapshot lives on the same disk, so disk failure or ransomware with admin rights destroys both.
  • Choosing XFS for a volume you may need to shrink: XFS can grow but cannot shrink.
  • Running fsck on a mounted file system: always unmount first (or use the file system's online check tool), or you may corrupt it.

docs.title: 3.12 The Block Layer, Storage Stack & I/O Schedulers
docs.text:
Below the file system sits the block layer: the part of the kernel that turns file-system requests into reads and writes of numbered blocks on disks, SSDs and virtual devices. It can merge and reorder requests with an I/O scheduler, and stack virtual devices such as RAID, LVM volumes and encrypted disks on top of real ones.

A typical Linux storage stack. Each layer looks like a block device to the one above it.

Think of it like…

The block layer is a post office sorting room: letters (I/O requests) arrive from many senders, get bundled by street (merged), possibly reordered for the van's route (scheduled) and sent through the right depot (device driver).

Real-world example

Siobhan runs a mixed server at fictional Coastline Data. Her NVMe SSDs use the 'none' scheduler because they have deep internal queues, while the 18 TB hard-disk backup array uses mq-deadline so reads are not starved during huge writes. On top sits LUKS encryption, then LVM, then XFS, all visible in one lsblk tree.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The file system or page cache builds a bio (block I/O request) describing sectors and memory pages.
  2. Requests enter per-CPU software queues in the multi-queue block layer (blk-mq).
  3. An optional I/O scheduler merges neighbours and orders them for fairness or latency.
  4. Requests are dispatched to hardware queues; NVMe drives expose many queues, one or more per CPU.
  5. The driver sends commands to the device and a completion interrupt (or polling) finishes the request.

Who uses it

Storage engineers, Linux administrators, database administrators, and cloud engineers tuning disks for performance.

Key takeaway

Check and change the scheduler per device in /sys/block/<dev>/queue/scheduler; the active one is shown in [brackets].

Going deeper

  • blk-mq arrived in Linux 3.13 (2014) for fast SSDs, and the old single-queue block layer and its CFQ, deadline and noop schedulers were removed in Linux 5.0.
  • The NVMe specification allows up to 65,535 I/O queues, each up to 65,536 commands deep, compared with SATA AHCI's single queue of 32 commands (NCQ).
  • mq-deadline gives each request a deadline (500 ms for reads, 5 s for writes by default) to prevent starvation; BFQ allocates I/O budgets per process for desktop responsiveness; Kyber targets latency goals.
  • Distributions typically pick 'none' for NVMe and mq-deadline or BFQ for rotational and slower devices, usually through udev rules.
  • The device mapper is the kernel framework behind LVM, dm-crypt, dm-verity (used by Android and ChromeOS for verified boot) and thin provisioning.
  • TRIM/discard tells SSDs which blocks are free so they can maintain write performance; most distributions run fstrim.timer weekly instead of using the continuous discard mount option.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Applying old advice ('use noop/deadline/CFQ'): those single-queue schedulers no longer exist; the modern choices are none, mq-deadline, BFQ and Kyber.
  • Assuming RAID is a backup: RAID protects against disk failure, not deletion, corruption or ransomware.
  • Using RAID 5 on very large hard disks without considering long rebuild times and the risk of a second failure during rebuild.

docs.title: 3.13 Device Drivers, the Driver Model, DMA & the IOMMU
docs.text:
A device driver is code — usually running inside the kernel — that knows how to talk to one kind of hardware and presents it to the rest of the OS in a standard way. The driver model discovers devices, matches them with drivers and manages their power. Fast devices move data directly to and from RAM using DMA, and an IOMMU acts like an MMU for devices, limiting which memory each one can touch.

A network card receiving a packet with DMA. The CPU is involved only at the start and the end; the IOMMU checks the DMA write.

Think of it like…

Drivers are interpreters: the OS speaks one common language and each interpreter translates for a particular foreign guest (device). DMA is the guest walking straight into the storeroom, and the IOMMU is the security guard who only lets each guest into its assigned shelves.

Real-world example

Kofi plugs a new Wi-Fi card into a Linux workstation at fictional Summit Robotics. The PCI bus reports vendor and device IDs, udev loads the matching iwlwifi module, the driver requests its firmware file from /lib/firmware, sets up DMA rings for packets and an MSI-X interrupt per queue, and the IOMMU confines the card to those buffers only.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. A bus (PCIe, USB, platform/device tree, ACPI) enumerates a device and reports its identity.
  2. The driver core matches IDs against registered drivers; udev loads the right module if needed.
  3. The driver's probe() function maps device registers (MMIO), requests interrupts and allocates DMA buffers.
  4. The OS uses the driver through a standard interface: block device, network interface, input device, GPU and so on.
  5. Data moves by DMA; the device raises an interrupt when done, and the IOMMU checks every DMA address.

Who uses it

Embedded and kernel engineers, hardware vendors, Linux and Windows support engineers, and security teams worried about DMA attacks.

Key takeaway

Know the three classic Unix device classes: character (byte streams: terminals, serial), block (disks) and network interfaces (eth0, wlan0 — no /dev node).

Going deeper

  • The Linux driver model represents everything as buses, devices, drivers and classes, exported in sysfs under /sys/bus, /sys/devices and /sys/class; udev reacts to its events to create /dev nodes.
  • PCIe devices expose configuration space with vendor/device IDs and Base Address Registers (BARs) that map device registers into the physical address space for memory-mapped I/O.
  • Interrupt handling is split: a short top half acknowledges the device, and deferred work (softirqs, threaded IRQs, workqueues, NAPI polling for networks) does the heavy lifting.
  • IOMMUs — Intel VT-d, AMD-Vi and Arm SMMU — translate device addresses (IOVAs) through per-device page tables, blocking DMA attacks and enabling safe device passthrough to VMs via VFIO.
  • Thunderbolt DMA attacks such as Thunderclap (2019) and Thunderspy (2020) motivated Windows Kernel DMA Protection (since Windows 10 1803) and default IOMMU use for external ports on Linux and macOS.
  • Windows drivers use the Windows Driver Frameworks (KMDF in kernel, UMDF in user mode) and must be signed through Microsoft's Hardware Dev Center; macOS moved most third-party drivers to user-space DriverKit.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Installing random driver downloads from third-party sites: drivers run with full kernel privilege; use the OS vendor's or hardware vendor's signed packages.
  • Disabling the IOMMU to 'fix' a device problem: it removes DMA protection; prefer updating firmware or drivers, or adjusting IOMMU passthrough settings deliberately.
  • Blaming the driver when firmware is missing: many devices need a firmware blob, so check dmesg for 'failed to load firmware' first.

docs.title: 3.14 Power Management: ACPI, Sleep States & CPU Frequency
docs.text:
Power management lets the OS save energy and heat by slowing or switching off hardware that is not busy. ACPI is the standard through which firmware describes power features to the OS. The OS chooses sleep states for the whole machine (sleep, hibernate), idle states for CPUs (C-states), speeds for CPUs (P-states, chosen by a governor) and low-power states for devices.

ACPI power states, from the system down to devices. The OS manages power at several independent levels at once.

Think of it like…

It is like running a house: you dim lights in empty rooms (device power states), slow the fan when it is cool (CPU frequency), switch most things off at night but keep the fridge running (sleep), or close up the house completely when on holiday (hibernate).

Real-world example

Nadia manages laptops at fictional Ashgrove Council. Battery complaints lead her to check powertop: a USB webcam never enters autosuspend and the CPU stays in shallow C-states. Enabling runtime power management, using the balanced power profile and a firmware update for Modern Standby extend battery life from 6 to 9 hours.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. At boot, firmware hands the OS ACPI tables describing devices, sleep states, thermal zones and CPU performance controls.
  2. When CPUs are idle, the cpuidle governor picks a C-state: deeper states save more power but take longer to wake.
  3. When busy, the cpufreq driver and governor (or the CPU itself, via CPPC/HWP) pick a performance level (P-state).
  4. Idle devices are suspended by runtime power management (PCIe ASPM, USB autosuspend, D3 device states).
  5. On lid close the OS enters a system sleep state — suspend-to-idle/S0ix, suspend-to-RAM (S3) or hibernate (S4).

Who uses it

Laptop and mobile engineers, embedded developers, data-centre operators managing energy bills, and IT staff fixing sleep and battery problems.

Key takeaway

Memorise ACPI system states: S0 working (with S0ix modern standby), S3 suspend-to-RAM, S4 hibernate, S5 soft off, G3 mechanical off.

Going deeper

  • ACPI was created in 1996 by Intel, Microsoft and Toshiba (later with HP and Phoenix) and has been maintained by the UEFI Forum since 2013; firmware supplies tables such as DSDT, SSDT, FADT and MADT in AML bytecode.
  • Many modern laptops support only S0ix ('Modern Standby' on Windows, s2idle on Linux) instead of S3, keeping the system nominally on while hardware drops into very low-power states.
  • Linux cpufreq offers governors such as performance, powersave, schedutil (driven by scheduler utilisation), ondemand and conservative; intel_pstate and amd-pstate drivers can let the CPU choose speeds itself (HWP/CPPC).
  • Energy Performance Preference (EPP) hints from the OS — performance, balance_performance, balance_power, power — tell hardware-managed P-states how to trade speed for energy.
  • Deep CPU C-states can take tens to hundreds of microseconds to exit, so latency-critical servers sometimes limit them (for example with tuned's latency-performance profile).
  • Desktop Linux uses power-profiles-daemon (or tuned-ppd on Fedora) for performance/balanced/power-saver modes; Windows exposes power plans and modes through powercfg and Settings.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Setting the performance governor everywhere: it wastes energy and heat, and on modern CPUs often gives little benefit over schedutil or balanced EPP.
  • Assuming 'sleep' means S3: many laptops use S0ix, so background activity or a misbehaving device can drain the battery overnight.
  • Ignoring firmware updates: many sleep, battery and thermal bugs are in BIOS/UEFI ACPI tables rather than the OS.

docs.title: Try it: Check sleep modes and CPU frequency settings

cat /sys/power/mem_sleep                      # [s2idle] deep
cat /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu0/cpufreq/scaling_driver
cat /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu0/cpufreq/scaling_governor
powerprofilesctl get 2>/dev/null
# Windows (admin)
powercfg /a

A rendering laptop drops from 4.8 GHz to 2.1 GHz; cat /sys/class/thermal/thermal_zone*/temp reveals 98 °C. powertopIntel (open source) · Tool · Current · Intermediate Shows which processes and devices wake the system and suggests power-saving tunables. sudo powertop --auto-tune applies all suggested runtime-PM settings for a quick battery test. power-profiles-daemon, TLP and tunedfreedesktop.org; TLP project; Red Hat · Software · Current · Intermediate Linux services that apply power or performance profiles: simple desktop modes, detailed laptop tuning, or server profiles. sudo tuned-adm profile throughput-performance tunes a database server's CPU and disk settings. powercfgMicrosoft Windows · Command · Current · Intermediate Windows tool to inspect and change power plans, list sleep states and diagnose wake and battery issues. powercfg /batteryreport creates an HTML report of battery capacity and recent usage.

docs.title: Chapter 1: Operating System Foundations
docs.text: This chapter builds the mental model the rest of the guide rests on: what an operating system is for, the hardware it manages, the wall between user mode and kernel mode, and how programs cross it with system calls and interrupts. It then tours kernel designs and OS types, follows a computer from power-on to login, explains POSIX, traces OS history from CTSS to Android, maps the 2026 market and gets you started at the command line.

docs.title: 1.1 What an Operating System Does
docs.text:
An operating system (OS) is the master program that runs a computer. It shares out the processor, memory, storage and devices among programs, hides messy hardware details behind simple ideas like files and windows, and stops programs from harming each other or the system. Everything else — browsers, games, databases — runs on top of it.

Where the OS sits. Applications never touch hardware directly; every request passes through the system-call door into the kernel.

Think of it like…

An OS is like the management of a busy hotel: it assigns rooms (memory), schedules the shared lifts and staff (CPU time), gives guests a simple front desk instead of letting them wander into the boiler room (abstraction), and makes each guest's key open only their own room (protection).

Real-world example

Amara, a student at the fictional Lakeside College, opens Spotify, a browser with 30 tabs and VS Code on her 16 GB laptop. The OS gives each program its own private memory, switches the 8 CPU cores between roughly 300 processes many times per second, and turns a click on 'Save' into block writes on her NVMe drive. When one browser tab crashes, the OS cleans up only that process; everything else keeps running.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. At boot the kernel takes control of the CPU, memory and devices and starts the first user program.
  2. Programs ask for services (open a file, send a packet, get memory) through system calls instead of touching hardware directly.
  3. The scheduler shares CPU time, and the memory manager gives each process its own virtual address space.
  4. Device drivers translate generic requests into commands for specific hardware.
  5. Protection checks (privilege levels, permissions, memory isolation) stop one program or user harming another.
  6. When a program exits, the OS reclaims every resource it held.

Who uses it

Every software developer, system administrator, DevOps/SRE engineer, security analyst and embedded engineer relies on OS knowledge daily — it is the foundation under virtualization, containers and the cloud.

Key takeaway

Memorise the three classic roles — resource manager (allocator), extended machine (abstraction) and protector (isolation); they frame most OS exam answers.

Going deeper

  • Tanenbaum describes two complementary views: top-down, the OS is an 'extended machine' offering clean abstractions; bottom-up, it is a 'resource manager' multiplexing hardware in time (CPU) and in space (memory, disk).
  • The core abstractions are few: processes and threads for the CPU, virtual address spaces for memory, files and directories for storage, sockets for networks, and handles or file descriptors that name them all.
  • 'Operating system' is used loosely: strictly it is the privileged kernel; broadly it includes system libraries, shells, the init system, utilities and the desktop — the root of the 'Linux vs GNU/Linux' naming argument.
  • Kernels are large: the Linux source tree passed roughly 40 million lines in 2025, though any one build compiles only a fraction of it, mostly the drivers for that machine's hardware.
  • Good OS design separates mechanism (how to switch tasks or map pages) from policy (which task to pick, which page to evict), so policies can change without rewriting the core.
  • The kernel's own overhead is normally a few percent of CPU, but pathological OS behaviour — thrashing, lock contention, excessive context switches — can make fast hardware feel slow.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Thinking the desktop or GUI is the OS: the graphical shell is just another program, and most servers run the same kernel with no GUI at all.
  • Believing apps talk to hardware directly: ordinary programs must go through the kernel via system calls; direct hardware access is blocked.
  • Equating 'Linux' with a complete OS: Linux is the kernel; distributions add GNU tools, systemd, package managers and desktops.

docs.title: Try it: See what your OS is managing right now
docs.text:
# Linux / macOS
uname -a            # kernel name and version
ps aux | wc -l      # roughly how many processes are running
free -h             # memory use (Linux)

# Windows PowerShell
Get-ComputerInfo -Property OsName,OsVersion
(Get-Process).Count

Windows 11, macOS, Ubuntu Linux, Android and iOS are all operating systems built around a kernel. KernelComponent · Current · Beginner The privileged core of the OS, running with full hardware access and handling scheduling, memory, devices and system calls. Linux's /boot/vmlinuz-* file and Windows' ntoskrnl.exe are loaded at boot and stay in memory until shutdown. Resource manager roleConcept · Current · Beginner The OS divides CPU time, memory, disk and network bandwidth fairly and efficiently among competing programs and users. A video render and a video call share 8 cores; the OS favours the call so its audio never stutters. Time and space multiplexingConcept · Current · Beginner Sharing a resource by taking turns (CPU time slices) or by dividing it into parts (memory regions, disk blocks). Four programs take turns on one core every few milliseconds, while each also owns a separate slice of the 16 GB RAM. Abstraction (extended machine)Concept · Current · Beginner Turning raw hardware into simple, uniform ideas — files, processes, sockets, windows — so programmers needn't know device details. A Python program calls open('notes.txt') and works identically on an SSD, a USB stick or a network share. Protection and isolationConcept · Current · Beginner Mechanisms ensuring one process or user cannot read, change or crash another's memory, files or the kernel itself. A crashing game shows an error and exits, while your unsaved document in another app is unaffected. Linux's scheduler mechanism stays the same while sched_ext lets administrators plug in a different scheduling policy. MultiprogrammingConcept · Current · Beginner Keeping several programs in memory so the CPU can run another whenever the current one waits for I/O. While a payroll job waits for a tape or disk read, the mainframe runs a second job instead of sitting idle. Preemptive multitaskingConcept · Current · Beginner The OS forcibly switches between tasks using timer interrupts, so no single program can monopolise the CPU. An infinite loop in one app cannot freeze Windows 11 or macOS; other windows stay responsive. Multi-user operating systemConcept · Current · Beginner An OS that lets several users work at once or in turn, each with separate accounts, files and permissions. Forty students log in by SSH to one university Linux server, each confined to their own home directory. Ubuntu uses GNOME by default and Kubuntu uses KDE Plasma, yet both run on the same Linux kernel.

docs.title: 1.2 The Hardware an OS Manages
docs.text:
To understand an OS you need a mental picture of the machine underneath: a CPU with cores and registers that execute instructions, memory (RAM) that holds running programs, storage that keeps data when the power is off, and devices connected through buses. The OS's job is to share all of these safely.

Typical access latency (log scale). Each step down the hierarchy is roughly 10-1,000 times slower, so the OS works hard to keep hot data high up.

Think of it like…

The computer is a kitchen: CPU cores are chefs, registers are what each chef holds in their hands, cache is the worktop, RAM is the fridge, the SSD is the storeroom down the corridor — and the OS is the head chef handing out work.

Real-world example

Ravi's fictional start-up, PixelPress, rents a cloud server with 16 vCPUs, 64 GB of RAM and a 1 TB NVMe disk. Reading from L1 cache takes about 1 ns, from RAM about 100 ns, and from the NVMe disk around 100 µs — roughly 100,000 times slower than cache. That gap is why the OS keeps recently used file data in RAM and why PixelPress's database is sized to fit its hot data in memory.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The CPU repeatedly fetches an instruction, decodes it and executes it, using registers for working values.
  2. The instruction pointer (program counter) says which instruction comes next; the stack pointer tracks function calls.
  3. The memory management unit (MMU) translates every virtual address a program uses into a physical RAM address.
  4. Devices (disks, network cards, GPUs) are driven through control registers, move data to RAM by DMA, then raise interrupts.
  5. A hardware timer interrupts the CPU periodically so the OS can regain control and switch tasks.

Who uses it

OS developers, performance engineers, embedded engineers and anyone sizing servers or troubleshooting slowness need this hardware picture.

Key takeaway

Memorise the latency ladder in rough powers of ten — register < cache < RAM < SSD < network/disk — interviewers love 'why does the page cache matter so much?'

Going deeper

  • A modern x86-64 core has 16 general-purpose 64-bit registers (RAX-R15), the instruction pointer RIP, RFLAGS and, with AVX-512, 32 vector registers of 512 bits — all part of the state saved on every context switch.
  • Caches come in levels: L1 is typically 32-64 KB per core, L2 one to a few megabytes per core, and a shared L3 tens of megabytes; cache lines are 64 bytes on x86 and most Arm cores.
  • Symmetric multiprocessing (SMP) means all cores share memory and run one kernel; NUMA servers give each socket its own local memory, so the OS tries to keep each thread near its data.
  • Hybrid CPUs — Intel's P-cores and E-cores since 12th-gen Core (2021), Arm big.LITTLE and Apple's performance and efficiency cores — force the scheduler to decide where a thread runs, not just when.
  • Simultaneous multithreading (Intel Hyper-Threading, AMD SMT) exposes two logical CPUs per core that share execution units, so 16 logical CPUs are not sixteen times one core's speed.
  • Devices are reached through memory-mapped I/O or x86 I/O ports; PCI Express links connect NVMe drives, GPUs and NICs, and an IOMMU restricts which memory each device may access.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming more cores always means faster programs: single-threaded code uses one core; the OS can only spread work that is already split into threads or processes.
  • Confusing RAM with storage: 'memory' is volatile working space, while 'storage' (SSD, disk) keeps data without power and is thousands of times slower.
  • Ignoring NUMA on large servers: a thread on socket 0 reading memory attached to socket 1 pays a noticeable latency penalty.

docs.title: Try it: Inspect your CPU, memory and disks
docs.text:
# Linux
lscpu | head -20        # cores, threads, caches, NUMA nodes
lsblk                   # disks and partitions
head -3 /proc/meminfo

# macOS
sysctl -n machdep.cpu.brand_string hw.ncpu hw.memsize

# Windows PowerShell
Get-CimInstance Win32_Processor | Select-Object Name,NumberOfCores,NumberOfLogicalProcessors

docs.text: Name What it does Example CPU coreIntel, AMD, Arm licensees, RISC-V vendors · Component · Current · Beginner An independent execution unit that fetches, decodes and runs instructions; one chip may contain dozens of cores. An AMD Ryzen 7 9700X has 8 cores and 16 hardware threads, so the OS sees 16 logical CPUs. RegistersComponent · Current · Beginner The fastest, tiny storage inside a core, holding current values, the instruction pointer and the stack pointer. On x86-64 the RIP register holds the address of the next instruction and RSP points to the top of the stack. Instruction set architecture (ISA)Intel/AMD (x86-64), Arm (AArch64), RISC-V International · Standard · Current · Beginner The contract between software and CPU: instructions, registers, privilege modes and memory model. Apple M-series Macs and Windows on Arm laptops run Arm64 code; most cloud servers run x86-64, with Arm instances such as AWS Graviton growing. Cache hierarchyConcept · Current · Beginner Small, fast memories (L1, L2, L3) between core and RAM that keep recently used data close to the CPU. A loop over a 20 KB array stays in L1 cache and runs many times faster than code jumping randomly through 4 GB. RAM (DRAM)JEDEC (DDR5, LPDDR5X standards) · Component · Current · Beginner Main memory holding running programs and their data: fast but volatile, so its contents vanish at power-off. A laptop with 16 GB of DDR5 holds the OS, browser and editor; when it fills, the OS compresses or swaps out pages. Storage device (SSD/HDD)NVM Express, SATA-IO · Component · Current · Beginner Non-volatile storage for files and the OS itself, read and written in blocks through device drivers. A PCIe 4.0 NVMe SSD reads around 7 GB/s sequentially, yet small random reads are still far slower than RAM. Hardware timerComponent · Current · Intermediate A clock device that interrupts the CPU at set intervals, letting the OS regain control for scheduling and timekeeping. Linux kernels typically tick at 250 or 1,000 Hz (CONFIG_HZ), meaning every 4 ms or every 1 ms. PCI ExpressPCI-SIG · Standard · Current · Intermediate High-speed serial interconnect linking CPUs to GPUs, NVMe drives and network cards; each generation roughly doubles per-lane bandwidth. A PCIe 5.0 x4 NVMe SSD can reach about 14 GB/s; the OS discovers it by enumerating the PCIe bus at boot. SMP and multicoreConcept · Current · Intermediate Symmetric multiprocessing: all cores share memory and any core can run kernel code, so the kernel needs careful locking. `nproc` prints how many logical CPUs the OS sees; Linux supports systems with thousands of them. NUMAConcept · Current · Advanced Non-Uniform Memory Access: on multi-socket servers each CPU has local RAM that is faster than another socket's RAM. `numactl --hardware` on a 2-socket database server shows two nodes; binding PostgreSQL to one node cuts memory latency. Hybrid (heterogeneous) coresIntel, Arm, Apple · Concept · Current · Intermediate Chips mixing fast performance cores with power-saving efficiency cores, requiring smarter OS scheduling. An Intel Core Ultra laptop runs background indexing on E-cores while the game in focus stays on P-cores. SMT / Hyper-ThreadingIntel (Hyper-Threading), AMD (SMT) · Concept · Current · Intermediate One physical core presents two logical CPUs that share its execution units to fill idle cycles. A 4-core, 8-thread laptop shows 8 CPUs in Task Manager, but heavy maths may gain only 10-30% from the extra threads.

docs.title: 1.3 Kernel Space vs User Space and Privilege Rings
docs.text:
The CPU has at least two modes: a privileged kernel mode where any instruction and any memory is allowed, and a restricted user mode for ordinary programs. The kernel runs in kernel mode; apps run in user mode and must ask the kernel for anything sensitive. This split is what stops one buggy app from crashing the whole machine.

Privilege levels, least to most powerful. Each level can see and control everything above it; bugs lower down are the most dangerous.

Think of it like…

It is like a bank: customers (user mode) stay in the public hall and hand forms across the counter, while only staff (kernel mode) may enter the vault — the counter window is the system call.

Real-world example

Leo, a student at the fictional Northgate University, writes a C program that executes the privileged x86 instruction `hlt` to halt the CPU. Because his program runs in ring 3, the CPU raises a general-protection fault instead; Linux catches it and kills the program with SIGSEGV while every other program keeps running. The same instruction in the kernel's idle loop, running in ring 0, works normally.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. At power-on the CPU starts in its most privileged mode; the kernel sets up page tables and interrupt tables, then drops to user mode to run the first program.
  2. Every memory page is marked user or supervisor; user-mode code touching a supervisor page triggers a fault.
  3. Privileged instructions (loading page tables, disabling interrupts, port I/O) fault if executed in user mode.
  4. To request a service, user code executes a special instruction (syscall, svc or ecall) that switches to kernel mode at a fixed entry point.
  5. The kernel validates the request, does the work and returns to user mode with a result.

Who uses it

Kernel and driver developers, security researchers, exploit analysts and anyone debugging crashes ('kernel panic' versus 'segfault') work with this boundary.

Key takeaway

x86 has four rings but mainstream OSes use only ring 0 (kernel) and ring 3 (user); on Arm the equivalents are EL0 (apps) and EL1 (kernel), with EL2 for hypervisors and EL3 for secure firmware.

Going deeper

  • On x86 the current privilege level (CPL) is held in the low two bits of the CS register; the interrupt descriptor table and the page-table user/supervisor bit together decide what ring-3 code can reach.
  • Linux maps the kernel into the upper half of every process's virtual address space, so a system call does not need a full address-space switch, while user programs live in the lower half.
  • The 2018 Meltdown flaw let user code speculatively read kernel memory; Kernel Page-Table Isolation (KPTI, called KVA Shadow on Windows) now unmaps most of the kernel while user code runs, costing a few percent on syscall-heavy workloads.
  • SMEP (Intel Ivy Bridge, 2012) and SMAP (Broadwell, 2014), with AMD equivalents, stop the kernel from executing or casually reading user pages, blocking a whole class of privilege-escalation exploits.
  • Arm defines four exception levels — EL0 applications, EL1 kernel, EL2 hypervisor, EL3 secure monitor for TrustZone — while RISC-V uses U, S and M modes plus a hypervisor extension.
  • Some code runs 'below ring 0': hypervisors (informally ring −1), System Management Mode (ring −2) and management engines (ring −3); flaws there are serious because the OS cannot observe them.
  • Moving code out of the kernel improves robustness: Windows' UMDF and Linux FUSE run drivers and file systems as ordinary processes, so their crashes do not take the system down.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Thinking 'running as root or Administrator' means kernel mode: admin processes still run in user mode; they are simply allowed to make more privileged requests.
  • Picturing the kernel as a separate process running beside apps: most kernel code runs on behalf of a process during its system calls and interrupts.
  • Assuming user-mode programs can't hurt the system: they can't directly, but a faulty kernel-mode driver (as in the July 2024 CrowdStrike outage) crashes the whole machine.

docs.title: Try it: Watch time spent in user mode vs kernel mode
docs.text:
# Linux/macOS: 'user' vs 'sys' time of one command
time ls -R /usr > /dev/null

# Linux: per-second user (us) vs system (sy) CPU percentages
vmstat 1 5

# Windows: Task Manager > Performance > CPU, right-click graph > 'Show kernel times'

docs.text: Name What it does Example User modeConcept · Current · Beginner Restricted CPU mode for applications: privileged instructions and kernel memory are off-limits. Your web browser, text editor and even a root shell all execute in user mode. Kernel mode (supervisor mode)Concept · Current · Beginner Privileged CPU mode in which code may run any instruction and access all memory and devices. The Linux scheduler, the ext4 file-system code and the Wi-Fi driver all run in kernel mode. Protection rings (x86)Intel / AMD · Concept · Current · Intermediate Four privilege levels (0-3) on x86; ring 0 is most privileged and mainstream OSes use only rings 0 and 3. A ring-3 program executing `cli` (disable interrupts) gets a general-protection fault instead of freezing the PC. Arm exception levels (EL0-EL3)Arm · Concept · Current · Intermediate Arm's privilege model: EL0 applications, EL1 OS kernel, EL2 hypervisor, EL3 secure-monitor firmware. On recent Pixel phones apps run at EL0, the Linux kernel at EL1 and Google's pKVM hypervisor at EL2. RISC-V privilege modesRISC-V International (Privileged Specification) · Concept · Current · Advanced User (U), Supervisor (S) and Machine (M) modes, plus a hypervisor extension, defined in the RISC-V privileged spec. OpenSBI firmware runs in M-mode and provides services to a Linux kernel running in S-mode on a RISC-V board. Privileged instructionConcept · Current · Intermediate A CPU instruction only kernel mode may execute, such as loading page tables, halting or disabling interrupts. Writing the x86 CR3 register switches page tables — only the kernel does this, on every process switch. Mode switchConcept · Current · Intermediate The CPU moving between user and kernel mode via a system call, interrupt or exception; cheaper than a full context switch. A program calling getpid() makes a mode switch into the kernel and back, usually in well under a microsecond. Kernel address spaceConcept · Current · Intermediate The region of every process's virtual memory reserved for kernel code and data, mapped but inaccessible from user mode. On 64-bit Linux, user programs live in the lower half of the address space and the kernel in the upper half. KPTI (Kernel Page-Table Isolation)Linux 4.15 (2018); Windows 'KVA Shadow' · Component · Current · Advanced Separate page tables that hide kernel memory from user mode, defeating the Meltdown attack. `cat /sys/devices/system/cpu/vulnerabilities/meltdown` prints 'Mitigation: PTI' on affected Intel CPUs. SMEP / SMAPIntel / AMD · Concept · Current · Advanced CPU features that stop the kernel executing (SMEP) or unexpectedly accessing (SMAP) user-space memory. `grep -o -w -E 'smep|smap' /proc/cpuinfo | sort -u` shows whether your CPU supports them. Vulnerable SMM handlers let attackers hide code that even the OS kernel cannot detect or remove. Windows UMDF drivers for some USB devices and Linux's sshfs (a FUSE file system) run outside the kernel. Kernel panic / Blue ScreenConcept · Current · Beginner The OS halts deliberately when kernel-mode code hits an unrecoverable error, to avoid corrupting data. A faulty driver triggers a Linux 'kernel panic' or a Windows stop error (BSOD); a user-mode crash just ends one app.

docs.title: 1.4 System Calls End to End
docs.text:
A system call is how a program asks the kernel to do something it isn't allowed to do itself — read a file, start a process, send network data. The program places a request number and arguments in CPU registers, executes a special instruction, and the CPU jumps into the kernel, which does the work and returns a result or an error code.

One read() from app to disk and back. The app sees one function call; underneath, the CPU changes mode twice and the kernel may sleep until the disk interrupt arrives.

Think of it like…

It is like ordering at a drive-through: you can't walk into the kitchen, so you speak your order number into the speaker (the syscall number), drive to the window (the mode switch) and receive your food — or a 'sorry, sold out' (an error code).

Real-world example

When Sofia runs `cat notes.txt` on her Ubuntu laptop, cat calls the C library's open(), read() and write(). glibc puts system-call number 257 (openat) in the RAX register and the file path in RSI, then executes the `syscall` instruction. The kernel checks permissions, finds the file in the page cache and returns file descriptor 3; a later read() copies 1,200 bytes into cat's buffer. Running `strace cat notes.txt` shows every one of these calls.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The program calls a library wrapper such as read() in libc (on Windows, a Win32 function such as ReadFile, which calls into ntdll.dll).
  2. The wrapper loads the system-call number and arguments into registers — on Linux x86-64 the number goes in RAX and arguments in RDI, RSI, RDX, R10, R8 and R9.
  3. It executes the trap instruction — `syscall` on x86-64, `svc #0` on Arm64, `ecall` on RISC-V — switching the CPU to kernel mode.
  4. Kernel entry code saves user registers, looks the number up in the system-call table and calls the matching handler.
  5. The handler validates pointers and permissions, does the work (perhaps sleeping until I/O completes) and sets a return value.
  6. The kernel restores registers and returns to user mode; on failure libc stores a code such as ENOENT in errno and returns −1.

Who uses it

Systems programmers, performance engineers, security engineers writing seccomp or EDR rules, and anyone answering 'why is this program hanging?' with strace.

Key takeaway

Know a few Linux x86-64 numbers (read = 0, write = 1, execve = 59) and the tracing tools: strace on Linux, dtruss/DTrace on macOS and Process Monitor on Windows.

Going deeper

  • Linux x86-64 defines more than 450 system-call numbers in arch/x86/entry/syscalls/syscall_64.tbl; new calls are appended and old numbers are never reused, so binaries keep working for decades.
  • The vDSO is a small kernel-provided library mapped into every Linux process so calls such as clock_gettime() and gettimeofday() run entirely in user mode without any mode switch.
  • Windows does not document its system-call numbers and changes them between builds; programs must call ntdll.dll (NtReadFile and friends) or Win32 APIs, so Windows compatibility is kept at the API level.
  • Linux's stable system-call ABI ('we do not break user space') lets containers run an Alpine userland on an Ubuntu host kernel and lets gVisor and WSL 1 reimplement the interface.
  • A trivial system call costs very roughly 100 nanoseconds on modern x86, but security mitigations can multiply that, which is why batching interfaces such as io_uring and sendmmsg exist.
  • Older entry mechanisms (int 0x80, sysenter) gave way to `syscall`; Intel's FRED (Flexible Return and Event Delivery), enabled by default in recent Linux 7.x kernels on supporting CPUs, redesigns ring transitions.
  • seccomp lets a process install a filter restricting which system calls it may make — the basis of Docker's default profile and Chrome's sandbox, covered with OS security later in this guide.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Confusing library functions with system calls: printf() is a libc function that buffers text and only occasionally calls write(); many libc functions make no system call at all.
  • Reading errno after a successful call: errno is meaningful only after a function reports failure, usually by returning −1; check the return value first.
  • Assuming system calls are free: a loop doing one-byte read() calls can be hundreds of times slower than reading 64 KB at once.

docs.title: Try it: Watch every system call a command makes (Linux)
docs.text:
strace -c ls /tmp                       # summary table of system calls
strace -e trace=openat cat /etc/hostname # only file opens
strace -f -e trace=network curl -sI https://example.com

# Windows: Sysinternals Process Monitor shows file, registry and process calls
