Opening, reading and closing a file takes at least three system calls: openat, read and close. System-call tableComponent · Current · Intermediate Kernel array mapping each system-call number to its handler function. On Linux x86-64, entry 0 is read, 1 write, 39 getpid, 59 execve and 60 exit. syscall / svc / ecall instructionsIntel/AMD, Arm, RISC-V · Concept · Current · Advanced The CPU instructions that trap into the kernel on x86-64, Arm64 and RISC-V respectively. Disassembling glibc's read() with objdump shows a `syscall` instruction right after the number is loaded into EAX. C standard library (libc)GNU glibc, musl, Apple libSystem, Microsoft UCRT · Software · Current · Beginner Library wrapping system calls in friendly C functions, plus strings, memory allocation, maths and more. Alpine Linux uses musl and Ubuntu uses glibc; the same C source compiles against either. ntdll.dll and the Native APIMicrosoft · API · Current · Advanced Windows' lowest user-mode layer: Win32 calls such as CreateFileW end in ntdll stubs like NtCreateFile that enter the kernel. Malware analysts watch calls such as NtWriteVirtualMemory in ntdll to spot code being injected into other processes. read() / write()POSIX · System call · Current · Beginner Copy bytes between a file descriptor and a memory buffer — the basis of nearly all Unix I/O. write(1, "hi\n", 3) prints 'hi' on standard output without using printf. openat() / close()POSIX · System call · Current · Intermediate openat opens a file by path (relative to a directory) and returns a file descriptor; close releases it. strace shows openat(AT_FDCWD, "/etc/hostname", O_RDONLY) = 3 when you run cat /etc/hostname. getpid()POSIX · System call · Current · Intermediate Returns the calling process's ID — one of the simplest system calls, often used to measure raw syscall overhead. A microbenchmark calling getpid() a million times measures the cost of entering and leaving the kernel. errnoPOSIX / ISO C · Concept · Current · Beginner Thread-local variable holding the error code after a failed call, such as ENOENT (no such file) or EACCES (permission denied). Opening a missing file returns −1 with errno = ENOENT, and perror() prints 'No such file or directory'. vDSOLinux kernel · Component · Current · Advanced Kernel-supplied shared library mapped into each process that runs selected time-related calls entirely in user mode. `ldd /bin/ls` lists linux-vdso.so.1 with no file path, because the kernel itself provides it. straceOpen source (Linux) · Tool · Current · Intermediate Traces the system calls and signals of a process using ptrace, showing arguments and return values. strace -f -e trace=network curl example.com shows the socket, connect and sendto calls that curl makes. Process MonitorMicrosoft Sysinternals · Tool · Current · Intermediate Windows tool logging real-time file, registry, network and process activity of every program. A help-desk engineer filters ProcMon on 'NAME NOT FOUND' to find the missing DLL that stops an app starting. DTrace / dtrussOriginally Sun Microsystems; macOS and FreeBSD · Tool · Current · Advanced Dynamic tracing framework; its dtruss script shows a process's system calls on macOS. sudo dtruss ls lists the open and getdirentries calls ls makes; System Integrity Protection may limit full tracing. Stable syscall ABI ('don't break user space')Linux kernel policy · Concept · Current · Intermediate Linux promises that system-call numbers and behaviour visible to programs never change incompatibly. A statically linked program built in 2005 still runs on a 2026 Linux 7.x kernel.

docs.title: 1.5 Interrupts, Exceptions and Traps
docs.text:
Interrupts are signals that make the CPU stop what it is doing and run kernel code. Hardware interrupts come from devices ('a network packet arrived'); exceptions come from the running instruction itself ('divide by zero', 'that page isn't in memory'); traps are deliberate, like a system call or a debugger breakpoint.

Life of a hardware interrupt. Keep the top half tiny; the heavy lifting happens later in a bottom half with interrupts re-enabled.

Think of it like…

A chef cooking (the CPU) can be interrupted by the doorbell (hardware interrupt), by burning a hand on the pan (exception) or by deliberately ringing for the manager (trap) — each time they put the pan down, deal with it and carry on.

Real-world example

On the fictional Riverside Hospital's file server, a 25 Gbit network card receives a burst of packets. Instead of interrupting for every packet, it raises one MSI-X interrupt on CPU 3; the handler acknowledges it within microseconds and schedules NAPI polling in a softirq, which processes up to 64 packets per batch. Meanwhile CPU 5 takes a page-fault exception when the database touches memory that was swapped out, and the kernel loads the page before re-running the instruction.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. A device asserts an interrupt (or the CPU detects an exception); the interrupt controller (APIC on x86, GIC on Arm) delivers a vector number to a CPU.
  2. The CPU finishes or abandons the current instruction, saves the instruction pointer and flags, and switches to kernel mode and a kernel stack.
  3. It looks up the vector in the interrupt descriptor table (IDT) or Arm vector table and jumps to the handler.
  4. The 'top half' does the minimum: acknowledge the device, grab urgent data, schedule deferred work.
  5. Deferred 'bottom half' work (softirqs, tasklets, workqueues, threaded IRQs; DPCs on Windows) runs soon after with interrupts enabled.
  6. The kernel returns from the interrupt (iretq on x86, eret on Arm), possibly switching to a different task if a reschedule is due.

Who uses it

Kernel and driver developers, embedded and firmware engineers, real-time engineers, and performance tuners who set IRQ affinity on busy network servers.

Key takeaway

Interview classic: hardware interrupts are asynchronous (independent of the current instruction), while exceptions and traps are synchronous (caused by it); a page fault is a restartable fault.

Going deeper

  • x86 has 256 interrupt vectors: 0-31 are reserved for CPU exceptions (0 divide error, 3 breakpoint, 6 invalid opcode, 13 general protection, 14 page fault) and the rest serve devices and inter-processor interrupts.
  • Exceptions come in three kinds: faults are restartable (a page fault re-runs the instruction), traps are reported after the instruction (int3 breakpoint) and aborts are unrecoverable (double fault, machine check).
  • Message-Signalled Interrupts replace interrupt wires with memory writes; MSI-X allows up to 2,048 vectors per device, so a multi-queue NIC or NVMe drive can steer each queue to its own CPU.
  • Windows orders interrupt work by Interrupt Request Level: device ISRs run at high IRQL and queue Deferred Procedure Calls at DISPATCH_LEVEL; touching pageable memory at high IRQL causes the IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL blue screen.
  • At very high packet rates interrupts can starve real work (interrupt livelock), so drivers switch to polling: Linux NAPI, NIC interrupt coalescing and busy-polling for ultra-low-latency systems.
  • Non-maskable interrupts cannot be disabled; Linux uses them for the hard-lockup watchdog and perf sampling, and a server's NMI button can force a crash dump of a hung machine.
  • Inter-processor interrupts let one CPU poke another — to reschedule, run a function remotely or shoot down stale TLB entries after a page-table change.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Doing slow work in an interrupt handler: handlers must not sleep or wait; defer heavy processing to a bottom half or kernel thread.
  • Calling every unusual event a 'trap': strictly, hardware interrupts are asynchronous, while traps and faults are caused by the current instruction.
  • Assuming every page fault is an error: most are normal (demand paging, copy-on-write); only invalid accesses become segmentation faults.

docs.title: Try it: Watch interrupts arrive
docs.text:
# Linux: interrupt counts per CPU and per device
head -15 /proc/interrupts
watch -n1 "grep -i -E 'nvme|eth|enp|LOC' /proc/interrupts"

# Windows: interrupts per second
typeperf "\Processor(_Total)\Interrupts/sec" -sc 5

docs.title: Key kernels, commands, tools, standards & concepts
docs.text: Name What it does Example Hardware interrupt (IRQ)Concept · Current · Beginner Asynchronous signal from a device asking the CPU for attention, such as completed disk I/O or a key press. Each keystroke on a USB keyboard ends in an interrupt that wakes the kernel's input driver. Exception (fault, trap, abort)Concept · Current · Intermediate Synchronous event caused by the current instruction, such as divide-by-zero, an invalid opcode or a page fault. Integer division by zero in C triggers x86 vector 0, and Linux sends the process SIGFPE. Trap (software interrupt)Concept · Current · Intermediate An intentional exception used to enter the kernel or a debugger, such as a system-call instruction or int3. A debugger sets a breakpoint by overwriting an instruction's first byte with int3 (0xCC). General protection fault (#GP)Intel / AMD · Concept · Current · Intermediate x86 exception for privilege and segment violations, such as user code running a privileged instruction. A ring-3 program executing `hlt` gets #GP (vector 13); Linux delivers SIGSEGV and the shell prints 'Segmentation fault'. Interrupt Descriptor Table (IDT)Intel / AMD · Component · Current · Advanced x86 table of up to 256 entries mapping each interrupt or exception vector to its handler. Old rootkits hooked IDT entries; modern kernels protect the table and Windows PatchGuard checks it for tampering. APIC / GICIntel/AMD (APIC); Arm (GIC) · Component · Current · Advanced Interrupt controllers that route device interrupts to CPU cores: the APIC family on x86, the Generic Interrupt Controller on Arm. The Raspberry Pi 4's BCM2711 chip uses an Arm GIC-400 to route interrupts to its four cores. MSI / MSI-XPCI-SIG · Standard · Current · Advanced Message-signalled interrupts: PCIe devices raise interrupts by writing to a special address instead of using a wire. An NVMe SSD gives each I/O queue its own MSI-X vector so completions land on the CPU that issued the request. Interrupt handler (ISR) / top halfConcept · Current · Intermediate Short, fast kernel routine run immediately on an interrupt; acknowledges the device and defers the rest. A network driver's ISR masks further receive interrupts and schedules NAPI polling. Bottom halves: softirq, tasklet, workqueueLinux kernel · Component · Current · Advanced Linux mechanisms for deferred interrupt work that runs later with interrupts enabled; workqueues may even sleep. The ksoftirqd/N kernel threads in `ps` output process network softirqs when there is too much to finish inline. DPC and IRQLMicrosoft Windows · Concept · Current · Advanced Windows' Deferred Procedure Calls and Interrupt Request Levels, which order interrupt work by priority. LatencyMon reveals which driver's DPCs cause audio crackles on a Windows music-production PC. Non-maskable interrupt (NMI)Concept · Current · Advanced High-priority interrupt that cannot be disabled, used for critical hardware errors, watchdogs and debugging. Linux's hard-lockup detector uses NMIs to report 'NMI watchdog: hard LOCKUP' when a CPU stops responding. Inter-processor interrupt (IPI)Concept · Current · Advanced An interrupt one CPU sends to another, for rescheduling, TLB shootdowns or remote function calls. The RES and TLB lines in /proc/interrupts count rescheduling and TLB-shootdown IPIs on each CPU. Timer interrupt and tickless kernelConcept · Current · Intermediate Periodic timer interrupts drive scheduling and timekeeping; tickless (NO_HZ) kernels stop the tick on idle CPUs to save power. With CONFIG_NO_HZ_IDLE, an idle laptop core sleeps deeply instead of waking 1,000 times a second.

docs.title: 1.6 OS Architectures: Monolithic, Microkernel, Hybrid, Unikernel, Exokernel
docs.text:
Kernels are built in different shapes. A monolithic kernel puts almost everything — drivers, file systems, networking — into one big privileged program; a microkernel keeps only the bare minimum privileged and runs everything else as separate user-mode servers; hybrid kernels mix the two. Unikernels and exokernels are more radical designs for special uses.

Three classic kernel designs

Monolithic Microkernel Hybrid In kernel mode Everything: drivers, FS, network Scheduling, memory, IPC only Core plus most services Drivers run Inside the kernel As user-mode servers Mostly inside the kernel Driver crash Can panic the system Restart that server Can crash the system Service calls Function calls IPC messages Mostly function calls Examples Linux, FreeBSD, OpenBSD seL4, QNX, MINIX 3, Zircon Windows NT, Apple XNU

The real difference is what runs in kernel mode, and therefore what a single bug can take down.

Think of it like…

A monolithic kernel is an open-plan office where everyone shouts across desks (fast, but one fire spreads everywhere); a microkernel is a building of locked rooms passing notes under the doors (safer, slower); a unikernel is a food truck built to serve exactly one dish.

Real-world example

The fictional carmaker Volta Motors chooses QNX, a microkernel real-time OS, for its digital dashboard: if the graphics driver crashes, it restarts in milliseconds while the speedometer keeps updating. Its cloud back-end runs on Linux, a monolithic kernel, for raw throughput, and its research team is testing a Unikraft unikernel that boots a small web service in a few milliseconds.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Decide what must run privileged: at minimum, address-space management, thread scheduling and inter-process communication (IPC).
  2. Monolithic: link drivers, file systems and the network stack into the kernel; components call each other as plain functions.
  3. Microkernel: run drivers and services as separate user processes that talk by message passing through the kernel.
  4. Hybrid: keep a microkernel-like structure but run performance-critical services in kernel mode (Windows NT, XNU).
  5. Unikernel: compile one application plus only the OS library pieces it needs into a single image that runs directly on a hypervisor.
  6. Exokernel: the kernel only multiplexes raw hardware securely; applications bring their own 'library OS' abstractions.

Who uses it

OS designers, embedded and automotive engineers choosing an RTOS, security architects needing verified kernels, and cloud engineers experimenting with lightweight VMs.

Key takeaway

Remember the trade-off: monolithic means fast function calls and simplicity; microkernel means isolation, reliability and verifiability at the cost of IPC overhead.

Going deeper

  • The 1992 Tanenbaum–Torvalds debate on comp.os.minix argued Linux was obsolete because it was monolithic; decades later Linux dominates general computing, while microkernels won safety-critical niches such as cars, avionics and modems.
  • Early microkernels like Mach were slow because each service request needed several context switches; Jochen Liedtke's L4 (1993) showed IPC could be roughly an order of magnitude faster, founding the L4 family.
  • seL4 (2009) was the first general-purpose OS kernel with a machine-checked proof that its C implementation matches its specification — about 10,000 lines of code backed by a far larger proof.
  • Linux is monolithic but modular: loadable modules (.ko files) add drivers at runtime, yet they run in ring 0 with full privileges, so one bad module can still crash or compromise the system.
  • Windows NT's executive, kernel and HAL share one kernel-mode address space, and macOS's XNU merges Mach and BSD into one kernel image, so both 'hybrids' behave much like monolithic kernels in practice.
  • Unikernels such as MirageOS (OCaml), Unikraft and Nanos remove the user/kernel split entirely, giving tiny images and millisecond boots but making debugging and multi-process programs harder.
  • MIT's exokernel research (Aegis and ExOS, 1995) exposed hardware securely to library operating systems; its ideas live on in kernel-bypass networking such as DPDK and in unikernel library OSes.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Calling Windows a microkernel: NT borrowed microkernel ideas, but its drivers, file systems and much of the graphics stack run in kernel mode.
  • Thinking microkernels are inevitably slow: L4-family kernels make IPC very fast; real overhead depends on design and workload.
  • Assuming loadable modules make Linux a microkernel: modules are linked into the same privileged address space as the rest of the kernel.

docs.title: Try it: See the loadable pieces of your monolithic kernel
docs.text:
# Linux: modules extend the monolithic kernel at runtime
lsmod | head
modinfo ext4 | head -5

# macOS: kernel extensions loaded into XNU
kmutil showloaded 2>/dev/null | head

docs.title: Key kernels, commands, tools, standards & concepts
docs.text: Name What it does Example Monolithic kernelConcept · Current · Beginner All core OS services, drivers and file systems run together in kernel mode as one large program. Linux, FreeBSD and OpenBSD are monolithic: a network driver hands packets to the TCP/IP stack with an ordinary function call. MicrokernelConcept · Current · Beginner Minimal privileged kernel providing address spaces, threads and IPC; drivers and services run as isolated user-mode servers. In QNX, a crashed USB driver process is restarted by a supervisor while the rest of the car's software keeps running. Hybrid kernelConcept · Current · Beginner Microkernel-inspired structure that keeps many services in kernel mode for speed. Windows NT and Apple's XNU are usually described as hybrid kernels. UnikernelConcept · Emerging · Intermediate Single-purpose machine image linking one application with just the OS libraries it needs, running directly on a hypervisor. A Unikraft image running NGINX can be only a few megabytes and boot in milliseconds on QEMU/KVM or Firecracker. ExokernelMIT (Dawson Engler, Frans Kaashoek) · Concept · Legacy · Advanced Research design where the kernel only allocates hardware securely and applications implement abstractions in library OSes. MIT's Aegis and Xok exokernels showed that web servers with application-specific I/O could run much faster than on conventional kernels. Modular monolithic designLinux, FreeBSD · Concept · Current · Intermediate A monolithic kernel that loads and unloads modules at runtime, gaining flexibility without gaining isolation. `sudo modprobe vfio-pci` loads a driver into the running Linux kernel without rebooting — but it runs fully privileged. MachCarnegie Mellon University (from 1985) · Kernel · Legacy · Intermediate Influential research microkernel that introduced tasks, threads and ports; its code lives on inside Apple's XNU. Every Mac and iPhone still uses Mach ports for low-level messaging between processes. L4 microkernel familyJochen Liedtke (1993) and successors · Kernel · Current · Advanced Second-generation microkernels built for extremely fast IPC; members include Fiasco.OC, OKL4 and seL4. OKL4, an L4 variant, has shipped inside the modem firmware of many mobile phones. seL4seL4 Foundation (originally NICTA / Data61) · Kernel · Current · Advanced High-assurance L4 microkernel with a machine-checked mathematical proof of functional correctness. DARPA's HACMS programme used seL4 in an unmanned Boeing Little Bird helicopter that resisted red-team hacking. MINIX 3Andrew Tanenbaum, Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam · Operating system · Legacy · Intermediate Teaching-oriented microkernel OS whose drivers restart themselves after crashes; earlier MINIX inspired Linus Torvalds. A MINIX 3 derivative runs inside the Intel Management Engine on many Intel PCs. QNX NeutrinoBlackBerry QNX · Kernel · Current · Intermediate Commercial real-time microkernel used in cars, medical devices and industrial systems. Many car infotainment and digital-cockpit systems run on QNX, where a crashed service restarts without a reboot. ZirconGoogle (Fuchsia project) · Kernel · Emerging · Advanced Capability-based microkernel at the heart of Google's Fuchsia OS; every resource is reached through a handle. Google moved its first-generation Nest Hub smart displays from a Linux-based OS to Fuchsia on Zircon in 2021. Redox OSOpen-source community · Operating system · Emerging · Advanced Unix-like microkernel operating system written in Rust, aimed at memory safety and reliability. Students can boot Redox in QEMU to explore a system whose drivers and file system run as user-space daemons. UnikraftUnikraft open-source project · Software · Emerging · Advanced Modular toolkit for building specialised unikernel images for many applications and hypervisors. A team packages a small Python API with Unikraft to get a tiny VM image that boots in milliseconds. Tanenbaum–Torvalds debatecomp.os.minix, 1992 · Concept · Legacy · Beginner Famous Usenet argument over monolithic versus microkernel design, opened by Tanenbaum's post 'LINUX is obsolete'. OS courses still use the debate to discuss trade-offs between raw performance and modular, isolated design.

docs.title: 1.7 Inside a Kernel: A Map of the Main Subsystems
docs.text:
A general-purpose kernel is really a set of cooperating subsystems: process and thread management, the scheduler, memory management, file systems, the networking stack, device drivers, IPC and security. Learning this map first makes every later chapter easy to place.

Main kernel subsystems. In a monolithic kernel all of these share one privileged address space and call each other directly.

Think of it like…

A kernel is like a city hall with departments — housing (memory), transport (scheduler), records office (file systems), post office (networking), utility contractors (drivers) and police (security) — all in one building and talking constantly.

Real-world example

When Kenji's photo app at the fictional SnapLeaf uploads a 5 MB picture, nearly every subsystem helps. The file-system layer and ext4 read the file, the page cache keeps it in RAM, the scheduler runs the upload thread, the TCP/IP stack splits the data into about 3,600 packets, the Wi-Fi driver transmits them, and the security module checks that the app may use the network at all.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The system-call layer receives requests and dispatches them to the right subsystem.
  2. Process management creates processes and threads; the scheduler decides which one runs on each CPU.
  3. Memory management maps virtual pages to physical frames and manages caches and swap.
  4. The file-system layer offers one interface over many file systems, and the block layer queues disk requests.
  5. The networking stack implements sockets, TCP/IP and packet filtering; drivers talk to the actual hardware.
  6. Security hooks (Linux Security Modules, the Windows Security Reference Monitor) check permissions throughout.

Who uses it

Students mapping the field, kernel developers deciding where to contribute, and SREs who must decide which subsystem to blame for a slowdown.

Key takeaway

When troubleshooting, ask 'which subsystem?' first — CPU (scheduler), memory, disk (file system/block) or network — then pick the matching tool; this is the start of the USE method used later in the guide.

Going deeper

  • In the Linux source tree, drivers/ is by far the largest directory — well over half of all code — while the core scheduler (kernel/sched/) and memory manager (mm/) are comparatively small but performance-critical.
  • Each subsystem has maintainers listed in the MAINTAINERS file; patches flow through subsystem trees such as net-next, mm and tip into Linus Torvalds's mainline during each two-week merge window.
  • Windows organises its kernel-mode executive into managers — Object, Process, Memory, I/O, Cache, Configuration (registry) and Security Reference Monitor — layered above the kernel and the hardware abstraction layer.
  • Handle-based designs (Unix file descriptors, Windows handles, Fuchsia handles) let one mechanism — reference-counted references with access rights — cover files, processes, events, sockets and more.
  • Shared infrastructure — locking, RCU, workqueues, timers, memory allocators and tracing (ftrace, eBPF) — is used by every subsystem, and is where many subtle bugs hide.
  • Kernels are slowly adopting memory-safe languages: Linux has accepted Rust code since 6.1 (December 2022), mainly for new drivers, and Microsoft has begun shipping Rust components in the Windows kernel.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming the kernel is mostly scheduler and memory code: most of it is device drivers, which is also where most kernel bugs are found.
  • Thinking subsystems are isolated like microservices: in a monolithic kernel they share memory, so a bug in one can silently corrupt another.

docs.title: Try it: Browse the Linux kernel's subsystem layout
docs.text:
# Each top-level directory of the source tree is roughly one subsystem
git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/torvalds/linux.git
ls linux/        # arch/ block/ drivers/ fs/ kernel/ mm/ net/ security/ ...
du -sh linux/drivers linux/fs linux/net linux/mm linux/kernel

docs.title: Key kernels, commands, tools, standards & concepts
docs.text: Name What it does Example Process managementComponent · Current · Beginner Creates, tracks and destroys processes and threads, and handles signals and exit codes. Running `python app.py` makes process management build a new task, load Python and record the shell as its parent. CPU schedulerComponent · Current · Beginner Picks which ready thread runs on each CPU and for how long. Linux's EEVDF scheduler chooses a new thread whenever the current one blocks or uses up its time slice. Memory managerComponent · Current · Beginner Maintains virtual address spaces, page tables, physical page allocation, caching and swapping. When RAM runs low, the Linux memory manager reclaims page-cache pages before resorting to swap or the OOM killer. File-system layerComponent · Current · Beginner Common kernel layer giving one API (open, read, write) over many different on-disk and network file systems. The same `cp` command copies from an ext4 disk to a FAT32 USB stick because this layer hides the differences. Network stackComponent · Current · Beginner Implements sockets, TCP/UDP/IP, routing, packet filtering and queuing between applications and network drivers. A web server's accept() and send() calls pass through the kernel's TCP code before the NIC driver transmits frames. Driver subsystemComponent · Current · Beginner Kernel code that operates particular hardware and presents it through standard interfaces such as block or network devices. Plugging in a USB webcam loads the uvcvideo driver, which exposes /dev/video0 to any video app. IPC subsystemComponent · Current · Beginner Kernel mechanisms letting processes exchange data and notifications: pipes, sockets, shared memory and message queues. `ls | grep txt` relies on the kernel's pipe code to carry ls's output into grep. Linux Security Modules (LSM)Linux kernel · Component · Current · Intermediate Hooks throughout the kernel that let modules such as SELinux, AppArmor and Landlock enforce extra access rules. On Fedora, SELinux stops a hijacked web-server process reading /home even where file permissions would allow it. Windows ExecutiveMicrosoft · Component · Current · Intermediate Upper layer of the NT kernel: the object, process, memory, I/O, cache, configuration and security managers. Every handle a Windows program opens — file, registry key or event — is tracked by the Executive's Object Manager. Hardware abstraction layer (HAL)Microsoft (hal.dll); per-architecture code in other kernels · Component · Current · Intermediate Thin layer hiding platform differences such as interrupt controllers and timers from the rest of the kernel. Windows' hal.dll, and Linux's per-architecture arch/ code in a similar role, let one core kernel run on many boards. Kernel threadsConcept · Current · Intermediate Threads that run only in kernel mode, doing housekeeping such as flushing data, reclaiming memory or deferred work. Names in square brackets in `ps -ef`, such as [kswapd0] and [kworker/0:1], are Linux kernel threads.

docs.title: 1.8 Types of Operating Systems
docs.text:
Operating systems are tuned for very different jobs. Batch systems run queued jobs without interaction; time-sharing systems let many users interact at once; desktop, server and mobile OSes balance responsiveness, throughput and battery life; real-time OSes guarantee deadlines; embedded OSes fit inside small devices; distributed OSes make many computers act like one.

Operating system types by purpose. One kernel can fill several roles: Linux appears in almost every box here.

Think of it like…

Like vehicles: a freight train (batch) is efficient but you can't hop off anywhere; a bus (time-sharing) serves many riders in turn; an ambulance (real-time) must arrive on time; a bicycle (embedded) is light and does one job well.

Real-world example

The fictional Harbourview Port uses five kinds of OS in one day: a payroll batch job on an IBM z/OS mainframe at 2 a.m., Windows 11 desktops for clerks, Linux servers for the shipping database, Android tablets for dock workers, and FreeRTOS on sensors in every crane, which must stop a load within 10 ms of a fault signal.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Identify the main goal: throughput (batch, server), responsiveness (desktop, mobile), deadlines (real-time) or size and power (embedded).
  2. Choose scheduling and memory policies that serve that goal.
  3. Decide the interaction model: none (batch), terminal or GUI (time-sharing, desktop), touch (mobile), or none at all (embedded).
  4. Match the hardware footprint: from kilobytes of RAM on a microcontroller to terabytes on mainframes and servers.
  5. Distributed and cluster systems add networking, replication and failure handling across many machines.

Who uses it

Solution architects, embedded engineers, mainframe operators, mobile developers and IoT designers choose between OS types on every project.

Key takeaway

Distinguish hard real-time (a missed deadline is a failure, e.g. an airbag) from soft real-time (a miss only degrades quality, e.g. video playback) — a frequent exam question.

Going deeper

  • Mainframe batch processing is far from dead: IBM z/OS still runs core banking, insurance and airline workloads, with JCL describing jobs much as it did in the 1960s.
  • Time-sharing, pioneered by CTSS and Multics, introduced ideas modern OSes take for granted: multiple users, preemptive scheduling, file permissions and an interactive command shell.
  • Real-time OSes are judged by worst-case latency rather than average speed: a good RTOS bounds interrupt-to-task latency to microseconds, and deterministic priority scheduling matters more than throughput.
  • Embedded devices range from 32-bit microcontrollers with tens of kilobytes of RAM running FreeRTOS or Zephyr up to embedded Linux systems built with Yocto or Buildroot on Arm SoCs.
  • Distributed operating systems such as Amoeba, Sprite and Plan 9 tried to make a network look like one computer; today orchestrators like Kubernetes, sometimes called a 'datacenter OS', largely fill that role.
  • Server OSes favour throughput, stability and remote management; they usually run headless, support huge memory and core counts, and offer ten-year-plus support lifecycles (RHEL, Windows Server).
  • Network devices run their own OSes too: Cisco IOS XE, Juniper Junos (FreeBSD-based) and SONiC (Debian-based) are operating systems specialised for forwarding packets.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Thinking 'real-time' means 'fast': it means predictable — a slower system that always meets its deadline is real-time; a fast one that sometimes misses is not.
  • Assuming embedded means no OS: tiny devices may run a bare-metal loop, but anything with networking, files or several tasks usually runs an RTOS or embedded Linux.
  • Treating the categories as exclusive: Linux serves as a server, desktop, mobile (Android), embedded and even real-time OS (PREEMPT_RT).

docs.title: Try it: What kind of system are you on?
docs.text:
# Linux/macOS: kernel and CPU architecture
uname -s -m
# Linux: how preemptible is this kernel? (look for PREEMPT, PREEMPT_DYNAMIC or PREEMPT_RT)
uname -v
# Windows PowerShell: client or server edition?
(Get-CimInstance Win32_OperatingSystem).ProductType   # 1 = workstation, 3 = server

docs.title: Key kernels, commands, tools, standards & concepts
docs.text: Name What it does Example Batch operating systemConcept · Current · Beginner Runs queued jobs one after another without user interaction, maximising throughput. A bank's nightly interest calculation runs as a batch job submitted with JCL on IBM z/OS. Time-sharing systemConcept · Legacy · Beginner Many users share one computer interactively; the CPU switches between them so quickly that each feels in control. In the 1960s, dozens of MIT users at teletype terminals shared one IBM 7094 through CTSS. Desktop operating systemConcept · Current · Beginner OS for personal computers emphasising a GUI, responsiveness, application compatibility and broad hardware support. Windows 11, macOS and desktop Linux distributions such as Ubuntu and Fedora are desktop OSes. Server operating systemConcept · Current · Beginner OS tuned for many simultaneous network clients, stability, remote administration and long support lifecycles. RHEL, Ubuntu Server and Windows Server 2025 run web, database and file servers, mostly with no monitor attached. Mobile operating systemConcept · Current · Beginner OS for phones and tablets focused on touch interfaces, battery life, app sandboxing and app stores. Android and iOS both suspend or kill background apps aggressively to save memory and battery. Real-time operating system (RTOS)Concept · Current · Beginner OS that guarantees tasks respond within bounded, predictable time limits. A car's brake controller running an RTOS must react to a wheel-sensor interrupt within a few milliseconds, every single time. Hard vs soft real-timeConcept · Current · Beginner Hard: a missed deadline is a system failure. Soft: occasional misses only reduce quality. Airbag deployment is hard real-time; dropping one frame in a video call is soft real-time. Embedded operating systemConcept · Current · Beginner Compact OS built into a dedicated device, often with little RAM, no disk and no display. A smart thermostat runs Zephyr or FreeRTOS on a microcontroller with 256 KB of RAM. Distributed operating systemConcept · Legacy · Intermediate Software making a network of computers appear as a single system that shares resources transparently. Bell Labs' Plan 9 let a user's terminal use a remote server's CPU and files as if they were local. Network operating systemConcept · Current · Intermediate OS specialised for network devices or, historically, for LAN file and print servers. Novell NetWare served office files in the 1990s; today Cisco IOS XE and SONiC run routers and switches. z/OSIBM · Operating system · Current · Intermediate IBM's flagship mainframe OS for very high-reliability, high-throughput transaction and batch processing. z/OS on IBM Z mainframes processes card payments and account updates for many of the world's largest banks. Datacenter OS (cluster orchestrator)Concept · Current · Intermediate Informal term for software that manages a whole data centre's machines as one pool of resources. Engineers call Kubernetes 'the operating system of the cloud' because it schedules containers across thousands of machines.

docs.title: 1.9 The Boot Process: From Power-On to Login
docs.text:
Booting is a relay race from pressing the power button to seeing a login screen. Firmware (UEFI, or the old BIOS) tests and initialises the hardware and finds a bootloader; the bootloader loads the kernel; the kernel sets up memory and drivers and starts the first user process (init), which starts everything else.

Boot chain from power button to login. Each stage loads and (with Secure Boot) verifies the next before handing over control.

Think of it like…

It is like opening a theatre: the caretaker switches on the power and checks the building (firmware), the stage manager arrives with the script (bootloader), the director takes charge (kernel), and front-of-house opens the doors to the audience (init and login).

Real-world example

Marta's Fedora laptop at the fictional Bayside Design: UEFI firmware runs its power-on self-test, verifies Secure Boot signatures and loads shim and GRUB from the EFI System Partition. GRUB loads the kernel and initramfs; the initramfs asks for her disk-encryption passphrase, mounts the real root file system and hands over to systemd as PID 1, which starts about 200 units in parallel. `systemd-analyze` reports the whole boot took 9.8 seconds.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Power-on: the CPU starts executing firmware from flash memory at a fixed reset address.
  2. Firmware (UEFI or legacy BIOS) runs the power-on self-test, initialises RAM and devices, and chooses a boot device from its boot order.
  3. UEFI loads a bootloader (.efi file) from the EFI System Partition, checking signatures if Secure Boot is on; legacy BIOS loads the 512-byte master boot record instead.
  4. The bootloader (GRUB, systemd-boot, Windows Boot Manager) loads the kernel and an initial RAM disk and passes a command line.
  5. The kernel sets up memory management, interrupts and drivers, mounts the root file system and starts the first process (PID 1).
  6. Init (systemd, launchd, or Windows' smss and wininit) starts services, networking and finally the login screen.

Who uses it

System administrators, firmware and platform engineers, security teams hunting boot-level malware, and anyone rescuing an unbootable machine.

Key takeaway

Be able to recite both chains: UEFI → shim/GRUB → vmlinuz + initramfs → systemd (Linux) and UEFI → bootmgfw.efi → winload.efi → ntoskrnl.exe → smss.exe → wininit/winlogon (Windows).

Going deeper

  • UEFI, specified by the UEFI Forum, replaced the 1981-era PC BIOS: it reads FAT-formatted EFI System Partitions, boots from GPT disks larger than 2 TiB and runs signed 64-bit boot applications.
  • Secure Boot checks each boot component against keys stored in firmware variables (PK, KEK, db and the dbx revocation list); Linux distributions use a Microsoft-signed shim that then verifies GRUB and the kernel with the distribution's own key.
  • Microsoft's original 2011 Secure Boot certificates start expiring in 2026, so firmware, Windows and Linux boot media have been moving to newer 2023 certificates — a major 2025-2026 maintenance task for IT teams.
  • The initramfs is a compressed cpio archive unpacked into RAM, built by tools such as dracut or initramfs-tools, holding just enough drivers and scripts to find, decrypt and mount the real root file system.
  • Measured boot records a hash of each stage in the TPM, so disk-encryption unlocking or remote attestation can prove that the boot chain was not modified.
  • Phones and embedded boards follow the same pattern with different names: a boot ROM in the chip, bootloaders such as U-Boot or Android's ABL, then the kernel, protected by schemes like Android Verified Boot.
  • PID 1 must never exit — if it dies, the Linux kernel panics. Modern init systems start services in parallel from dependency graphs, which is why boots shrank from minutes to seconds.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Confusing BIOS with UEFI: almost every PC made since about 2012 uses UEFI; 'BIOS settings' is simply the old name for the firmware setup screen.
  • Thinking Secure Boot encrypts anything: it only verifies signatures on boot code; disk encryption such as BitLocker or LUKS is a separate layer.
  • Deleting the small EFI System Partition to reclaim space: without it the firmware has no bootloader to start.

docs.title: Try it: Inspect how your machine booted
docs.text:
# Linux: how long did each stage take?
systemd-analyze
systemd-analyze blame | head
# Booted with UEFI or legacy BIOS?
[ -d /sys/firmware/efi ] && echo UEFI || echo BIOS

# Windows (admin PowerShell): boot entries
bcdedit /enum

Installing the vendor's firmware update on a laptop fixes CPU microcode bugs and refreshes Secure Boot certificates. Old machines in 'Legacy/CSM' mode boot from MBR-partitioned disks limited to 2 TiB partitions. An encrypted Ubuntu laptop's initramfs prompts for the LUKS passphrase before the root file system can be mounted. U-BootDas U-Boot open-source project · Software · Current · Advanced Popular bootloader for embedded and Arm boards that loads Linux from flash, SD card or the network. Many routers and development boards start via U-Boot, whose console lets engineers load a test kernel over TFTP. Measured bootTrusted Computing Group · Concept · Current · Advanced Each boot stage hashes the next and records it in the TPM, creating evidence of exactly what software started. systemd-cryptenroll --tpm2-pcrs=7 ties disk unlocking to Secure Boot state recorded in the TPM.

docs.title: 1.10 POSIX and the Single UNIX Specification
docs.text:
POSIX is a family of IEEE standards that defines what a Unix-like operating system must offer programs: system interfaces such as fork and open, C library functions, a shell language and standard utilities like ls and grep. The Single UNIX Specification is the same core plus extras; passing its tests lets a vendor call a product UNIX.

How POSIX and SUS evolved. One standard, maintained jointly since 2001, revised roughly once a decade.

Think of it like…

POSIX is like a standard plug and socket: if every wall socket follows the specification, any appliance (program) built to it works in any house without rewiring.

Real-world example

The fictional analytics firm DataFjord writes its log tool in C using only POSIX interfaces (open, read, getopt, pthread_create). The same source compiles unchanged on Ubuntu, Alpine, FreeBSD and macOS; only the Windows port needed extra work, which they solved by shipping it inside WSL. Their shell scripts start with #!/bin/sh and avoid bash-only features, so they also run under dash and BusyBox.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. 1988: IEEE publishes POSIX.1, standardising the C interface to Unix-like systems.
  2. Later parts add the shell and utilities (POSIX.2, 1992), real-time extensions (1993) and threads (POSIX.1c, 1995).
  3. The Open Group's Single UNIX Specification and POSIX merge in 2001; the Austin Group maintains both as one document.
  4. Revisions follow in 2008, 2017 and 2024 — POSIX.1-2024 equals SUS Version 5's core (Base Specifications Issue 8).
  5. Vendors may certify products against the specification to use the UNIX trademark; others are 'mostly POSIX-compliant' without certification.

Who uses it

Systems programmers writing portable code, shell scripters, OS vendors, and anyone porting software between Linux, BSD, macOS and commercial Unix.

Key takeaway

Know the distinction: Linux distributions are largely POSIX-compatible but generally not certified, while macOS releases have been certified UNIX 03 since Mac OS X Leopard (2007).

Going deeper

  • POSIX.1-2024 (IEEE Std 1003.1-2024, published June 2024) is technically identical to The Open Group Base Specifications Issue 8 and has four volumes: Base Definitions, System Interfaces, Shell and Utilities, and Rationale.
  • The 2024 revision standardised interfaces that had long been common in practice, such as strlcpy() and strlcat(), reallocarray(), asprintf(), ppoll() and getentropy(), and aligned the standard with C17.
  • Certified UNIX products have included IBM AIX, HP-UX, Oracle Solaris and Apple macOS; a few Linux-based systems (such as Huawei's EulerOS) were certified, but mainstream distributions never seek certification.
  • Feature-test macros such as _POSIX_C_SOURCE=200809L or _XOPEN_SOURCE=700 tell the C library which version of the standard a program expects, hiding non-standard extensions.
  • The Linux Standard Base tried to standardise binary compatibility between distributions on top of POSIX but stalled after version 5.0 (2015); in practice, glibc versions and packaging define compatibility today.
  • Windows is not natively POSIX-compliant: its old POSIX subsystem and later Services for UNIX were removed, and today Cygwin, MSYS2 and WSL supply Unix-like environments.
  • The name POSIX was suggested by Richard Stallman; the X signals its Unix heritage, and the IEEE standard number 1003 is still how most specifications cite it.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Writing #!/bin/sh but using bash features such as [[ ]] or arrays: on Debian and Ubuntu /bin/sh is dash, so the script breaks; use #!/bin/bash or stick to POSIX syntax.
  • Assuming 'POSIX-compliant' means 'certified': only systems that pass The Open Group's test suites may use the UNIX trademark.
  • Expecting identical command flags everywhere: GNU tools add extensions (such as sed -i with no suffix) that behave differently on macOS and the BSDs.

docs.title: Try it: Ask your system about POSIX values and limits
docs.text:
getconf _POSIX_VERSION     # e.g. 200809 = POSIX.1-2008 interfaces
getconf ARG_MAX            # max bytes of arguments passed to exec
getconf PAGESIZE           # 4096 on most x86-64 Linux, 16384 on Apple silicon
# Check a script for bash-only syntax before running it with /bin/sh
shellcheck --shell=sh myscript.sh

docs.text: Name What it does Example POSIXIEEE 1003 / The Open Group / ISO/IEC 9945 · Standard · Current · Beginner Portable Operating System Interface: standards defining Unix-like system interfaces, C library, shell and utilities. Code using fork(), pipe() and the POSIX shell runs on Linux, macOS and FreeBSD with minimal changes. POSIX.1-2024 finally standardised strlcpy() and reallocarray(), long available on the BSDs and in newer glibc. Vendors test against the SUS to put the UNIX trademark on products such as IBM AIX and Apple macOS. Anyone can report defects or propose changes for the next POSIX revision on the Austin Group's public bug tracker. Cygwin / MSYS2Cygwin (Red Hat-sponsored); MSYS2 open source · Software · Current · Intermediate Windows environments providing a POSIX API layer and Unix tools so Unix software can compile and run on Windows. Git for Windows ships an MSYS2-based bash so Git's shell scripts work on Windows. Linux Standard Base (LSB)Linux Foundation · Standard · Legacy · Intermediate Former standard for binary compatibility across Linux distributions, built on POSIX; largely abandoned after version 5.0 (2015). Old commercial installers checked `lsb_release` output; Debian dropped most LSB support in 2023.

docs.title: 1.11 A Short History of Operating Systems
docs.text:
Operating systems grew from simple job loaders in the 1950s into the layered systems on every device today. The key milestones are time-sharing (CTSS, Multics), Unix in 1969 and its many descendants (BSD, Linux, macOS, Android), MS-DOS and Windows on PCs, and the smartphone OSes of the late 2000s.

Milestones in operating-system history. Most of today's systems trace back to two lines: Unix (1969) and Windows NT (1993).

Think of it like…

OS history is a family tree: Multics is the grandparent, Unix the famous parent, and today's Linux, macOS, iOS and Android are cousins who inherited the same habits — files, processes, shells and pipes.

Real-world example

Grace, a junior engineer at the fictional Old Mill Software, types `ls -l` on a 2026 MacBook and on a Linux server and sees almost the same output. Both systems descend from ideas first shipped at Bell Labs in 1969-1971: hierarchical files, rwx permissions and small tools joined by pipes. Even Windows PowerShell defines `ls` as an alias for Get-ChildItem.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. 1950s-60s: batch monitors and IBM's OS/360 (shipped 1966) manage jobs on mainframes.
  2. 1961-69: CTSS and Multics invent interactive time-sharing and hardware-enforced protection.
  3. 1969-80s: Unix spreads from Bell Labs; Berkeley's BSD adds virtual memory and TCP/IP sockets.
  4. 1980s: PCs arrive with CP/M and MS-DOS, the Macintosh brings the GUI, and GNU begins a free Unix-like system.
  5. 1990s: Windows NT and Linux appear, and the open-source movement grows.
  6. 2000s-today: Mac OS X/macOS, iOS and Android put Unix-like kernels into billions of devices.

Who uses it

Anyone in computing benefits — interviewers like history questions, and design choices such as fork(), everything-is-a-file and Windows drive letters only make sense with this background.

Key takeaway

Anchor dates: Unix 1969, MS-DOS 1981, Linux 1991, Windows NT 1993, Mac OS X 2001, iPhone 2007, first Android phone 2008.

Going deeper

  • CTSS (Compatible Time-Sharing System) was first demonstrated at MIT in 1961 and later ran on the IBM 7090/7094; it is credited with early forms of e-mail, text formatting and password-protected accounts.
  • Multics (from 1965; MIT, GE and Bell Labs) pioneered hierarchical file systems, dynamic linking, protection rings and a single-level store; after Bell Labs left in 1969, Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie built Unix as a simpler reaction.
  • Rewriting Unix in C in 1973 made it portable; AT&T's licensing let universities study the source, and Berkeley's BSD added virtual memory, a faster file system and the sockets TCP/IP stack in 4.2BSD (1983).
  • The Unix wars and the USL v. BSDi lawsuit (settled 1994) held back BSD exactly when Linux appeared, which helps explain Linux's rapid rise in the 1990s.
  • Linus Torvalds announced Linux on 25 August 1991 as 'just a hobby'; combined with GNU tools (begun by Richard Stallman in 1983) and licensed under GPLv2, it became a complete free OS.
  • Windows NT 3.1 (1993), led by Dave Cutler, formerly of DEC's VMS team, introduced a portable, preemptive, protected-memory kernel; every consumer Windows since XP (2001) is NT-based.
  • Mac OS X 10.0 (2001) combined NeXTSTEP's Mach-and-BSD XNU kernel with a new interface; the same core powers iOS (2007), while Android (first phone 2008) put a Linux kernel into billions of pockets.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Saying Linux is a version of Unix: Linux is a from-scratch Unix-like kernel with no AT&T code; the BSDs descend from the original source.
  • Believing Windows grew straight out of MS-DOS: Windows 95, 98 and ME were DOS-based, but all current Windows versions use the separate NT kernel.
  • Thinking macOS is based on Linux: macOS uses XNU (Mach plus BSD); Android, by contrast, really does use the Linux kernel.

docs.title: Try it: Spot your Unix heritage
docs.text:
man 1 ls | head -20      # man pages descend from the 1971 Unix manual
echo $SHELL
uname -a
cal 9 1752               # Unix 'cal' still shows the 1752 calendar change

docs.text: Name What it does Example IBM OS/360IBM (announced 1964, shipped 1966) · Operating system · Legacy · Intermediate OS for IBM's System/360 mainframes, the first to span a whole range of compatible machines; ancestor of z/OS. Fred Brooks's book 'The Mythical Man-Month' draws its lessons from managing the OS/360 project. CTSSMIT (Fernando Corbató), 1961 · Operating system · Legacy · Intermediate Compatible Time-Sharing System: one of the first time-sharing OSes, letting many users work interactively at once. CTSS users exchanged some of the earliest electronic messages, an early form of e-mail, in the mid-1960s. MulticsMIT, General Electric, Bell Labs (from 1965) · Operating system · Legacy · Intermediate Influential time-sharing OS that introduced hierarchical file systems, protection rings and dynamic linking. The x86 protection rings echo Multics, which used hardware rings to separate users from the supervisor. UnixBell Labs (Ken Thompson, Dennis Ritchie), 1969 · Operating system · Legacy · Beginner Small, elegant multi-user OS whose ideas — hierarchical files, processes, shells, pipes — underlie most modern systems. The first Unix ran on a PDP-7 minicomputer; the 1973 Fourth Edition kernel was rewritten in C. The Linux, Windows NT and XNU kernels are written mostly in C, with growing amounts of Rust and C++. BSDUniversity of California, Berkeley · Operating system · Legacy · Intermediate Berkeley Software Distribution: Unix variant that added virtual memory and TCP/IP sockets; ancestor of FreeBSD, OpenBSD and NetBSD. The sockets API from 4.2BSD (1983) is still how almost every program opens a network connection. MS-DOSMicrosoft (1981), from Seattle Computer Products' 86-DOS · Operating system · Legacy · Beginner Single-user, single-tasking disk OS for the IBM PC and compatibles. Microsoft has published the source code of MS-DOS 1.25, 2.0 and 4.0 on GitHub for historians and hobbyists. Classic Mac OSApple (1984) · Operating system · Legacy · Beginner The original Macintosh system software that brought a mouse-driven graphical interface to the mass market. Mac OS 9 (1999) was the last classic version before Mac OS X replaced it with a Unix-based core. Windows NTMicrosoft (Dave Cutler), 1993 · Operating system · Current · Beginner Microsoft's portable, preemptive, protected-memory OS family — the base of every Windows version since XP. Running `ver` on Windows 11 still reports an internal NT version of 10.0. Linux (1991)Linus Torvalds · Kernel · Current · Beginner Free Unix-like kernel announced in August 1991, now the most widely deployed OS kernel in the world. Linux 0.01 had about 10,000 lines of code; by 2025 the kernel source tree had passed roughly 40 million. Mac OS X / macOSApple (2001) · Operating system · Current · Beginner Apple's Unix-based desktop OS built on the XNU kernel from NeXTSTEP; renamed macOS in 2016. In 2025 Apple jumped from macOS 15 Sequoia to macOS 26 Tahoe to align version numbers with the year. iPhone OS / iOSApple (2007) · Operating system · Current · Beginner Mobile OS derived from Mac OS X, launched with the first iPhone and renamed iOS in 2010. The App Store opened in 2008 with iPhone OS 2.0, creating the modern mobile-app economy. AndroidAndroid Inc. / Google (2008) · Operating system · Current · Beginner Linux-kernel-based mobile OS; first shipped on the HTC Dream (T-Mobile G1) in 2008. Because Android's core is open source (AOSP), makers such as Samsung and Xiaomi ship their own customised versions.

docs.title: 1.12 The OS Landscape and Market Shares in 2026
docs.text:
No single OS rules everywhere. Android is the most-used OS overall because of phones; Windows dominates traditional desktops and laptops; Apple's iOS and macOS hold a large premium share; and Linux runs most servers, clouds, supercomputers and embedded devices even though it is a small slice of desktops.

Share of worldwide web traffic, all devices. StatCounter, July 2026 (approximate); web-traffic share is not the same as installed devices.

Think of it like…

The OS market is like a city's transport: cars (Windows) fill the roads, scooters (Android) are everywhere, premium taxis (Apple) take a profitable share, and the trains and power lines nobody notices (Linux in servers and devices) carry most of the freight.

Real-world example

Nadia, an IT student, audits the fictional Greenway Logistics: 380 Windows 11 laptops, 40 MacBooks, 600 Android scanners and phones, 90 iPhones, 120 Linux virtual machines in the cloud and a Kubernetes cluster on Linux nodes. Her report concludes: 'Linux is about 3% of our desktops but 100% of our servers.'

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Decide which population you mean: desktops, phones, servers, embedded devices or web traffic.
  2. Pick a data source: web-traffic trackers (StatCounter), shipment trackers (IDC, Counterpoint), surveys (Steam) or server scans.
  3. Treat numbers as approximate and check how large the 'unknown' share is — methods differ by several percentage points.
  4. Compare trends over many months rather than quoting one month in isolation.

Who uses it

IT managers planning device fleets, developers choosing target platforms, security teams prioritising patches, and students deciding which OS skills to learn first.

Key takeaway

Quote ranges, not precise figures: in mid-2026 Android was roughly two-thirds of mobile and about 40% of all web traffic, Windows roughly 60% of desktops, and Linux around 4% of desktops but most cloud servers.

Going deeper

  • StatCounter counts page views on sites using its tracker, so it measures web activity rather than installed devices; mid-2026 desktop figures swung by several points month to month, partly because of a large 'unknown' category.
  • On phones, StatCounter showed Android at about 67-69% and iOS about 31-33% worldwide in mid-2026, while iOS leads in some richer markets such as the United States and Japan.
  • Windows 10 reached end of support on 14 October 2025; Windows 11 (versions 24H2 and 25H2) is now the majority Windows version, with paid Extended Security Updates bridging organisations that could not upgrade in time.
  • Linux has run on every TOP500 supercomputer since November 2017 and on most public-cloud virtual machines; Microsoft has said that more than half of Azure's VM cores run Linux.
  • Apple moved to year-based version numbers in 2025 (iOS 26, macOS 26 Tahoe); the 27 releases shipped in September 2026, and macOS 27 supports only Apple silicon Macs.
  • In China, Huawei's HarmonyOS — including the non-Android HarmonyOS NEXT generation launched in 2024 — has become a significant third mobile platform alongside Android and iOS.
  • Embedded and IoT devices such as routers, TVs, cars and cameras vastly outnumber PCs; most run embedded Linux, Android variants or RTOSes like FreeRTOS and Zephyr, so 'most-used OS' depends on what you count.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Treating one month's StatCounter figure as exact: shares move by several points between months and between desktop-only and all-device views.
  • Concluding that Linux is unimportant from its desktop share: nearly every website and cloud service you use is served from Linux.
  • Forgetting ChromeOS, consoles and embedded devices: education fleets, gaming and IoT are sizeable worlds with their own operating systems.

# macOS

# Windows PowerShell

docs.title: 1.13 Shells and Command-Line Basics
docs.text:
A shell is a program that reads the commands you type, runs other programs for you and shows their output. It is an ordinary user program: the terminal window draws the text, the shell interprets it, and the kernel runs the resulting processes. Learning a shell (bash, zsh or PowerShell) is the single most useful practical OS skill.

What the shell does with one command line. Parsing and expansion happen in the shell; only the final program runs in a new process.

Think of it like…

The shell is a waiter: you speak in a short, precise language ('two coffees, no sugar'), the waiter passes the order to the kitchen (the kernel) and brings back what comes out — and you can write your regular order on a card (a script).

Real-world example

On her first day at the fictional CloudNest support desk, Aisha opens a terminal and types `cd /var/log`, `ls -lh`, then `tail -n 50 syslog | grep -i error`. The shell expands and splits the line, starts tail and grep as two processes joined by a pipe, and within seconds she spots 'No space left on device' — something that would take minutes of clicking in a GUI.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The terminal emulator shows a prompt and passes your keystrokes to the shell.
  2. The shell parses the line: words, quotes, variables ($HOME), wildcards (*.txt), pipes and redirections.
  3. It finds the program by searching each directory in the PATH variable, unless the command is a built-in such as cd.
  4. It creates a child process (fork and exec on Unix, CreateProcess on Windows) and waits for it — or runs it in the background with &.
  5. When the command ends, the shell records its exit status ($? in Unix shells, $LASTEXITCODE in PowerShell) and prints a new prompt.

Who uses it

Every sysadmin, DevOps engineer, developer, data scientist and security analyst; interviews for these roles routinely include live command-line tasks.

Key takeaway

Learn to help yourself: `man ls`, `ls --help`, `help cd` (bash built-ins), `Get-Help Get-Process` (PowerShell) and `tldr` pages answer most questions faster than a web search.

Going deeper

  • Terminal, console and shell are different things: a terminal emulator (GNOME Terminal, iTerm2, Windows Terminal) draws characters and handles keys, and a pseudo-terminal (pty) device connects it to the shell process.
  • bash (GNU, 1989) is the default interactive shell on most Linux distributions; macOS switched its default to zsh in Catalina (2019); Debian and Ubuntu use the small, fast dash as /bin/sh for system scripts.
  • PowerShell pipes .NET objects rather than text, so `Get-Process | Sort-Object CPU -Descending | Select-Object -First 5` sorts on a real numeric property; PowerShell 7 is cross-platform and open source.
  • Exit status 0 means success and anything else failure: 127 means 'command not found', 126 'not executable', and 128 + N means the process was killed by signal N (130 after Ctrl+C).
  • Built-ins such as cd, export and exit must run inside the shell itself, because a child process cannot change its parent's working directory or environment variables.
  • Startup files shape your environment: ~/.bashrc and ~/.bash_profile for bash, ~/.zshrc for zsh and $PROFILE for PowerShell — aliases, functions and PATH changes belong there.
  • Remote administration is mostly shell-based: OpenSSH gives a shell on servers (and ships with current Windows), often inside tmux or screen so long jobs survive a dropped connection.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Running `rm -rf "$DIR"/` when DIR is unset or misspelt can delete far more than intended; quote variables and use `set -u` in scripts.
  • Pasting commands from a web page straight into a root shell: read them first — malicious pages can hide extra commands in copied text.
  • Expecting cmd.exe syntax to work in PowerShell or bash (or vice versa): quoting, variables and escape characters all differ.

docs.title: Try it: Your first ten minutes at a shell
docs.text:
pwd                 # where am I?
ls -la ~            # list home directory, including hidden files
echo "$SHELL"; echo "$PATH"
type cd ls          # built-in vs external program
false; echo "exit status: $?"   # prints 1

# PowerShell equivalents
Get-Location; Get-ChildItem ~ -Force; $env:Path

docs.title: Chapter 9: Operations, Security, Careers & Learning
docs.text: Knowing how operating systems, containers and Kubernetes work is only half the job — the other half is running them well. This chapter covers hardening hosts and clusters, patching and live patching, methodical troubleshooting with real commands, observability and SRE, automation with infrastructure as code, and platform engineering. It then maps the careers, certifications, books, home-lab plan, interview questions and study schedule that take you from beginner to job-ready.

docs.title: 9.1 Hardening Operating Systems: CIS Benchmarks, STIGs & Least Privilege
docs.text:
Hardening means switching off everything a system does not need, locking down what is left and proving it against a checklist. Published baselines such as the CIS Benchmarks and DISA STIGs turn hundreds of settings into a repeatable standard that scanners can check automatically.

The hardening workflow. Hardening is a loop, not a one-off: drift creeps back as people change systems.

Think of it like…

It is like moving into a new house: change the locks, close the windows you never open, hand keys only to people who need them, and keep a checklist the insurer can inspect.

Real-world example

Priya, a junior Linux admin at fictional Harbourline Logistics, must harden 40 new Ubuntu 24.04 servers. She applies the CIS Level 1 Server profile with Ubuntu Security Guide, disables SSH passwords, turns on automatic security updates and auditd, then runs an OpenSCAP scan. Auditors receive a 96% pass report with two documented exceptions for a legacy application.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Inventory every host: OS and version, role, owner and exposed ports — you cannot harden what you do not know exists.
  2. Choose a baseline for the exact OS version: CIS Level 1 for most servers, CIS Level 2 or a DISA STIG for regulated systems.
  3. Shrink the attack surface: remove unused packages and services, close ports and set a default-deny host firewall.
  4. Lock down access: SSH keys only, no direct root login, least-privilege sudo, central accounts and MFA where possible.
  5. Turn on logging, auditing and integrity checking (journald forwarding, auditd, AIDE) and keep patches flowing.
  6. Scan, fix, document justified exceptions, and rescan on a schedule to catch drift.

Who uses it

Linux and Windows administrators, security engineers, compliance auditors and anyone building golden images for government, finance or healthcare.

Key takeaway

Know the difference: CIS Benchmarks are free consensus guides from the Center for Internet Security, while STIGs are mandatory DISA configuration standards for US Department of Defense systems.

Going deeper

  • CIS Benchmarks come in profiles: Level 1 gives practical protection with little impact on function, while Level 2 adds defence in depth for high-security systems and may break applications. More than 100 benchmarks cover OSes, clouds, containers and apps.
  • DISA STIG findings are graded CAT I (high, such as a default password), CAT II (medium) and CAT III (low); SCAP content and the STIG Viewer let you check most rules automatically.
  • OpenSCAP with the SCAP Security Guide (from the ComplianceAsCode project) ships CIS, STIG and PCI DSS profiles for RHEL, Ubuntu, SUSE and others; 'oscap xccdf eval' produces an HTML report plus Bash or Ansible remediation.
  • Least privilege on Linux means sudo rules limited to specific commands, file capabilities instead of setuid-root binaries, service accounts without login shells, and systemd sandboxing such as ProtectSystem=strict and NoNewPrivileges=yes.
  • On Windows, Microsoft publishes security baselines in the Security Compliance Toolkit, applied through Group Policy or Intune; Windows LAPS, built in since April 2023, gives each device a unique rotated local admin password.
  • SSH essentials: Ed25519 keys, PasswordAuthentication no, PermitRootLogin no, AllowGroups to restrict users, and rate limiting with tools such as fail2ban; never leave secrets in scripts or shell history.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Applying Level 2 or STIG settings blindly in production: some break applications, so test in staging and record justified exceptions.
  • Treating a 100% scan score as 'secure': benchmarks check configuration, not unpatched software, weak application code or stolen credentials.
  • Hardening each server by hand: drift follows; encode settings in Ansible, Group Policy or a golden image so they are reapplied automatically.

docs.title: Try it: Quick hardening checks on your own Linux machine
docs.text:
# Which services listen on the network?
sudo ss -tulpn
# Is SSH password or root login allowed?
sudo sshd -T | grep -Ei 'passwordauthentication|permitrootlogin'
# Who is in the admin groups?
getent group sudo wheel
# Lynis audit (Debian/Ubuntu: sudo apt install lynis)
sudo lynis audit system --quick

An audit rule on /etc/sudoers logs who edited it; AIDE's nightly check flags a modified /usr/bin/ls for investigation.

docs.title: 9.2 Hardening Containers & Kubernetes Clusters: Benchmarks, Scanners and the 4Cs
docs.text:
Containers and clusters add new layers to secure: images, the container runtime, worker nodes, the Kubernetes control plane and the cloud account underneath. Benchmarks and scanners such as kube-bench, Trivy and Kubescape check those layers against published hardening guides so you can find and fix the gaps.

The 4Cs of cloud-native security. Each layer relies on the one around it; a weak outer layer undermines everything inside.

Think of it like…

A cluster is like a block of flats: you secure the grounds (cloud), the building and lobby (cluster), each flat (container) and what people keep inside (code) — a strong front door does not help if a flat window is open.

Real-world example

Tomás inherits a three-year-old cluster at fictional Kestrel Games. kube-bench flags anonymous kubelet access and no API audit log; Trivy finds 40 critical CVEs in an old base image; Kubescape shows 12 privileged pods. Over two sprints he fixes the kubelet settings, enables audit logging, rebuilds images on a minimal base and enforces the 'restricted' Pod Security level.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Secure the cloud account and nodes first: private API endpoint, a minimal hardened node OS and a patched kernel.
  2. Run kube-bench against the CIS Kubernetes Benchmark (or your managed service's variant) and fix control-plane and kubelet findings.
  3. Scan images and running workloads with Trivy, Grype or Kubescape, and rebuild on minimal, patched base images.
  4. Enforce workload rules: non-root users, read-only root file systems, no privileged pods, resource limits and NetworkPolicies.
  5. Enable audit logging, encrypt Secrets at rest, rotate certificates and add runtime detection such as Falco.
  6. Rescan in CI and continuously inside the cluster so new drift and new CVEs are caught early.

Who uses it

Platform engineers, DevSecOps and cloud security engineers, Kubernetes administrators and auditors working towards SOC 2, PCI DSS or government accreditation.

Key takeaway

Memorise the 4Cs of cloud-native security — Cloud, Cluster, Container, Code — and be ready to name one control at each layer in an interview.

Going deeper

  • The CIS Kubernetes Benchmark covers control-plane components, etcd, kubelet and policies; managed services have their own CIS EKS, AKS and GKE benchmarks because customers cannot configure the provider's control plane.
  • kube-bench (Aqua Security, open source) detects the Kubernetes version and runs the matching CIS checks, printing PASS, FAIL or WARN with remediation text; run it as a Job per node type.
  • The NSA/CISA Kubernetes Hardening Guidance (version 1.2, August 2022) recommends non-root containers, immutable file systems, network separation, strong authentication, audit logging and regular configuration review.
  • Falco, a CNCF project that graduated in February 2024, watches system calls (via eBPF) and Kubernetes audit events, alerting on behaviour such as a shell spawned in a container or writes below /etc.
  • Encrypting Secrets at rest needs an EncryptionConfiguration on the API server, ideally with a KMS v2 provider; without it, Secrets sit in etcd merely base64-encoded.
  • Container-optimised node OSes such as Bottlerocket, Talos Linux and Flatcar Container Linux drop the package manager (and usually SSH) and update by swapping whole images, shrinking the attack surface.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming a managed cluster is secure by default: the provider hardens the control plane, but workloads, RBAC, network policies and node pools remain your job.
  • Scanning images only at build time: new CVEs appear daily, so rescan images in registries and in running clusters.
  • Believing base64-encoded Secrets are encrypted: anyone who can read etcd or the Secret object can decode them in one command.

docs.title: Try it: Audit a disposable lab cluster (kind, minikube or k3s)
docs.text:
# CIS checks with kube-bench, run as a Job
kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/aquasecurity/kube-bench/main/job.yaml
kubectl logs job/kube-bench | grep -E '\[FAIL\]' | head

# Scan an image, then summarise the whole cluster
trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL nginx:1.27
trivy k8s --report summary

docs.title: 9.3 Patch Management, Live Patching & Upgrade Cadence
docs.text:
Patching means installing updates that fix security holes and bugs. Good teams patch on a regular rhythm, rush the dangerous fixes, test before rolling out widely, and use live patching or rolling restarts so services stay up.

A month in a ring-based patch cycle. Actively exploited critical flaws skip the queue and are fixed or mitigated within days.

Think of it like…

It is like servicing a fleet of buses: routine checks happen on schedule, a brake recall jumps the queue, and buses are swapped in and out so the route never stops.

Real-world example

At fictional Meridian Health, Patch Tuesday updates reach a 5% pilot ring on day 2 and every Windows server by day 14. When a critical Linux kernel flaw appears on CISA's KEV list, Ravi live-patches 300 RHEL hosts within 48 hours, then schedules proper reboots into the fixed kernel at the next maintenance window.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Keep an accurate inventory and subscribe to vendor advisories (Ubuntu USNs, Red Hat RHSAs, Microsoft MSRC, Kubernetes security announcements).
  2. Prioritise: actively exploited (CISA KEV) and internet-facing first, then by CVSS severity and EPSS likelihood.
  3. Test in staging, then roll out in rings — pilot, early, broad — with automatic health checks.
  4. Use live patching for urgent kernel fixes, and rolling restarts or node replacement to avoid downtime.
  5. Verify with a fresh scan and report patch compliance and mean time to patch.
  6. Upgrade whole platforms — OS releases and Kubernetes minor versions — before they reach end of support.

Who uses it

Systems administrators, vulnerability management teams, SREs and platform teams responsible for fleets of servers, laptops and clusters.

Key takeaway

Know the cadences: Microsoft releases security updates on Patch Tuesday (the second Tuesday of each month), and Kubernetes ships about three minor releases a year, each patched for roughly 14 months.

Going deeper

  • CVSS v4.0 (FIRST, November 2023) rates severity from 0 to 10; EPSS estimates the probability a CVE will be exploited in the next 30 days; CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogue lists flaws already used in real attacks.
  • US federal civilian agencies must fix KEV entries by their due dates under Binding Operational Directive 22-01 (November 2021); many private companies use the same list as a priority signal.
  • Linux live patching: Red Hat's kpatch and SUSE's kGraft led to the mainline livepatch framework in kernel 4.0 (2015); Canonical Livepatch and Oracle Ksplice are commercial services built on similar ideas.
  • Live patches replace individual functions in memory, not the whole kernel; some fixes (for example data-structure changes) cannot be live-patched, so you still reboot into the fixed kernel at the next window.
  • Windows hotpatching applies monthly security updates without restarts on supported editions such as Windows Server 2025 (Azure Edition, or via Azure Arc) and Windows 11 Enterprise 24H2; quarterly baseline months still need a reboot.
  • Kubernetes supports the three newest minor releases; upgrade the control plane first, one minor version at a time, then the nodes — kubelets may lag the API server by up to three minor versions.
  • Immutable infrastructure patches by replacement: bake a new image (Packer, a new node-pool image), roll it out gradually and delete old instances instead of updating in place.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Patching without rebooting: a new kernel or glibc is not active until restart (or a live patch); check needs-restarting or reboot-required.
  • Using the CVSS score alone: an actively exploited 7.5 on your VPN gateway matters more than a 9.8 on an isolated lab machine.
  • Skipping Kubernetes minor versions: you must step one minor at a time, and falling a year behind turns routine upgrades into risky projects.

docs.title: Try it: Check for updates and pending reboots
docs.text:
# Debian/Ubuntu
apt list --upgradable
[ -f /var/run/reboot-required ] && echo 'reboot needed'

# RHEL / Fedora family
sudo dnf updateinfo list --security
sudo dnf needs-restarting -r

# Windows PowerShell: most recent updates
Get-HotFix | Sort-Object InstalledOn -Descending | Select-Object -First 5
