'sudo pro enable livepatch' then 'canonical-livepatch status' shows patches applied to a home-lab server. SUSE Live Patching & Oracle KspliceSUSE; Oracle · Service · Current · Advanced Commercial live-patching services for SUSE Linux Enterprise and Oracle Linux; Ksplice can also patch some user-space libraries. A bank running SUSE Linux Enterprise for SAP applies urgent kernel fixes without breaking its uptime targets. Windows hotpatchMicrosoft · Service · Current · Intermediate Installs monthly security updates in memory without restarts on supported Windows Server 2025 and Windows 11 Enterprise setups. A retailer's hotpatch-enabled Windows Server 2025 hosts restart about four times a year instead of twelve. Ring-based rolloutDeployment practice · Concept · Current · Intermediate Releasing updates to progressively larger groups — test, pilot, broad — and halting automatically if health checks fail. A faulty driver update crashed three pilot machines, so it never reached Meridian's 4,000 laptops. Kubernetes upgrade cadence & version skewKubernetes release team · Concept · Current · Intermediate About three minor releases a year, each patched for roughly 14 months; upgrade the control plane first, one minor at a time. Kestrel upgrades 1.33 to 1.34 to 1.35 across two quarters, never jumping straight from 1.33 to 1.35. Immutable infrastructureCloud operations practice · Concept · Current · Intermediate Never patch servers in place: build a new patched image and replace instances, so every machine matches a known version. Meridian's autoscaling group rolls to a freshly baked image every week; old instances are terminated, not updated.

docs.title: 9.4 Troubleshooting Methodology & Host Problems on Linux and Windows
docs.text:
Troubleshooting is detective work: gather facts, guess the most likely cause, test that guess, fix it and check the fix worked. A small set of standard commands answers most first questions — is the CPU busy, is memory or disk full, is the network working, and what do the logs say?

The troubleshooting loop. Go round the loop again if the symptom is not gone — and never skip the last step.

Think of it like…

It is like a doctor's visit: take the symptoms, check vital signs, order tests that rule causes in or out, treat, and confirm the patient recovers — rather than prescribing pills by guesswork.

Real-world example

The fictional Larkspur Books website is slow. Amara runs uptime (load 18 on 4 CPUs), then vmstat (high I/O wait), then iostat (disk 100% busy) and iotop, which points to a log-rotation job compressing 40 GB at peak time. She moves the job to 03:00, confirms page times recover, and writes a short incident note.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Define the problem precisely: what is broken, for whom, since when — and what changed?
  2. Check the basics: is it up and reachable, out of disk, out of memory, CPU saturated?
  3. Read the logs and recent changes (deploys, patches, config edits); most outages follow a change.
  4. Form one hypothesis, test it with a specific command, and change only one thing at a time.
  5. Fix, verify against the original symptom, then document the cause and how to prevent it.

Who uses it

Every help-desk technician, sysadmin, SRE and support engineer; troubleshooting skill is what hiring managers probe hardest.

Key takeaway

Learn Brendan Gregg's 60-second checklist: uptime, dmesg | tail, vmstat 1, mpstat -P ALL 1, pidstat 1, iostat -xz 1, free -m, sar -n DEV 1, sar -n TCP,ETCP 1 and top.

Going deeper

  • Load average counts runnable plus uninterruptible (D-state) tasks, averaged over 1, 5 and 15 minutes; compare it with nproc — a load of 8 is busy on 8 CPUs but overloaded, or stuck on I/O, on 2.
  • 'Disk full' has two forms: no free blocks (df -h) or no free inodes (df -i). Deleted files that a process still holds open keep using space until it closes them; find them with lsof +L1.
  • strace -f -p PID shows system calls live, revealing permission errors, missing files or slow network calls; on Windows, Sysinternals Process Monitor plays a similar role for file and registry activity.
  • Classic boot faults: a bad /etc/fstab entry drops you into emergency mode (fix the UUID or add nofail), a full /boot blocks kernel updates, and SELinux denials appear in the audit log.
  • Windows triage: Event Viewer or Get-WinEvent for logs, Reliability Monitor for a crash timeline, Resource Monitor for usage, and sfc /scannow plus DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth for corrupted system files.
  • Network checks go bottom-up: link (ip link), address (ip addr), route (ip route), name resolution (dig, resolvectl), port (ss, nc -zv, Test-NetConnection), then TLS and the application itself.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Changing several things at once: if it starts working you will not know why, and you may introduce new faults.
  • Rebooting first: it can destroy the evidence (memory state, temporary logs) you need to stop the problem recurring.
  • Ignoring 'what changed?': most incidents follow a deploy, patch, expired certificate or config edit, so check change records early.

docs.title: Try it: First five minutes of triage on a Linux machine
docs.text:
uptime            # load averages; compare with: nproc
free -h           # memory and swap
df -h; df -i      # disk space AND inodes
journalctl -p err -b --no-pager | tail -20   # errors this boot
systemctl --failed                           # failed units
sudo dmesg -T | tail                         # kernel: OOM, disk errors
sudo ss -tulpn                               # listening ports and owners
vmstat 1 5        # watch r, si/so and wa columns

docs.text: Name What it does Example uptime & load averageprocps-ng · Command · Current · Beginner Shows how long the system has run and the 1-, 5- and 15-minute averages of runnable and blocked tasks. A load of 18.2 on a 4-CPU server told Amara work was queueing, so she checked I/O wait next. vmstatprocps-ng · Command · Current · Beginner Prints rolling summaries of processes, memory, swap, I/O and CPU; the r, si/so and wa columns matter most. 'vmstat 1' showing wa at 60% points to slow storage rather than a CPU-hungry process. iostat & iotopsysstat; iotop · Command · Current · Intermediate iostat -xz shows per-disk utilisation, queueing and latency; iotop shows which processes are doing the I/O. iostat showed nvme0n1 at 100% utilisation with 45 ms waits; iotop pointed straight at gzip run by logrotate. journalctlsystemd · Command · Current · Beginner Queries the systemd journal by unit, boot, priority or time, for example journalctl -u nginx --since '1 hour ago'. 'journalctl -b -1 -p err' lists errors from the previous boot after an unexpected restart. dmesgutil-linux · Command · Current · Beginner Prints the kernel ring buffer: hardware errors, driver messages, OOM-killer events and file-system problems. 'sudo dmesg -T | grep -i "out of memory"' reveals the kernel killed a Java process at 14:02. stracestrace project · Tool · Current · Intermediate Traces the system calls a process makes, exposing failing opens, permission errors and slow calls. 'strace -f -e trace=openat ./app' shows the app looking for /etc/app/config.yml, which does not exist. ssiproute2 · Command · Current · Beginner Shows sockets — listening ports, established connections and owning processes; the modern replacement for netstat. 'ss -tlnp | grep :5432' shows PostgreSQL listening only on 127.0.0.1, explaining refused remote connections. dig & resolvectlISC BIND utilities; systemd-resolved · Command · Current · Beginner dig queries DNS servers directly; resolvectl shows which resolvers and search domains the host actually uses. 'dig +short api.example.com @1.1.1.1' works but normal lookups fail, so the local resolver configuration is wrong. Event Viewer & Get-WinEventMicrosoft Windows · Tool · Current · Beginner Windows' central System, Application and Security logs; Get-WinEvent filters them from PowerShell. 'Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName="System"; Level=2} -MaxEvents 20' lists recent system errors. Reliability Monitor & Resource MonitorMicrosoft Windows · Tool · Current · Beginner Reliability Monitor shows a day-by-day timeline of crashes, failed updates and installs; Resource Monitor shows live per-process CPU, disk, network and memory. Reliability Monitor shows application crashes began the day a new antivirus driver was installed. sfc & DISMMicrosoft Windows · Command · Current · Beginner sfc /scannow checks and repairs protected system files; DISM /RestoreHealth repairs the component store sfc relies on. A server failing updates is fixed by running DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth, then sfc /scannow. Linux performance analysis in 60 secondsBrendan Gregg (Netflix, 2015) · Resource · Current · Intermediate Ten-command checklist for the first minute on a slow Linux server, from uptime through vmstat and iostat to top. Amara keeps the list in the team runbook so every on-call engineer starts an investigation the same way. Rescue & emergency modesystemd (rescue.target, emergency.target) · Concept · Current · Intermediate Minimal boot targets for repairs: rescue mounts file systems and starts little else; emergency gives a root shell with almost nothing. A typo in /etc/fstab drops a server into emergency mode; Amara remounts root read-write, fixes the UUID and reboots.

docs.title: 9.5 Troubleshooting Containers & Kubernetes: CrashLoopBackOff, OOMKilled, DNS and Image Pulls
docs.text:
In Kubernetes most problems show up as a pod stuck in a bad status. The status name, the events and the logs usually tell you which layer is failing — the image, the application, its resources, the network or the scheduler — so you know where to look next.

Pod symptom → likely cause → first move

Likely cause First command CrashLoopBackOff app exits repeatedly logs --previous OOMKilled (137) memory limit too low describe pod, top pod ImagePullBackOff bad tag, auth, rate limit describe pod (Events) Pending no node fits the pod describe: FailedScheduling CreateContainerConfigError missing Secret/ConfigMap describe, get secret Running, not Ready readiness probe failing describe: probe events Service no reply no ready endpoints get endpointslices DNS lookups fail CoreDNS or NetworkPolicy nslookup from a pod Evicted node memory/disk pressure describe node

The status name narrows the search before you open a single log.

Think of it like…

It is like a parcel-tracking page: 'held at depot', 'address not found' or 'returned to sender' each tell you which team to call.

Real-world example

After a release at fictional Lumen Bank, the payments pod shows CrashLoopBackOff. Kai runs kubectl describe and sees 'Last State: Terminated, Reason: OOMKilled, Exit Code: 137'. kubectl top shows memory hitting the 256Mi limit during start-up. He raises the limit to 512Mi, sizes the JVM heap to match, and the pod becomes Ready.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Find unhealthy pods and their nodes with kubectl get pods -A -o wide.
  2. Run kubectl describe pod for events, last state, exit code and probe failures.
  3. Read the application's own error with kubectl logs, adding --previous for the crashed container.
  4. List recent events sorted by time for scheduling, image-pull and volume problems.
  5. Check dependencies: Service endpoints, DNS, NetworkPolicies, Secrets, ConfigMaps, PVCs and node health.
  6. Go deeper with kubectl debug (ephemeral containers), crictl on the node, or kubelet and runtime logs.

Who uses it

Kubernetes administrators, SREs, platform and DevOps engineers, and developers on call for services running in clusters; troubleshooting is the largest domain (30%) of the CKA exam.

Key takeaway

Memorise container exit codes: 137 = killed by SIGKILL (often OOMKilled), 143 = SIGTERM, 139 = segmentation fault, 127 = command not found, 1 = general application error.

Going deeper

  • CrashLoopBackOff is a waiting state, not an error itself: the kubelet restarts the failing container with exponential back-off starting at 10 seconds, doubling up to a 5-minute cap, and resets after 10 minutes of healthy running.
  • OOMKilled means a container exceeded its memory limit and the kernel's cgroup OOM killer ended it; node-wide memory shortage instead triggers kubelet eviction, reported as Evicted.
  • ImagePullBackOff causes include a misspelled image or tag, a private registry without imagePullSecrets, an architecture mismatch (arm64 versus amd64), and anonymous pull rate limits on Docker Hub.
  • Pod DNS goes through CoreDNS with 'ndots:5' in /etc/resolv.conf, so short external names try several cluster search domains first; a NetworkPolicy blocking port 53 to kube-system breaks every lookup.
  • Pending pods: read the FailedScheduling event — 'Insufficient cpu', an untolerated taint, an affinity mismatch or an unbound PersistentVolumeClaim; an autoscaler may need to add nodes.
  • On the node, crictl (cri-tools) commands such as 'crictl ps -a' and 'journalctl -u kubelet' show what the kubelet and runtime saw; 'kubectl debug node/NAME -it --image=busybox' starts a pod with the host file system mounted at /host.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Deleting a crashing pod and hoping: its controller recreates it with the same bug; read logs --previous and events first.
  • Over-aggressive liveness probes: slow-starting apps get killed in a loop; add a startupProbe or longer delays.
  • Assuming 'Running' means healthy: check the READY count, readiness probes and whether the Service actually has endpoints.

docs.title: Try it: Debug a broken pod on a lab cluster
docs.text:
kubectl get pods -o wide
kubectl describe pod web-7c9d5 | sed -n '/Last State/,/Events/p'
kubectl logs web-7c9d5 --previous
kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | tail

# Test cluster DNS from a throwaway pod
kubectl run dnstest --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never -- nslookup kubernetes.default

# Attach a debug container that shares the app's process namespace
kubectl debug -it web-7c9d5 --image=busybox:1.36 --target=web

docs.title: Key kernels, commands, tools, standards & concepts
docs.text: Name What it does Example CrashLoopBackOffKubernetes (kubelet status) · Concept · Current · Beginner Status shown while the kubelet waits, with growing delays, before restarting a container that keeps exiting. A pod restarts every 40 seconds; logs --previous shows 'permission denied' on /data, owned by root while the app runs as UID 1000. OOMKilled (exit code 137)Linux cgroup OOM killer, reported by Kubernetes · Concept · Current · Beginner Container ended because it used more memory than its limit; describe shows Reason: OOMKilled and exit code 137. Kai raised the limit from 256Mi to 512Mi and set -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75 so the JVM heap fits inside it. ImagePullBackOff / ErrImagePullKubernetes (kubelet status) · Concept · Current · Beginner The node cannot pull the image: wrong name or tag, missing registry credentials, wrong architecture or rate limiting. Events show 'manifest unknown': the pipeline pushed tag v2.4.1 but the Deployment asks for 2.4.1. Pending & FailedSchedulingkube-scheduler · Concept · Current · Beginner The pod is accepted but no node fits it, because of resource requests, taints, affinity rules or unbound volumes. '0/3 nodes are available: 3 Insufficient memory' — the pod requests 16Gi on nodes with 8Gi each. CreateContainerConfigErrorKubernetes (kubelet status) · Concept · Current · Intermediate The kubelet cannot build the container's configuration, usually because a referenced Secret, ConfigMap or key is missing. The Deployment references Secret 'db-creds' in the prod namespace, but it was only created in staging. Probe failureskubelet liveness, readiness and startup probes · Concept · Current · Intermediate Failing readiness removes a pod from Service endpoints; failing liveness restarts it; events say which probe failed. A readiness probe on /healthz returns 503 while the cache warms, so traffic waits until it passes. Evicted podskubelet node-pressure eviction · Concept · Current · Intermediate The kubelet removes pods when a node runs short of memory, disk or process IDs, starting with BestEffort pods. A runaway log file fills a node's disk; the kubelet reports DiskPressure and evicts six pods. kubectl describeKubernetes (kubectl) · Command · Current · Beginner Human-readable details of an object: status, conditions, last container state and recent events. 'kubectl describe pod api-5f6' shows 'Back-off pulling image' together with the exact registry error. kubectl logs --previousKubernetes (kubectl) · Command · Current · Beginner Prints logs from the previous, crashed instance of a container — vital because the current one may have just started. 'kubectl logs api-5f6 -c api --previous' reveals a stack trace that vanished after the restart. kubectl get eventsKubernetes (kubectl) · Command · Current · Beginner Lists recent cluster events — scheduling, image pulls, kills, volume mounts; by default events are kept for about one hour. 'kubectl get events -n prod --sort-by=.lastTimestamp' shows a FailedMount just before the outage. kubectl debug & ephemeral containersKubernetes (stable since 1.25) · Command · Current · Intermediate Adds a temporary debugging container to a running pod, or a debugging pod on a node, without rebuilding images. A distroless pod has no shell, so Kai attaches busybox with --target=app to inspect its processes and files. Cluster DNS troubleshootingCoreDNS (CNCF graduated) · Concept · Current · Intermediate Checking CoreDNS pods and logs, the kube-dns Service, the pod's resolv.conf and NetworkPolicies that must allow port 53. nslookup kubernetes.default fails from every pod: a new default-deny egress policy had blocked DNS traffic. kubectl topKubernetes (requires metrics-server) · Command · Current · Beginner Shows current CPU and memory use of pods and nodes, needing metrics-server installed in the cluster. 'kubectl top pod --sort-by=memory' shows the payments pod at 250Mi of its 256Mi limit.

docs.title: 9.6 Observability & SRE Basics: SLIs, SLOs, Error Budgets, USE and RED
docs.text:
Observability means being able to tell what a system is doing from the outside, using metrics, logs and traces. Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) turns that into promises: measure what users feel (SLIs), set targets (SLOs), and spend the allowed failure (the error budget) to balance new features against stability.

Downtime allowed per 30 days. Each extra nine cuts the allowance tenfold — and usually raises cost sharply.

Think of it like…

It is like a bus company promising '99% of buses within five minutes of the timetable': it measures every arrival, and once this month's lateness allowance is used up it pauses timetable changes and fixes reliability.

Real-world example

Fictional QuickCart sets an SLO: 99.9% of checkout requests succeed in under 300 ms over 30 days — an error budget of about 43 minutes of full outage. A bad deploy burns 30 minutes in one evening, so the team freezes risky releases, fixes its rollout pipeline and holds a blameless postmortem.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Choose SLIs that reflect user experience: availability, latency, correctness or freshness.
  2. Set SLOs a little below what users actually need, and tighter than any external SLA.
  3. Calculate the error budget (100% minus the SLO) and alert on fast budget burn, not every blip.
  4. Instrument with metrics, logs and traces (for example OpenTelemetry); build dashboards with USE for resources and RED for services.
  5. Run incidents with clear roles, then hold blameless postmortems with tracked actions.
  6. Reduce toil by automating repetitive manual work.

Who uses it

SREs, platform and DevOps engineers, on-call developers and engineering managers balancing feature delivery against reliability.

Key takeaway

Know the numbers: 99.9% allows about 43 minutes of downtime per 30 days and 99.99% about 4.3 minutes — and an SLI is a measurement, an SLO an internal target, an SLA a contract.

Going deeper

  • Google's Site Reliability Engineering (2016) and The Site Reliability Workbook (2018) are free online at sre.google and define SLIs, SLOs, error budgets, toil and blameless postmortems.
  • Multi-window burn-rate alerts page when the budget is spent fast: a burn rate of 14.4 sustained for one hour consumes 2% of a 30-day budget, so it deserves a page, whereas a brief spike does not.
  • USE (Brendan Gregg): for every resource check Utilisation, Saturation and Errors. RED (Tom Wilkie): for every service track Rate, Errors and Duration. Google's four golden signals are latency, traffic, errors and saturation.
  • Metrics (cheap numeric time series), logs (detailed events) and traces (one request's path across services) are increasingly collected with OpenTelemetry, a CNCF project offering vendor-neutral APIs, SDKs and a Collector.
  • DORA research measures delivery with deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate and time to restore service; its top performers deploy on demand and restore service in under an hour.
  • Incident response borrows the Incident Command System: an incident commander, a communications lead and an operations lead, severity levels such as SEV1-SEV4, and regular status-page updates.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Setting a 100% SLO: it is impossible and freezes all change — users cannot tell 99.99% from 100% because their own networks fail more often.
  • Alerting on causes (CPU at 80%) instead of symptoms (users seeing errors): it creates noisy pages that often do not matter.
  • Treating postmortems as blame sessions: people start hiding mistakes; blameless reviews focus on systems and fixes.

docs.title: Try it: Error-budget arithmetic in Python
docs.text:
slo = 0.999                      # 99.9 %
minutes = 30 * 24 * 60           # 30-day window
print(f"Error budget: {(1 - slo) * minutes:.1f} minutes")    # 43.2

requests = 10_000_000            # requests this month
print(f"Allowed failures: {(1 - slo) * requests:,.0f}")     # 10,000

docs.title: Key kernels, commands, tools, standards & concepts
docs.text: Name What it does Example SLI (service level indicator)Google SRE practice · Concept · Current · Beginner A measured ratio of good events to all events, such as successful requests or requests served faster than 300 ms. QuickCart's SLI: checkout requests returning success within 300 ms, divided by all checkout requests. SLO (service level objective)Google SRE practice · Concept · Current · Beginner An internal target for an SLI over a time window, for example 99.9% over 30 days. The search team picks a 99.5% latency SLO because users barely notice occasional slow results. SLA (service level agreement)Contracts between providers and customers · Concept · Current · Beginner A contractual promise with penalties such as service credits, usually looser than the provider's internal SLOs. A hosting firm's SLA promises 99.9% uptime with credits, while its internal SLO is 99.95% for a safety margin. Error budgetGoogle SRE practice · Concept · Current · Intermediate The allowed unreliability (100% minus the SLO) that teams may spend on releases and experiments; an empty budget pauses risky changes. With 10,000 failed requests allowed per month, a bad deploy using 8,000 of them pauses feature launches. Burn-rate alertingThe Site Reliability Workbook (Google) · Concept · Current · Advanced Alerts based on how fast the error budget is being consumed over short and long windows, cutting noisy pages. A page fires when the one-hour burn rate exceeds 14.4, meaning 2% of the monthly budget gone in an hour. USE methodBrendan Gregg (2012) · Concept · Current · Intermediate For every resource — CPU, memory, disks, network — check Utilisation, Saturation and Errors to find bottlenecks systematically. Disk utilisation is only 40%, but its queue is long and errors are rising: a failing SSD, not a busy one. RED methodTom Wilkie (2015) · Concept · Current · Intermediate For every request-driven service, track Rate, Errors and Duration — a simple dashboard pattern for microservices. The checkout dashboard shows a steady rate, 4% errors and p99 duration of 2 s, so the fault is inside the service. Four golden signalsGoogle SRE book · Concept · Current · Beginner Latency, traffic, errors and saturation: the first four things to monitor on any user-facing system. Monitoring only CPU missed an outage; an alert on the error-rate golden signal would have paged immediately. Metrics, logs and tracesObservability practice · Concept · Current · Beginner The three main kinds of telemetry: numeric time series, timestamped event records and end-to-end request paths. A metric shows p99 latency rose, a trace shows the slow step is a database call, and the log shows a lock timeout. OpenTelemetryCNCF · Specification · Current · Intermediate Vendor-neutral standard, SDKs and Collector for producing and exporting metrics, logs and traces to any back end. QuickCart instruments its services once with OpenTelemetry, then switches tracing vendors without changing application code. ToilGoogle SRE practice · Concept · Current · Beginner Manual, repetitive, automatable operational work that grows with the service; Google aims to keep SREs below 50% toil. Renewing certificates by hand every month was toil until cert-manager automated it. Blameless postmortemSRE and incident-management practice · Concept · Current · Beginner Written review of an incident's timeline, impact, causes and actions, focused on improving systems rather than blaming people. QuickCart's postmortem led to automatic canary checks instead of a reprimand for the engineer who deployed. DORA metricsDORA research programme (Google Cloud) · Concept · Current · Intermediate Delivery measures: deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate and time to restore service. After adding automated tests, a team's change failure rate falls from 25% to 8% while deployments double. On-call & incident commandSRE practice; tools such as PagerDuty and incident.io · Concept · Current · Intermediate Rotations of engineers who respond to alerts, using incident roles — commander, communications, operations — and severity levels. During a SEV1 the incident commander coordinates fixes while another engineer updates the status page every 30 minutes.

docs.title: 9.7 Automation & Infrastructure as Code: Ansible, Terraform/OpenTofu, cloud-init and Packer
docs.text:
Infrastructure as code (IaC) means describing servers, networks and settings in text files kept in Git, so tools build and configure them automatically and identically every time. Provisioning tools such as Terraform and OpenTofu create infrastructure; configuration tools such as Ansible set up what runs on it.

Where each automation tool fits. Image, then infrastructure, then first boot, then configuration, then applications: each tool owns one stage.

Think of it like…

It is like cooking from a written recipe instead of from memory: anyone can follow it, every cake comes out the same, and you can see exactly what changed between versions.

Real-world example

Fictional Northwind Clinics needs identical web servers in two regions. Lena builds a hardened Ubuntu image with Packer, creates VMs and load balancers with OpenTofu, sets hostnames and SSH keys at first boot with cloud-init, and installs nginx with an Ansible playbook. A reviewed pull request now replaces a 40-step wiki page.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Keep every definition in Git; changes go through pull requests and review.
  2. Bake a base image with Packer, including OS hardening and agents.
  3. Provision infrastructure declaratively with Terraform or OpenTofu: plan, review the diff, apply; keep state remote and locked.
  4. Bootstrap each machine at first boot with cloud-init, then configure software idempotently with Ansible.
  5. Run everything from CI/CD and detect and correct drift on a schedule.

Who uses it

DevOps, cloud, platform and Linux engineers; most modern infrastructure job adverts list Terraform (or OpenTofu) and Ansible.

Key takeaway

Be ready to explain idempotency: running the same playbook or plan twice should change nothing the second time.

Going deeper

  • Terraform uses HCL and provider plugins for thousands of APIs; HashiCorp moved it from MPL 2.0 to the Business Source Licence in August 2023, and IBM completed its acquisition of HashiCorp in February 2025.
  • OpenTofu is the open-source (MPL 2.0) fork of Terraform created in 2023 under the Linux Foundation; it stays largely compatible with Terraform configurations and has added features such as client-side state encryption.
  • State files map code to real resources: store them remotely with locking (for example S3, Azure Blob Storage, Google Cloud Storage or HCP Terraform) and never commit them to Git, because they can contain secrets.
  • Ansible, owned by Red Hat since 2015, is agentless: it connects over SSH or WinRM, runs YAML playbooks of modules, and shares reusable content as roles and collections through Ansible Galaxy.
  • cloud-init, led by Canonical, reads user data at first boot to create users, write files, install packages and run commands; it works on the major clouds and on Proxmox and OpenStack VMs.
  • Puppet, Chef and Salt use agents and a pull model; Puppet is owned by Perforce, Chef by Progress Software, and Salt by Broadcom through VMware's 2020 SaltStack acquisition.
  • Policy-as-code scanners such as Checkov, Conftest (OPA) and Trivy's misconfiguration checks review IaC before apply, catching public storage buckets or SSH open to the internet in the pull request.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Clicking changes in the cloud console after adopting IaC: the next apply reverts or conflicts with them, so make every change through code.
  • Committing state files or secrets to Git: use remote encrypted state and a secrets manager or Ansible Vault.
  • Writing every Ansible task as a shell command: such tasks are not idempotent; prefer modules with state: present or absent.

docs.title: Try it: A tiny idempotent Ansible playbook (dry run against localhost)
docs.text:
# site.yml - run with:
#   ansible-playbook -i localhost, -c local site.yml --check --diff
- hosts: all
  become: true
  tasks:
    - name: Ensure chrony is installed
      ansible.builtin.package:
        name: chrony
        state: present
    - name: Ensure the time service is running and enabled
      ansible.builtin.service:
        name: chronyd        # 'chrony' on Debian/Ubuntu
        state: started
        enabled: true

docs.title: 9.8 Platform Engineering & Internal Developer Platforms (Backstage)
docs.text:
Platform engineering builds an internal product — an internal developer platform (IDP) — that lets developers create, deploy and run services through self-service, without mastering every Kubernetes, cloud and security detail. A developer portal such as Backstage is usually its front door.

What an internal developer platform bundles. Developers see one self-service interface; the platform team wires the tools together behind it.

Think of it like…

It is like a professional kitchen with prepared stations, sharp knives and tested recipes: the cooks concentrate on the dishes instead of building ovens and sourcing gas every morning.

Real-world example

At fictional Orbit Travel, a new service used to take two weeks of tickets. The platform team builds a Backstage 'golden path' template: one form creates a Git repository with CI, a Helm chart, an Argo CD application, dashboards and an SLO. New services now go live in a day, and every one is secured the same way.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Treat the platform as a product: interview developers and find their slowest, most painful tasks.
  2. Build golden paths: opinionated templates for common service types with security and observability built in.
  3. Offer self-service through a portal, CLI or API, backed by IaC, GitOps and Kubernetes-style infrastructure APIs.
  4. Keep a software catalogue of services, owners, documentation and dependencies.
  5. Measure adoption and outcomes (DORA metrics, developer surveys) and keep iterating.

Who uses it

Platform engineers, DevOps and SRE teams, and engineering leaders in mid-sized and large software organisations.

Key takeaway

Remember the motto: build a paved road, not a gate — developers should choose the platform because it is the easiest way to ship.

Going deeper

  • The CNCF Platforms White Paper (2023) describes a platform as an integrated collection of capabilities offered to users according to their needs; a companion CNCF Platform Engineering Maturity Model rates investment, adoption, interfaces, operations and measurement.
  • Backstage was built inside Spotify, open-sourced in 2020 and donated to the CNCF; its core features are the Software Catalog (catalog-info.yaml files), Software Templates (the scaffolder), TechDocs and a large plugin ecosystem.
  • Crossplane, a CNCF project, turns Kubernetes into a control plane for cloud resources: platform teams publish composite resource definitions so developers can request, say, a 'Database' without touching the cloud console.
  • Team Topologies (Skelton and Pais, 2019) describes platform teams serving stream-aligned product teams and reducing their cognitive load — the organisational idea behind platform engineering.
  • Gartner predicted that by 2026 about 80% of large software engineering organisations would have platform teams; in 2025 the CNCF launched the CNPA associate exam and the performance-based CNPE.
  • Commercial alternatives and add-ons include Roadie (hosted Backstage), Port, Cortex and Humanitec; many teams combine a portal with Argo CD, Crossplane and an observability stack.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Building a platform nobody asked for: without user research and product management, developers route around it.
  • Mandating a rigid platform: forced adoption breeds shadow IT; offer a paved road with documented escape hatches.
  • Renaming the operations team 'platform' without change: platform engineering needs self-service APIs and a product mindset, not a new job title.

docs.title: Try it: Create a local Backstage portal to explore (needs Node.js and Yarn)
docs.text:
npx @backstage/create-app@latest
cd backstage        # the app name you chose
yarn start          # then open http://localhost:3000
# Older app templates use: yarn dev

docs.title: 9.9 Careers: From Help Desk to SRE, Platform, Cloud and Kernel Engineering
docs.text:
Operating-system knowledge opens many doors: running servers, automating infrastructure, keeping large services reliable, building internal platforms, or writing the kernel itself. Most people start in support or junior admin roles, then specialise as they add Linux, scripting, cloud and Kubernetes skills.

Common career paths. There is no single route: most people move sideways as often as upwards.

Think of it like…

It is like a hospital career ladder: you might start as a healthcare assistant and become a nurse, a specialist or a surgeon — each role building on the same basic knowledge of how the body works.

Real-world example

Jordan starts on a university IT help desk, fixing laptops and resetting accounts. After a year of evening study and the RHCSA, Jordan becomes a junior Linux admin, automates patching with Ansible, passes the CKA, and three years later joins a fintech company as a site reliability engineer.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Build the fundamentals: one Linux distribution, the shell, networking basics and one scripting language.
  2. Get a first job touching real systems: help desk, NOC, technical support or junior sysadmin.
  3. Add automation (Bash, Python, Ansible), Git, a public cloud and containers.
  4. Specialise: SRE, platform, cloud, security, Windows and identity, or kernel and embedded work.
  5. Show evidence: home-lab write-ups, GitHub repositories, certifications and open-source contributions.

Who uses it

Students, career-changers and IT staff planning their next move; employers range from start-ups and cloud providers to banks, hospitals and governments.

Key takeaway

Job titles such as DevOps engineer, SRE, platform engineer and cloud engineer overlap heavily — read the responsibilities, not just the title.

Going deeper

  • The US Bureau of Labor Statistics reports a median pay of roughly US$95,000-97,000 for network and computer systems administrators in its recent surveys; SRE and platform roles at large technology firms often pay well above that.
  • Entry roles (help desk, NOC, technical support) reward troubleshooting, clear communication and ticket discipline; Linux skills, scripting and a certification such as Linux+ or RHCSA move you into administration.
  • Site reliability engineering began at Google in 2003 under Ben Treynor Sloss; Google's guidance caps SRE operational work at about 50% so the rest goes on engineering that removes toil.
  • Kernel and embedded developers need strong C, computer architecture and debugging skills — and increasingly Rust, supported in the Linux kernel since 6.1 (December 2022); many begin by sending small fixes to subsystem mailing lists.
  • Infrastructure interviews mix Linux and networking fundamentals, hands-on troubleshooting, scripting exercises, system design and behavioural questions about incidents you have handled.
  • Remote work is common in infrastructure, but on-call rotations, follow-the-sun support and maintenance windows outside office hours come with many of these jobs.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Collecting certifications without hands-on practice: interviewers expose paper knowledge quickly with 'show me how you would debug this'.
  • Jumping straight to Kubernetes without fundamentals: most cluster problems are Linux, networking or DNS problems underneath.
  • Ignoring soft skills: incident communication, clear tickets and well-written postmortems matter as much as commands.

docs.title: 9.10 Certifications: Linux, Windows, Kubernetes, Docker and Cloud
docs.text:
Certifications show employers you have a baseline of skills and help your CV pass automated filters. The most respected ones in this field are hands-on, performance-based exams — you fix real systems at a command line under time pressure — such as RHCSA, LFCS, CKA, CKAD and CKS.

A certification ladder. Climb one track at a time; the hands-on exams in the upper tiers impress employers most.

Think of it like…

It is like a driving licence: the theory test (multiple choice) shows you know the rules, but the practical test (performance-based) proves you can actually drive.

Real-world example

Mei plans a year of certifications: CompTIA Linux+ in spring, RHCSA in summer after daily lab practice, and the CKA in autumn using the two included killer.sh simulator sessions. She budgets roughly US$1,300-1,500 in exam fees (prices vary by country), and her employer's training budget covers half.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Start with one Linux certification that suits your target employers: RHCSA for Red Hat shops, LFCS or Linux+ for vendor-neutral roles.
  2. Add a Kubernetes path: KCNA as an optional foundation, then CKA or CKAD, then CKS.
  3. Add one cloud associate exam (AWS, Azure or Google Cloud) that matches local job adverts.
  4. Practise in labs until tasks are fast — performance-based exams are strictly timed.
  5. Track expiry dates: most certifications must be renewed every one to three years.

Who uses it

Students, career-changers and working admins who want to pass HR filters, earn promotions or meet employer and government-contract requirements.

Key takeaway

Performance-based exams (RHCSA, RHCE, LFCS, CKA, CKAD, CKS) carry the most weight with hiring managers because they cannot be passed by memorising answers.

Going deeper

  • CompTIA Linux+ V8 (exam XK0-006) launched on 15 July 2025: up to 90 questions in 90 minutes, pass mark 720 on a 100-900 scale, adding automation, containers and Python; XK0-005 retired in January 2026.
  • RHCSA (EX200) is a hands-on exam of about three hours on live systems, based on RHEL 10 since mid-2025; RHCE (EX294) requires RHCSA and tests Ansible automation. Red Hat certifications stay current for three years.
  • CKA, CKAD and CKS are two-hour, performance-based, remotely proctored exams listed at about US$445 each, including one free retake and two killer.sh simulator sessions; since April 2024 they are valid for two years, and CKS requires an active CKA.
  • KCNA and KCSA are 90-minute multiple-choice associate exams (about US$250). Holding KCNA, KCSA, CKA, CKAD and CKS earns the CNCF 'Kubestronaut' title; 'Golden Kubestronaut' adds every other CNCF certification plus LFCS.
  • LFCS (Linux Foundation Certified System Administrator) is a two-hour performance-based exam priced like the CKA; LPI's vendor-neutral LPIC-1 needs two multiple-choice exams (101 and 102) and is valid for five years.
  • Cloud associates that employers recognise include AWS Certified Solutions Architect – Associate, Microsoft Azure Administrator Associate (AZ-104) and Google Cloud Associate Cloud Engineer; HashiCorp's Terraform Associate covers IaC basics.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Buying exam 'dumps': it breaks exam agreements, can get certifications revoked, and does not help with performance-based exams anyway.
  • Forgetting expiry dates: CKA and CKAD now last two years, so plan renewal early or the credential lapses.
  • Choosing by hype rather than local job adverts: check which credentials employers in your region actually request.

docs.title: 9.11 Learning Resources: Books, Documentation and Courses
docs.text:
The best learning combines a solid theory book, official documentation and hands-on courses. Many of the most respected resources in this field are free — including the OSTEP textbook, the Linux kernel documentation, Google's SRE books and the Kubernetes docs.

A reading path from theory to practice. Build from the bottom: theory and the command line first, then internals, cloud native and current news.

Think of it like…

It is like learning to cook: a good cookbook explains why recipes work, the oven's manual tells you exactly how your oven behaves, and cooking classes make you practise.

Real-world example

Ade, a second-year student, reads OSTEP alongside his OS module, does MIT's xv6 labs over the summer, then works through How Linux Works and the free Introduction to Kubernetes course. He keeps notes in a public Git repository that he later shows in interviews.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Theory first: OSTEP or a classic OS textbook, chapter by chapter, with the exercises.
  2. Linux practice: a command-line book plus man pages and well-maintained wikis such as the Arch Wiki.
  3. Systems depth: The Linux Programming Interface and Systems Performance when you need detail.
  4. Containers and Kubernetes: the official docs, Kubernetes the Hard Way and an introductory book.
  5. Stay current: LWN.net, release notes, conference talks (KubeCon, Linux Plumbers) and vendor blogs.

Who uses it

Students, self-learners and working engineers preparing for exams, interviews or deeper specialisation.

Key takeaway

Learn to read primary sources — man pages, docs.kernel.org and kubernetes.io — because books age but these stay current.

Going deeper

  • OSTEP (Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces) by Remzi and Andrea Arpaci-Dusseau is free online, organised around virtualization, concurrency and persistence, and comes with homework simulators used by many universities.
  • Classic textbooks: Operating System Concepts (Silberschatz, Galvin and Gagne, 10th edition, 2018) and Modern Operating Systems (Tanenbaum and Bos, 5th edition) cover theory broadly with Linux and Windows case studies.
  • MIT 6.1810 (formerly 6.S081) publishes lectures and labs built on xv6, a small Unix-like teaching kernel for RISC-V; you add system calls, page-table features and file-system code to a real kernel.
  • docs.kernel.org hosts the kernel's own admin and developer guides; LWN.net, a subscription site whose articles become free after a week, is the leading source of in-depth kernel development news.
  • Brendan Gregg's Systems Performance (2nd edition, 2020) and BPF Performance Tools (2019) are the standard references for Linux performance methodology, perf and eBPF tracing.
  • The Linux Foundation offers free introductory courses such as LFS101 (Introduction to Linux) and LFS158 (Introduction to Kubernetes); paid lab platforms such as KodeKloud and the killer.sh simulators help with exam practice.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Reading without doing: type every command and break things in a VM — passive reading fades within weeks.
  • Following outdated tutorials: check dates, because ifconfig, dockershim and removed Kubernetes APIs still fill many older guides.
  • Trying to read everything: pick one resource per layer and finish it rather than starting ten.

docs.title: 9.12 Building a Home Lab: A Step-by-Step Plan
docs.text:
A home lab is your own practice environment where you can build, break and fix real systems without risk. An old PC, a mini PC or a few Raspberry Pis — or simply your laptop with free virtualization software — is enough to run Linux servers, Windows, containers and a small Kubernetes cluster.

A 32 GB home-lab memory plan. Plan memory before you buy: RAM, not CPU, is usually the first thing a lab runs out of.

Think of it like…

It is like a flight simulator for pilots: you practise engine failures and bad weather safely before facing them for real.

Real-world example

Sam buys a refurbished mini PC with 32 GB of RAM and a 1 TB SSD. He installs Proxmox VE and creates Ubuntu, Rocky Linux and Windows Server VMs, then a three-node k3s cluster. Over six months he adds Prometheus and Grafana, deploys apps with Argo CD from GitHub, and blogs each break-fix exercise — which his first interviewer has read.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Phase 1: use your laptop (VirtualBox, UTM or Hyper-V) with two Linux distributions to practise the shell, users, SSH and packages.
  2. Phase 2: install a hypervisor such as Proxmox VE on a spare machine and build services — DNS, file sharing, a web server, backups.
  3. Phase 3: automate everything with Ansible and OpenTofu and keep it in Git.
  4. Phase 4: run containers with Podman or Docker, then a k3s or kubeadm cluster with an ingress controller.
  5. Phase 5: add monitoring (Prometheus, Grafana, Loki), GitOps (Argo CD or Flux) and security scanning.
  6. Phase 6: run deliberate break-fix drills, write them up, and rebuild everything from code to prove it works.

Who uses it

Students, career-changers and working engineers preparing for certifications, interviews or new technologies.

Key takeaway

Treat your lab like production — everything in Git, documented, backed up and reproducible; that story impresses interviewers more than the hardware does.

Going deeper

  • Typical hardware: a used small-form-factor business PC or a mini PC with 32-64 GB of RAM and an NVMe SSD; such machines idle at roughly 10-25 W, far cheaper to run than an old rack server.
  • Raspberry Pi 5 boards (launched 2023, with a 16 GB model since early 2025) run arm64 Linux and k3s well, and teach multi-architecture image problems as a bonus.
  • Proxmox VE is a free, open-source, Debian-based virtualization platform combining KVM virtual machines and LXC containers with a web interface, snapshots, backups and clustering; paid support subscriptions are optional.
  • Lightweight Kubernetes choices: k3s (a single binary, CNCF sandbox project), kind (disposable clusters in Docker), minikube, and Talos Linux for an immutable, API-managed cluster.
  • Cloud free tiers and trial credits (AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Oracle Cloud) let you practise managed services alongside the lab; set a billing alert on day one.
  • Isolate the lab: its own VLAN or subnet, no port-forwarding to the internet without a VPN, and regular backups (vzdump or Proxmox Backup Server to an external disk).

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Buying an old enterprise rack server first: it is loud, power-hungry and costly to run; a small efficient PC teaches the same skills.
  • Exposing lab services directly to the internet: reach them through a VPN such as WireGuard or Tailscale instead of open ports.
  • Building everything by hand and writing nothing down: you cannot rebuild it or show employers what you learned.

docs.title: Try it: A throwaway Kubernetes cluster inside Docker with kind
docs.text:
kind create cluster --name lab
kubectl get nodes
kubectl create deployment hello --image=nginx:1.27
kubectl expose deployment hello --port=80
kubectl port-forward svc/hello 8080:80   # browse http://localhost:8080, Ctrl+C to stop
kind delete cluster --name lab

docs.title: 9.13 Interview Questions with Model Answers
docs.text:
Interviews for infrastructure jobs test whether you understand how systems really work and how you think under pressure. Each item below is a common question, with the core of a strong answer in 'what' and a hint for making it stand out in 'example'.

Model answer: what happens on 'kubectl apply'. Components never call each other directly — they all watch the API server and reconcile.

Think of it like…

It is like a driving examiner asking you to talk through a tricky junction: they want to hear your reasoning, not only the final move.

Real-world example

In an SRE interview at fictional Aurora Payments, Nia is asked why a pod keeps restarting. She describes kubectl describe, exit code 137 and the memory limit, explains how she would confirm it with kubectl top and logs --previous, and suggests a memory alert. The interviewer moves on to system design — a sign she passed that round.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Clarify the question and any assumptions before answering.
  2. Give a short definition or plan first, then explain the mechanism.
  3. Name real commands, files and numbers to show hands-on experience.
  4. Mention trade-offs and how you would verify the fix or prevent a repeat.
  5. For behavioural questions use STAR: Situation, Task, Action, Result.

Who uses it

Candidates for help-desk, sysadmin, Linux, DevOps, SRE, platform and cloud engineering roles.

Key takeaway

Practise thinking aloud at a live terminal — many interviews now include a hands-on troubleshooting exercise on a broken VM or cluster.

Going deeper

  • Expect layers of questions: Linux fundamentals (boot, processes, permissions, file systems), networking (DNS, TCP, HTTP, TLS), scripting, containers and Kubernetes, then system design and incident stories.
  • Hands-on rounds often hand you a broken VM: a full disk, a stopped service, a wrong permission, a bad DNS entry or a firewall rule — exactly the break-fix drills from a home lab.
  • Senior questions add trade-offs: when to use a StatefulSet, how to upgrade a cluster without downtime, how to design SLOs and alerts, or how to plan a migration off a hypervisor.
  • 'I don't know, but here is how I would find out' — naming man pages, logs, strace or documentation — scores far better than a confident guess.
  • Prepare three stories in advance: a hard problem you debugged, something you automated, and a mistake you made and what you changed afterwards.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Reciting definitions without examples: interviewers follow up with 'how would you check that?', so always connect concepts to commands.
  • Jumping to a fix in troubleshooting questions: first describe how you would confirm the cause.
  • Bluffing about tools you have never used: say what you know and relate it to something similar you have used.

docs.title: Try it: See the 'what happens when you run ls' answer for yourself
docs.text:
# The shell creates a child (clone), which execs ls; the parent waits
strace -f -e trace=clone,clone3,execve,wait4 bash -c 'ls > /dev/null; true'

# The system calls ls itself makes
strace -e trace=openat,getdents64,write ls > /dev/null

docs.title: Key kernels, commands, tools, standards & concepts
docs.text: Name What it does Example What happens when you type ls and press Enter?Linux fundamentals · Concept · Current · Beginner The shell parses the line, searches PATH, forks a child that execve()s /usr/bin/ls, which reads the directory and writes output; the shell waits. Mention system calls crossing from user space into the kernel, and offer to demonstrate with strace. What are zombie and orphan processes?Linux fundamentals · Concept · Current · Beginner A zombie has exited but its parent has not yet called wait(); an orphan's parent died, so PID 1 or a subreaper adopts it. Add that zombies hold only a process-table entry; fix or restart the parent so they get reaped. The server is slow. How do you investigate?Troubleshooting · Concept · Current · Intermediate Clarify the symptom and scope, ask what changed, then check CPU, memory, disk and network (USE) with uptime, vmstat, iostat and top, then logs. Walk through a real case, such as high I/O wait traced to a backup job and fixed by rescheduling it. The disk is full, but du shows little used. Why?Linux fundamentals · Concept · Current · Intermediate Deleted files still held open by a process, inode exhaustion, or files hidden underneath a mount point. Show 'lsof +L1' and 'df -i'; restarting or signalling the process releases the space. Explain Linux permissions. What does chmod 750 mean?Linux fundamentals · Concept · Current · Beginner Read 4, write 2, execute 1 for owner, group and others: 750 gives owner rwx, group r-x and others nothing. Extend to setuid, setgid, the sticky bit, ACLs and umask to show depth. Hard link versus symbolic link?Linux fundamentals · Concept · Current · Beginner A hard link is another name for the same inode; a symlink stores a path, so it can dangle or cross file systems. Note that deleting the original breaks symlinks but not hard links, and directories cannot normally be hard-linked. What happens when a Linux machine boots?Linux fundamentals · Concept · Current · Intermediate UEFI firmware, bootloader (GRUB or systemd-boot), kernel and initramfs, root file system mounted, systemd as PID 1, targets and services, login. Mention Secure Boot and where you would look when boot fails: firmware screen, GRUB menu, journalctl -b. Container versus virtual machine?Virtualization and containers · Concept · Current · Beginner VMs virtualize hardware and run their own kernel; containers share the host kernel, isolated by namespaces and limited by cgroups. Cover trade-offs: containers start fast and are small; VMs isolate more strongly; gVisor and Kata Containers sit between. What are namespaces and cgroups?Linux containers · Concept · Current · Intermediate Namespaces control what a process can see (PIDs, network, mounts, users); cgroups control how much it can use (CPU, memory, I/O). Demonstrate: 'sudo unshare --pid --fork --mount-proc bash' then 'ps' shows only a couple of processes. A pod is in CrashLoopBackOff. What do you do?Kubernetes operations · Concept · Current · Intermediate Describe the pod for exit code and events, read logs --previous, then check configuration, Secrets, probes and resource limits. Tell a story: exit code 137 meant OOMKilled; raising the limit and sizing the heap fixed it. What happens when you run kubectl apply?Kubernetes architecture · Concept · Current · Intermediate The API server authenticates, authorises, admits and stores the object in etcd; controllers create ReplicaSets and Pods; the scheduler binds; kubelets start containers. Stress the declarative reconciliation loop: components watch the API server rather than calling each other. How does a Kubernetes Service route traffic?Kubernetes networking · Concept · Current · Intermediate A Service gets a stable virtual IP and DNS name; EndpointSlices list ready pods; kube-proxy or an eBPF data plane load-balances to them. Mention label selectors, readiness, and that a Service with no ready matching pods has no endpoints. SLI, SLO and SLA — what is the difference?Site reliability engineering · Concept · Current · Beginner The SLI is the measurement, the SLO the internal target and the SLA the contract with penalties; error budget = 100% minus SLO. Add a number: a 99.9% monthly SLO allows about 43 minutes of downtime. What is idempotency and why does it matter?Automation · Concept · Current · Beginner An operation that gives the same result however many times it runs, enabling safe re-runs, drift correction and predictable deploys. Contrast 'echo line >> file', which appends every run, with Ansible's lineinfile module, which adds it once. How would you harden a new Linux server?Security operations · Concept · Current · Intermediate Patch, remove unused services, SSH keys only, no root login, default-deny firewall, least-privilege sudo, logging and auditd, then a CIS scan. Mention automating it with Ansible or a golden image so every server is identical and auditable. Tell me about an outage you handled.Behavioural question · Concept · Current · Beginner Use STAR: situation, task, actions, result — covering detection, communication, the fix and the change that prevented a repeat. Students can use a home-lab outage, such as DNS breaking after a config change, and the test added afterwards.

docs.title: 9.14 A 24-Week Study Plan from Zero to Job-Ready
docs.text:
A clear plan beats random tutorials. This 24-week plan, at about 8-10 hours a week, takes you from first Linux commands through administration, scripting, automation, containers and Kubernetes to a certification and a portfolio you can show employers.

24 weeks to job-ready. Each block ends with something you built or passed, ready for your portfolio.

Think of it like…

It is like training for a half marathon: a schedule of steadily longer runs gets you to race day ready, while random sprints just leave you sore.

Real-world example

Leila, who works in retail, follows the plan on evenings and weekends. She passes Linux+ in week 8, has a lab running on Ansible and k3s by week 16, passes the CKA in week 22 and starts applying in week 24 with a GitHub portfolio and three blog posts. Two months later she accepts a junior cloud support role.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Weeks 1-4: Linux basics and the shell, practised daily.
  2. Weeks 5-8: administration, storage, networking and a first certification.
  3. Weeks 9-12: scripting, Git and automation.
  4. Weeks 13-16: containers, then Kubernetes basics.
  5. Weeks 17-22: Kubernetes in depth, observability, troubleshooting and the CKA.
  6. Weeks 23-24: portfolio, CV, mock interviews and applications.

Who uses it

Beginners, students and career-changers who can commit regular hours each week and want a structured route into infrastructure jobs.

Key takeaway

Consistency beats intensity: a focused hour every day plus a weekend lab session builds more skill than an occasional 12-hour binge.

Going deeper

  • At 8-10 hours a week the plan totals roughly 200-240 hours — enough to cover one Linux certification and the CKA syllabus, provided most of the time is hands-on rather than watching videos.
  • Use spaced repetition (for example Anki flashcards for commands, ports and exit codes) and a weekly 'teach-back' write-up to make knowledge stick.
  • Interleave theory and practice: read an OSTEP chapter on virtual memory, then watch free, vmstat and /proc/meminfo on your own VM in the same week.
  • Book each exam at the start of its preparation block — a fixed date sharpens focus — and remember that Linux Foundation Kubernetes exams include one free retake.
  • A strong portfolio holds Ansible and OpenTofu code for your lab, Kubernetes manifests or a Helm chart, a CI pipeline, and two or three postmortem-style write-ups.
  • After the first job, continue with RHCE or CKS, a cloud associate exam, and one area of depth such as SRE, security or kernel development.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Tutorial hell — watching courses without building: every week should end with something you built or fixed yourself.
  • Skipping networking: DNS, routing and TLS problems dominate real incidents and interview questions.
  • Studying alone without feedback: join a community, meetup or user group and get your work reviewed.

docs.title: Chapter 2: Processes, Threads, Scheduling & Concurrency
docs.text: This chapter is about how an operating system runs many things at once. It starts with processes and threads — what they are, how they are created and how runtimes multiplex them — then explains context switching and the scheduling algorithms that decide who runs next, from textbook FCFS and Round Robin to Linux EEVDF and sched_ext, Windows priorities, macOS QoS and real-time scheduling with PREEMPT_RT. The second half covers concurrency: race conditions and locks, semaphores and RCU, deadlock, inter-process communication, and the asynchronous I/O interfaces (epoll, kqueue, IOCP, io_uring) behind every high-performance server.

docs.title: 2.1 Processes, the PCB and Process States
docs.text:
A process is a program in action: the code plus its own memory, open files, current position and other state. The kernel tracks each process in a record called the process control block (PCB) and moves it between states such as ready (waiting for a CPU), running, and blocked (waiting for something like the disk or the keyboard).

The five-state process model. A process spends most of its life bouncing between ready, running and blocked.

Think of it like…

A recipe book is a program; a cook actually making the dish, with ingredients out and a finger on step 4, is a process — and the head chef's clipboard noting where every cook is up to is the PCB.

Real-world example

On the fictional Brightwater Bank's Linux server, the nightly report job is PID 48213. While it calculates totals it shows state R (running); while waiting for the database to answer it shows S (sleeping); while the disk is busy writing it briefly shows D (uninterruptible). When it finishes it is a zombie (Z) for a split second, until its parent, cron, collects the exit status 0.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Creating a process allocates a PCB, a PID, an address space and initial resources such as open file descriptors.
  2. The new process joins the ready queue; the scheduler eventually dispatches it to a CPU (running).
  3. If it requests I/O or waits for an event, it becomes blocked (waiting) and another process runs.
  4. When the event completes, the kernel moves it back to ready.
  5. If its time slice ends it is preempted back to ready; when it exits it becomes terminated — a zombie on Unix — until its parent reads the exit status.

Who uses it

System administrators reading ps and top output, developers debugging hangs, SREs investigating load averages, and every OS exam.

Key takeaway

Know the Linux ps state letters — R runnable, S interruptible sleep, D uninterruptible sleep (usually I/O), T stopped, Z zombie, I idle kernel thread — and that Linux's load average counts R plus D tasks.

Going deeper

  • Linux's PCB is struct task_struct in include/linux/sched.h: state, PID and thread-group ID, scheduling data, a pointer to the memory descriptor (mm_struct), open-files table, credentials, signal handlers and parent/child links — several kilobytes per task.
  • Windows splits the same information into EPROCESS/KPROCESS for processes and ETHREAD/KTHREAD for threads; Process Explorer and WinDbg's !process command display them.
  • Linux PIDs historically maxed out at 32,768, but systemd usually raises /proc/sys/kernel/pid_max to 4,194,304 on 64-bit systems, so PID numbers are reused only after wrapping around.
  • Load average (shown by uptime and top) is an exponentially damped average over 1, 5 and 15 minutes; on Linux it counts runnable plus uninterruptible tasks, so stuck I/O can raise load while CPUs sit idle.
  • A zombie keeps only its PID and exit status and disappears when the parent calls wait(); an orphan whose parent died is re-parented to PID 1 or a designated 'subreaper' that reaps it.
  • A process bundles three things later systems pulled apart: execution contexts (threads), an address space, and resources plus credentials — containers wrap namespaces and cgroups around this same structure.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Trying to kill a zombie: it is already dead; fix the parent so it calls wait(), or end the parent so PID 1 adopts and reaps the zombie.
  • Treating a program and a process as the same thing: one program file can run as many independent processes, each with its own state.
  • Expecting kill -9 to remove a process stuck in D state: uninterruptible sleep ignores signals until the I/O completes, which is why hung NFS mounts hurt.

docs.title: Try it: Look at processes and their states
docs.text:
# Linux/macOS: PID, parent, state and command
ps -eo pid,ppid,stat,comm | head -20
# Linux: the kernel's view of one process
head -12 /proc/self/status
# Process tree (Linux; install psmisc if missing)
pstree -p | head

# Windows PowerShell: top CPU users
Get-Process | Sort-Object CPU -Descending | Select-Object -First 5

docs.text: Name What it does Example ProcessConcept · Current · Beginner A running instance of a program with its own address space, resources, security identity and one or more threads. Opening three terminal windows starts three separate bash processes, each with its own PID and command history. Process ID (PID)Concept · Current · Beginner Number that uniquely identifies a live process; the kernel assigns PIDs and reuses them after processes are gone. `echo $$` prints your shell's PID; `kill 48213` sends a signal to process 48213. Process control block (PCB)Concept · Current · Beginner Kernel data structure holding everything about a process: state, saved registers, memory info, open files, scheduling and accounting data. When the scheduler pauses a process, its saved registers go into its PCB so it can later resume exactly where it stopped. task_structLinux kernel · Component · Current · Advanced Linux's PCB, used for both processes and threads; one per task, linked into lists and scheduler run queues. /proc/<pid>/status and /proc/<pid>/sched expose many task_struct fields as readable text. EPROCESS / ETHREADMicrosoft Windows · Component · Current · Advanced Windows kernel structures describing a process and each of its threads. In WinDbg, `!process 0 0` walks the list of EPROCESS structures to show every process on a crashed system. Process statesConcept · Current · Beginner Life-cycle stages — new, ready, running, blocked (waiting), terminated — that the scheduler moves a process through. A text editor spends most of its life blocked, waiting for your next keystroke. Ready queue / run queueConcept · Current · Intermediate The set of processes or threads that are ready to run and waiting for a CPU. Linux keeps one run queue per CPU; vmstat's 'r' column shows how many tasks are waiting for CPU time. Zombie processConcept · Current · Intermediate A finished child whose exit status has not yet been collected by its parent; shown as Z or <defunct>. A buggy Python server that never calls wait() accumulates thousands of <defunct> entries in `ps` output. Orphan process and reapingConcept · Current · Intermediate A child whose parent has exited is adopted by PID 1 (or a subreaper), which collects its exit status. Container images use tiny init programs such as tini so orphaned processes inside the container are reaped properly. Process treeConcept · Current · Beginner Hierarchy formed because every process has a parent; the root of the tree is the init process. `pstree -p` shows systemd → sshd → bash → python, revealing who started a suspicious process. Process groups and sessionsPOSIX · Concept · Current · Intermediate Unix groupings of processes into jobs (process groups) and logins (sessions), used for job control and terminal signals. Ctrl+C sends SIGINT to the whole foreground process group, so every command in `cat log | grep x` stops together. Load averageConcept · Current · Beginner Average number of runnable (and, on Linux, uninterruptible) tasks over the last 1, 5 and 15 minutes. A load of 12.0 on a 4-CPU server means work is queuing for CPU or disk; 3.5 means busy but keeping up. Process ExplorerMicrosoft Sysinternals · Tool · Current · Intermediate Advanced Windows task manager showing the process tree, threads, handles, loaded DLLs and security details. A help-desk engineer uses Process Explorer's handle search (Ctrl+F) to find which process locks a file that won't delete.

docs.title: 2.2 Creating Processes: fork, exec, wait — and CreateProcess
docs.text:
On Unix-like systems a new process is born in two steps: fork() makes a near-identical copy of the current process, and exec() replaces the copy's program with a new one. The parent then calls wait() to collect the child's exit status. Windows does it in one step with CreateProcess, which builds a new process directly from a program file.

A shell running one command. The child keeps its PID across exec; the parent's wait collects the status and frees the zombie.

Think of it like…

fork is photocopying your whole desk, exec is clearing the copy and laying out a different project on it, and wait is checking back later to sign off the finished work; CreateProcess is ordering a brand-new desk already set up for the project.

Real-world example

When Tom types `python3 report.py` at the fictional Quayside Analytics, bash calls fork(); the child (PID 9102) sets up any redirections and calls execve("/usr/bin/python3", ...). bash then waits. When the script finishes with exit(0), the kernel wakes bash, which reads status 0 and prints the next prompt. On his Windows laptop, launching the same script from PowerShell uses a single CreateProcessW call.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The parent calls fork() (implemented on Linux with clone()); the kernel duplicates the PCB and marks memory pages copy-on-write instead of copying them.
  2. fork returns twice: 0 in the child and the child's PID in the parent, so each knows its role.
  3. The child adjusts its environment (redirects file descriptors, changes directory) and calls execve() to load a new program image.
  4. The parent calls wait() or waitpid() to block until the child exits and to collect its exit status, which also removes the zombie.
  5. On Windows, CreateProcess (via the native NtCreateUserProcess) creates the process object, maps the executable, creates the first thread and returns handles — nothing is copied from the parent.

Who uses it

Systems programmers, shell and container-runtime authors, security analysts reading process trees in EDR tools, and anyone writing daemons or job runners.

Key takeaway

Classic puzzle: a program that calls fork() three times in a row ends up with 2³ = 8 processes (7 new ones); remember that fork returns 0 in the child.

Going deeper

  • Linux implements fork, vfork and thread creation with one system call, clone(), whose flags (CLONE_VM, CLONE_FILES, CLONE_NEWPID and others) choose what is shared; clone3() (Linux 5.3) takes an extensible structure.
  • Copy-on-write makes fork cheap: page tables are copied but physical pages stay shared read-only until someone writes. Forking a process with a 50 GB heap still copies large page tables, which is why Redis snapshots can cause latency spikes.
  • vfork() and posix_spawn() avoid copying page tables entirely; glibc's posix_spawn uses clone with CLONE_VM and CLONE_VFORK, and a 2019 Microsoft Research paper, 'A fork() in the road', argued fork should be retired.
  • Linux pidfds (pidfd_open and friends, from Linux 5.3) give a stable file-descriptor handle to a process, avoiding races where a PID is recycled before you signal or wait on it — much like Windows process handles.
  • Win32 has no fork: NtCreateUserProcess builds the EPROCESS, maps the image, creates the PEB and first thread, and notifies csrss.exe; Cygwin and WSL 1 had to emulate fork, Cygwin's version being notoriously slow.
  • After exec, open file descriptors are inherited unless marked close-on-exec (O_CLOEXEC); leaking descriptors into children is a classic security and resource bug.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Forgetting to wait() for children: every finished child stays a zombie, eventually exhausting the process limit.
  • Doing complex work after fork() in a multithreaded program: only the calling thread is copied, so other threads' locks may stay held forever — exec at once or use posix_spawn.
  • Assuming exec returns on success: if execve succeeds the old program is gone; code after it runs only when exec has failed.

docs.title: Try it: fork, exec and wait in a few lines of Python (Linux/macOS)
docs.text:
import os
pid = os.fork()
if pid == 0:                          # child
    os.execvp('echo', ['echo', 'hello from child', str(os.getpid())])
else:                                 # parent
    _, status = os.waitpid(pid, 0)
    print('child', pid, 'exited with', os.waitstatus_to_exitcode(status))

A forked child whose exec fails should call _exit(127) so it doesn't flush the parent's duplicated output buffers a second time. clone() / clone3()Linux · System call · Current · Advanced Linux's general process and thread creation call; flags choose shared memory, files and signal handlers, or new namespaces. Container runtimes such as runc start container processes using clone flags like CLONE_NEWPID, CLONE_NEWNS and CLONE_NEWNET. vfork()BSD (obsolescent in POSIX) · System call · Legacy · Advanced Creates a child that borrows the parent's memory until it calls exec or _exit, avoiding page-table copies. Older shells used vfork to launch commands quickly on machines with very little memory. posix_spawn()POSIX · API · Current · Intermediate Creates a new process running a given program in one call, with options for file actions and attributes. Python's subprocess module uses posix_spawn in some cases, making process launches faster on Linux and macOS. Copy-on-write forkConcept · Current · Intermediate After fork, parent and child share memory pages read-only; a page is copied only when one of them writes to it. Redis forks to write a snapshot; only pages changed during the save are duplicated, so memory use rises modestly. pidfdLinux 5.3+ · Concept · Current · Advanced A file descriptor that refers to a process, allowing race-free signalling, waiting and polling. systemd uses pidfds so it never accidentally signals an unrelated process that inherited a recycled PID. CreateProcessMicrosoft Win32 · API · Current · Intermediate Windows API that creates a new process and its primary thread from an executable in a single call. Double-clicking notepad.exe makes Explorer call CreateProcessW, which returns process and thread handles plus their IDs.
